Chapter 1

Attack Vectors and the Challenge of Preventing Data Theft

David A.E. Haddon

The Processor Centre
david.haddon@ieee.org

ABSTRACT

As a matter of normal business operations, confidential documents, payment instructions and credit card data need to be exchanged between systems easily and securely. To improve efficiency and reduce costs, governments and local authorities provide portals through which data is regularly transmitted in the form of tax returns, social security returns, company registration returns and so on. Email has become the main form of communication in business and as such is the life blood of many organisations. At the same time, it is important that emails are not accidentally or otherwise sent to the wrong recipient, as the content of a misaddressed email could compromise an individual and even expose a company to claims against it. Making sure that data is easily communicated to the correct parties and minimising the likelihood of data being exfiltrated or sent to the wrong location is a challenge every business faces. The challenges of maintaining the availability, confidentiality and integrity of both data and services has never been greater. The evolution of State Sponsored Cyber Attack Units and Cyber Mercenaries (Maurer, 2018) have increased the sophistication of attacks way beyond what some lonely teenager hacking systems from a bedroom could have accomplished. Locking down access rights, patching systems, restricting the ports that are enabled on firewalls and keeping antivirus systems up to date are normal practices on corporate networks. This is a study of the attack vectors and the methods used to mitigate attacks. It is unusual in that it assumes reasonable security precautions have been adopted and its scope is limited to such systems.

Keywords: Next-generation firewall, state-sponsored, data exfiltration, cross-site scripting, emerging threats, threat landscape, advanced persistent threat, tunnelling, covert channel

1.1.Cyber Attack Vectors

Cyber attacks are various. Some are targeted against servers and others are targeted at users and workstations.

According to the Symantec 2018 annual security review the main cyber attack vectors are the following:

•SQL Injection (against web servers).

•Cross Site Scripting (links with hooks to other websites).

•Spear Phishing Emails (links to phony websites made to look like other legitimate sites).

•Business Email Compromise (predominately hacked webmail services).

•Email attachments with embedded code.

Other growing and emerging threats are:

•PowerShell exploits (scripts that exploit PowerShell’s vast command library).

•Command and Control exploits (these enable remote shell access to a victim’s system).

However, before examining the various methods of performing cyber attacks, we first look at some of the largest leaks to get an insight into the attack vectors used in these attacks. From there an examination will be made of other emerging attack methods, and the way an attacker could subsequently exfiltrate data. Only the methods that could be used on a secure system will be discussed as it is assumed other methods would not be possible on systems where users are logged in with restricted access rights. Then, from a review of exfiltration methods, an analysis is made of the methods and products that can be used to protect a system. Further ideas to prevent data exfiltration are also proposed.

Due to the threats to corporate networks, the potentially large fines resulting from breaches under the 2018 General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) law and the reputational damage associated with personal data theft, a company director’s worst nightmare is to learn that their company’s computer systems have been hacked and that client information might have been stolen. By studying this chapter, a company executive will understand some of the issues in protecting data, the vulnerabilities in the systems in which the data is held, and some of the emerging technologies, methods and products for preventing data theft.

Several firewall manufacturers now offer intrusion protection add-ons that use Deep Packet Inspection for detecting and preventing data exfiltration from on-premises networks. Yet, how effective they are at preventing data theft will depend on how well their detection methods are aligned with the exfiltration methods that an attacker or rogue user might use.

If an attack is targeted then an attacker will generally know what they are looking for, otherwise the most likely focus of an attack will be to search for files with credit card details, usernames, passwords, product keys, cryptocurrency wallets (aka crypto-jacking) and other confidential information. The number of files that an attacker would find of interest will generally be small as an attacker would generally have no reason to download all of a company’s data unless it is all of interest. An attacker could examine emails for signs of a future large transaction that could be intercepted with a notification telling the company to transfer the money to the attacker’s bank account, or he could use stolen user credentials to access other websites and obtain further confidential information. If the amount of data stolen is small, then it will be more difficult to detect the attack.

If a rogue user sends out emails to a personal email account with the company’s data attached, how can this be detected when emailing out attachments is an everyday occurrence? Could a rogue user exfiltrate data to a web storage system such as Dropbox, or could a user accidentally launch a “command and control” data exfiltration attack by simply visiting a rogue website through opening an email attachment? These are real concerns not only for company directors but also security professionals.

1.1.1.A brief look at the attack vectors in high profile leaks

When leaks are reported, the method by which data is stolen is often glossed over. As far as the news reporter is concerned, the headline generally focusses on how many thousands or millions of personal records or user credentials have been stolen, how many credit card numbers have been taken, the subsequent risks to individuals and the damage to the company. Once confidential data is in the public domain, how it happened is often a secondary issue.

The following is a list of methods used to leak data from historical records accessed on or before March 7, 2019.

1.Adultfriendfinder — 412 million accounts were hacked in 2016 due to a Structured Query Language (SQL) injection vulnerability. Of the accounts hacked 103 million were apparently stored in a database in plaintext (Storm, 2016).

2.Anthem — The USA’s largest healthcare insurers were hacked in 2015. 80 million records were accessed using malware that gave the attackers access to a user’s workstation (Abelson and Goldstein, 2015).

3.Appleby (Paradise Papers) — 13.4 million documents were leaked. Appleby claimed that the German newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung had obtained these because of a data theft. Appleby are a law firm, and sued newspapers such as the BBC News and the Guardian — which reported the story — for inaccuracies, arguing that the data was stolen, not hacked. Though they won this action and managed to prevent further publication, it was a hollow victory, as Appleby are still losing clients (Appleby, 2018).

4.British Airways (BA) — 380,000 credit card records were stolen for bookings made between 22 August and 5 September 2018 (FT, 2018). This was the first large theft of personal data in the UK national news since GDPR came into force. The transactions were believed to have been intercepted whilst being processed using an external partner's scripts. As the data controller, British Airways were responsible for reporting the breach even though they do not hold the CCV data. It is interesting to note that Air Canada’s data breach over the same period attracted far less publicity (Whittaker, 2018).

5.Bupa — 108,000 records were stolen in 2017 by a rogue employee who copied data and tried to sell it (Bupa, 2017). From the Bupa jobs advertised in 2015 we see that Bupa recognised the importance of compliance with security standards ISO27001:2013 and PCI DSS (Bupa, 2015).

6.Citibank — A hacker stole 200,000 customer details in 2011 (Packard, 2013). This was the second breach after the bank’s internet platform had been hacked (Kitten, 2011). The data was stolen after the hacker realized that once logged in a user could just alter the URL to access another person’s bank account, and automated the process (Wilson, 2011).

7.Deloitte was hacked through an account that did not have two-factor authentication (Daileda, 2017). This is despite Deloitte implementing ISO27001:2013 and being a company that promotes and assists companies with implementing the ISO27001 standard.

8.Dixons Carphone — 5.9 million payment cards and 1.2 million personal data records were stolen in 2017. The cards apparently have not been used maliciously as most of them were protected by their chips and PINs. The names, addresses and email addresses of more than one million people were also taken in the breach (Cellan-Jones, 2018).

9.eBay was hacked in 2014 due to the hacker obtaining access credentials from some eBay staff (Finkle, 2014). eBay itself does not process credit card transactions as these are done through a payment gateway provided by PayPal; however, eBay and Paypal would have been audited to the highest Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS) standards due to the volume of transactions processed. The standard PCI DSS questionnaire D (PCI DSS, 2018) is very stringent and can be very challenging to deploy.

10.Equifax had their website hacked due to a security flaw in Apache Struts, an open source Apache Java add-on (Sweet and Liedtke, 2017). The vulnerability is explained by Sophos on the Naked Security website (https://nakedsecurity.sophos.com/) (Ducklin, 2017).

11.Facebook — At least 87 million records were breached. An app was developed that scraped details about people’s personalities, social networks and engagement on the platform. The breach was disclosed on 17 March 2018 and Facebook were fined £500,000 (Hern and Pegg, 2018). Facebook lost over one million users as a result and its share price fell 20% over two weeks during the Cambridge Analytica scandal before recovering six weeks later, based on strong financial results.

12.Facebook 2 — A further leak in September 2018 was due to problems with Facebook’s code. A quiz app apparently allowed attackers to take control of accounts. Astonishingly, about 50 million accounts were affected (Matsacis and Lapowsky, 2018).

13.Google was hacked from China in 2009 and 2011 (Packard, 2013). This was due to a spear phishing attack that gave the attackers access to a Google employee’s system. The attack lasted for about one year (Nakashima, 2013).

14.Heartland Payment Systems — 134 million accounts of the 6th largest payment provider in the USA were hacked in 2008 using SQL injection (McGlasson, 2009; Vaas, 2018).

15.JPMorgan Chase was hacked by criminals who were not expert hackers. The attackers bought the tools to hack JPMorgan Chase (Economist, 2015). Personal data from 83 million accounts were accessed.

16.Mossack Fonseca (Panama Papers) — This leak was the result of the Outlook Web Access component of Exchange 2010 not being patched for three years (Wired, 2016).

17.MyHeritage — The hack was disclosed on 4 June 2018. A security researcher reached out to the Chief Information Security Officer of online genealogy platform MyHeritage and revealed they had found a file labeled “myheritage” on a private server outside the company. Upon inspection of the file, officials at MyHeritage determined that the asset contained the email addresses of all users who had signed up with MyHeritage prior to 26 October 2017.

18.RSA — 44 million account credentials were leaked in 2011. Two separate hacking groups launched a phishing attack against RSA employees. The leak cost the company $66 million (Armerding, 2018).

19.Sony warned that users of its PlayStation network might have had their personal information, including credit card details, stolen (Cellan-Jones, 2011). Sony was hacked due to weak passwords. The 2015 hack was extremely sophisticated and used Zero-day malware and sophisticated exfiltration methods. 77 million accounts were compromised and Sony paid $8 m to the affected employees (BBC, 2015).

20.TalkTalk was hacked by a teenager on 21 October 2015 (TalkTalk, 2016). 156,959 account details were taken including 21,000 bank details and email addresses. The leak cost TalkTalk £42 m and they were fined £400,000. The cause was SQL injection (ICO, 2016).

21.Target Stores — 110 million accounts were hacked in 2013 including 40 million credit card details. Federal law enforcement later discovered 11 GB of data from Target that the hackers had transferred to a temporary server (Smith, 2014).

22.Tesco — Cyber attackers exploited deficiencies in Tesco Bank’s design of its debit card, its financial crime controls and its Financial Crime Operations Team to carry out the attack. Those deficiencies left Tesco Bank’s personal current account holders vulnerable to the cyber attackers for over 48 hours and netted the cyber attackers £2.26 m. Tesco was fined £16.4 m on 1 October 2018 (FCA, 2018).

23.Ticketmaster — 40,000 people were affected over a period from February to June 2018. Ticketmaster revealed that the login information, payment data, addresses, names and telephone numbers of users were at risk. It would turn out that Ibenta Technologies, who operate a chatbot on Ticketmaster’s site, had modified a line of JavaScript code to customise its basic product to its client’s needs. Ticketmaster then used this code (without Ibenta’s knowledge) on its payments page. Hackers discovered this script, and then modified it to extract payment information, harvesting user information from February 2018 onwards (Wired, 2018).

24.Uber was hacked in 2016. Uber’s chief security officer Joe Sullivan was fired for concealing the October 2016 breach. Uber paid hackers $100,000 to delete data and keep the breach quiet (Wong, 2017). Personal information from 56 million accounts was accessed. Hackers managed to access Uber’s accounts on Amazon Web Services by hacking access credentials. The data was unencrypted.

25.US Office of Personnel Management — 22 million records were stolen in 2012. The hack was due to a compromised third party (OPM, undated).

26.Yahoo — 1 billion account details were stolen (Williams 2017). Yahoo notified users in December 2016 of the breach that occurred in 2014. Farivar (2018) highlights the seriousness of hacking for hire, and how an administrative tool was used to reset passwords for targeted accounts.

The accounts affected by the large data leaks have been collated into a database where one can check using an email address what leaks the email address may have been involved in. The site is run by Troy Hunt and is found at https://haveibeenpwned.com/.

1.1.2.Overview of the high-profile leaks

Looking at the high-profile attacks earlier, it is evident that only a few involved a sophisticated attack method (CitiBank, eBay and Sony). The majority of the attacks were due to SQL injection, deception and carelessness from employees and vulnerabilities due to unpatched systems. Deloitte, eBay and TalkTalk were all supposedly audited to ISO27001:2013; eBay and TalkTalk would have been PCI DSS compliant too. With so many of the systems examined not being patched correctly, the companies were not complying with the standards in practice despite having been audited.

Many of the attacks listed involved insiders. Of those that were outright hacks, the main method of attack was SQL injection. Organisations that have public web servers that interact with SQL servers are therefore particularly vulnerable.

Not all the exfiltration methods used in the listed attacks have been determined. Had there been a secured and properly patched system, only a few would have been successful.

1.1.3.High profile leaks and insider threat

The Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report shows that 75% of data exfiltration attacks were from external hackers and 25% from internal actors (Verizon, 2017), which is slightly at odds with the attacks listed, in which internal involvement is seen to have been more prevalent. The Anthem, Appleby, Bupa, eBay, Google, MyHeritage, RSA and Uber attacks all appear to involve insiders, either due to lack of diligence or dishonesty. Techniques that reduce the threat from insiders are therefore important to discuss. Insiders have access to systems and a user with a moderate level of technical expertise will have knowledge of internal systems and their architecture. There are a lot of psychological reasons why an employee may steal data and much has been written on this subject, notably “The CERT Guide to Insider Threats” (Cappelli and Moore, 2012).

“Insider IT Sabotage is typically committed by technical users with privileged access, such as system administrators, database administrators, and programmers. The motivation in those crimes is usually revenge for a negative workplace event, and the crimes are often set up while still employed but executed following termination.

Insider theft of intellectual property (IP) is usually committed by scientists, engineers, programmers, and salespeople. The insiders usually steal the information they worked on and take it with them as they leave the organization to start their own business, take with them to a new job, or give foreign government or organization.

Insider fraud is usually committed by lower-level employees such as help desk, customer service, and data entry clerks. The crimes are motivated by financial need or greed, and they typically continue for a long time. Many of these insiders are recruited by outsiders to steal information. Collusion with other insiders is very common in crimes involving modification of information for payment from the outside.”

It is clear from this quote from Cappelli and Moore (2012) that Risk Managers and HR departments need to work closely with IT departments to ensure an effective Information Governance security framework. Staff are moved from department to department gaining an ever-increasing knowledge of a company’s systems. Rotation of job duties and responsibilities is seen as a form of security control in many large organisations in that it exposes bad practices, but also familiarises the rogue employee with greater knowledge of a company’s systems and its vulnerabilities. Although job rotation and compulsory two-week holidays are standard methods that organisations use to expose fraud, build skills and provide variety, it is questionable whether these practices improve security. Office practices are clearly very different to military security practices. In the military, information is conveyed on a need-to-know basis.

1.1.4.What exfiltration methods are possible on a corporate network?

Although in practice malware and botnets might be used to exfiltrate data, one would expect these to be picked up by an antivirus scanner. Unwanted applications that come with new machines are removed as a matter of course and Potentially Unwanted Applications (PUAs) and the payloads that are downloaded due to Zero-day exploits are prevented from being installed by restricted access rights. Even so it must be assumed that there is still the possibility that some malware might get installed and not detected. Once installed, malware could provide the means to enable a command and control exploit like the Kali BEEF exploit and subsequently exfiltrate data.

Word macros that can launch fileless malware are a more sophisticated threat as an exploit is run in memory without the need to save a payload. Payloads may also be delivered using steganography to hide code in images which are generally ignored by Antivirus programs. Visiting a website’s images causes images with steganographic content to be automatically downloaded into a user’s internet cache, providing another means from which code could be extracted. This will be discussed later.

If a firewall is configured correctly, there are no inbound rules generally required other than for incoming email to an email gateway server configured for that purpose, and the only outbound rules allowed should be:

•DNS outbound using UDP DNS port 53 only. (Generally, from a DNS Caching server only).

•HTTPS outbound through a proxy server.

•Email outbound from a Microsoft Exchange Server, or an email gateway.

•NTP outbound for time synchronisation.

•ICMP outbound for diagnosing connectivity issues.

This chapter is therefore limited to these protocols and their related TCP/UDP ports.

1.2.Scope of Discussion on Data Exfiltration Methods

According to Rashid et al. (2017) an advanced persistent threat (APT) attack follows three distinct phases.

Stage 1: Reconnaissance, attack staging and initial host infection.

Stage 2: Network intrusion, remote control, data discovery, persistence.

Stage 3: Staging server selection, data preparation and data exfiltration.

This chapter focuses on the last stage where access is obtained to a user’s workstation or a server. Therefore,

•Data exfiltration by air-gapped methods is excluded from this discussion.

•Data exfiltration via USB devices is also excluded. Obviously stealing data using USB devices, either as backup media or otherwise is perhaps the easiest way to get substantial amounts of data from an organisation but this involves deception and unauthorised physical access which are outside the scope of this chapter. Also, it is assumed that the use of USB storage devices has been restricted either by a system Group Policy (GPO) or centrally managed antivirus endpoint management system like Sophos EMS. Where USB devices need to be used it would be assumed that they are encrypted and that their loss would not pose a threat.

•It is assumed that user access rights are set correctly, and that users do not have local administrative rights. The focus will be on methods that are theoretically possible using tools which are native to the operating system or that could be possible without installing programs — effectively living off the land (Symantec, 2017).

•Stolen Laptop. This is outside the scope of this discussion, though the following quote must not be forgotten: “The data leaks posed by accidents exceed the risks posed by vulnerable software” (Kaspersky, 2014).

•Wireless vulnerabilities like man-in-the-middle attacks are excluded as wireless connections to a corporate network are assumed to be unacceptable.

1.2.1.Web server attack — SQL injection

Structured Query Language injection occurs when code is input in forms. If the data entered is not validated, then any code placed in a search box is sent to the SQL engine with two possible undesirable outcomes. The first is that a buffer overflow is caused resulting in shell access using the SQL connect permissions and the second is that answers to unintended queries can be retrieved. To extract data, many queries might be required to establish a database’s structure. This sounds complex but has happened on many occasions, as is clear from the reported hacks.

The reality is and has always been that anything internet facing with an external IP address will be under attack, so web server operating systems need to be hardened and web interfaces need to be robust. Forensic investigations of web attacks on web servers such as Apache can be difficult because even if full forensic logging is turned on, if the attacker is using the TOR browser, then it will be the TOR endpoint IP address that is logged, not the attacker’s IP address.

Web servers must therefore be patched and scanned for vulnerabilities regularly, and when accessing confidential information, two-factor authentication should be used where possible.

1.2.2.Cross Site Scripting

Cross Site Scripting (XSS) involves appending a JavaScript string to the end of a URL. This is then sent in an email to a user who is meant to think that clicking on that URL will only lead him to a familiar site. This perception is reinforced by the fact that the displayed URL does not show the appended string. When a user clicks on the link they are taken to the site as expected but a JavaScript script also runs. This can be set to pop-up a window asking for credentials, a hook that launches a command and control attack.

According to the European Union Agency for Network and Information Security (ENISA), XSS attacks grew 39% in Q1 of 2017, and XSS vulnerabilities are thought to have grown by 166% in 2017 (ENISA, 2017, p. 36). There are various types of XSS attacks, the most common being a reflected attack whereby no change is made to the web server. Cross Site Scripting attacks are also a common way of stealing cookies for session hijacking and getting user credentials.

Preventing web attacks requires a combination of technology and awareness. XSS attacks commonly happen when users follow links in emails and on the internet to familiar websites. One effective way to prevent XSS attacks is to examine links before clicking on them. Many Antivirus solutions examine weblinks for suspicious content at the end of a web address, as do all the main browsers now, including Internet Explorer 11, Microsoft Edge, Google Chrome and Mozilla Firefox. Trustwave’s Blended Threats is an example of an option deployed on the Trustwave Secure Email Gateway that rewrites links in emails so that they can be verified by Trustwave. The primary precaution to avoid the consequences of rogue content is not to have systems that are vulnerable, which is largely achieved by keeping systems patched with the latest security updates.

Cutting edge firewalls that have XSS detection built into IDS/IPS features should be deployed as these can prevent XSS attacks and filter out Denial-of-Service (DoS) attacks. GeoIP filters, which can be used to block traffic from specific geographic locations, are now also a common feature of firewalls. They are seldom used, and their use should be considered.

1.2.3.PowerShell exploits

PowerShell exploits are fileless malware using PowerShell, PSExec or WMI that run simple scripts and shellcode directly in memory. They are increasingly being used in attacks by both targeted threat actors and cyber criminals as they avoid detection and make forensic investigations harder (Symantec, 2017). Symantec refer to these attacks as “living off the land” and “fileless attack methods”.

1.2.4.Command and Control

In a Command and Control attack, a staging server under the control of the attacker is used to mount the attack. This means that any tracing done on the target network will lead to the compromised system that is the staging server. The staging server might be controlled over the TOR network, thus protecting the anonymity of the attacker. An alternative approach that allows an attacker to protect their identity is ngrok (ngrok, 2018), a free utility available from GitHub which allows the attack to be proxied via ngrok’s server using a temporary URL (Hackersgrid, 2018). ngrok was developed as an educational tool to assist students to run web servers on the internet even though they might be behind routers and firewalls because students might not be able to configure port forwarding on the routers they use and might not want to pay for dynamic Domain Name System (DNS) services. The use of ngrok as a hacking tool is therefore not its intended use. ngrok can be purchased, which gives permanent URLs, or used for free, which has the limitation that the URL changes with each use. However, when attackers use the free version of ngrok, there is no payment trail to disclose the attacker.

The ChessMaster cyber espionage campaign (Hsieh and Kohei, 2017) is partly based on a technique that can be demonstrated with the use of Koadic (Takhion, 2018). Koadic (available from zerosum0x0’s github page) is a Command and Control tool built for educational purposes. It is like the Metasploit and Empire frameworks except that it exploits a Microsoft Windows JavaScript engine, mstha.exe, rather than using a payload. A user just needs to be persuaded to click on a web page link to launch the attack. These attacks work by creating a reverse proxy from the victim back to the attacker and could in practice use common ports like port 80 (HTTP) or 53 (DNS) which might be open to provide internet access.

1.2.5.Phishing emails

Phishing emails are often regarded as spam, but the difference is that they are generally targeted and have malicious links to code on external websites. By clicking on one a user might be doing no more than effectively confirming their email address.

By looking at the yearly reports from Symantec and Sophos it is seen that spear-phishing attacks are currently the most common attack vector. According to Symantec:

“If you’re going to be attacked, the chances are that initial compromise, the gap in the fence the attackers sneak through, is going to be created by social engineering rather than anything technically sophisticated such as exploit of a zero-day vulnerability. Spear-phishing emails are the number one means of attack we’ve seen used, meaning a well-crafted email, sent to an unsuspecting staff member is the most likely source of compromise and can be the trigger to a potentially serious security breach.” (Symantec, 2018) 74% of attacks involved phishing emails (Symantec, 2018, p. 76).

From Trustwave’s 2017 Security Report, targeted spear phishing attacks are the most common method to gain initial access (Trustwave, 2018).

To be successful in duping a victim, the emails used for the attacks must be convincing. This level of detail in spear-phishing emails, i.e. the use of familiar names, logos and style, is now becoming commonplace. Vigilance, the verification of email instructions by other means and good email filtering is paramount.

1.2.6.Documents with embedded code and other attachments

According to the Sophos Annual Report 2018 the two most common Office exploits in 2017 were CVE-2012-0158 and CVE-2017-0199 (Sophos, 2018). CVE-2012-0158 is the most exploited document vulnerability going back to 2012. Though patched it remains a popular exploit. This is a buffer overflow vulnerability in the ListView/TreeView ActiveX controls in the MSCOMCTL.OCX library (Janus, 2013). The CVE-2017-0199 vulnerability is exploited by malicious code that can be triggered by a specially crafted DOC or RTF file for Microsoft Office versions 2003, 2007 and 2010 (Jiang, 2017). This vulnerability allows a malicious actor to download and execute a Visual Basic script containing PowerShell commands when a user opens a document containing an embedded exploit.

1.2.7.Business Email Compromise

With so many email systems having web interfaces, improper use of webmail is not surprising, and the threat of Business Email Compromise (BEC) can easily be understood. The attack vector might be a link in an email, which leads a user to a clone website asking a user to change their password. The email looks legitimate and the website the user is directed to is a perfect clone of a web email service provider’s website. Another scam is an email that requests users to log on and upgrade storage quotas (Ragan, 2017). Having gained access to a user’s email, an attacker can gather information and look for an opportunity to intercept a future large transaction. An attacker will subsequently advise new bank details in relation to a payment at precisely the time the payment is expected. The sophistication can be extreme, and the sums defrauded in this way can be large. These attacks are targeted, customised and now extremely common. They are known as Business Email Compromise (BEC) and according to the FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center, BEC has been a bigger issue than ransomware since 2016 (FBI IC3, 2018). The FBI is therefore now tracking BEC as a single crime type (FBI IC3, 2017). The attack vector could be a shared computer in a hotel lobby that is set to record passwords.

1.2.8.Emerging threats: Knock-Knock and Office 365

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is seen as the concept that will make all our lives easier, although it can also be used as an attack tool. The Knock-Knock attack against Microsoft Office 365 servers is an example of this. Having determined an organisation to target, a company’s email domain name is easily deduced from a company’s website. The company’s web site is then trawled for employee names, and the internet is searched for email addresses related to the company. Once one is found then the format of all others in the company is deduced. One of the flaws of Office365 is that the usernames are generally the email addresses. AI is used to try each email address with just two passwords, then move on to the next email address, which is how the attack gets its name. The attacking machine then goes to sleep or performs an attack on another company. It then returns and tries the email addresses again with another two passwords, then goes to sleep again and so on. Eventually an account is cracked, and a user’s email is downloaded, which gives the attacker knowledge of everything a user is doing, including access to their calendar. Office365 accounts can be protected by the implementation of the Enterprise Security and Mobility Suite as this can be set to only allow registered devices to connect.

1.3.Exfiltration Methods

There are a couple of comprehensive reviews of data exfiltration methods, one published by Ullah et al. (2017), the other by Rashid et al. (2017); however, many of the methods discussed in Ullah et al. and Rashid et al. assume that an attacker has the necessary access rights to install malware. As mentioned earlier, locking down access rights, patching systems, restricting the ports that are enabled on firewalls and keeping antivirus systems up to date are normal practices on corporate networks, so this study will be limited to only the methods possible on such a system.

Rashid et al. highlights the concern that a growing number of attacks target remote users’ home PCs as these are likely to be used to access targeted information elsewhere (Rashid et al., 2017). Remote PCs are more likely not to have access rights set correctly and can be more easily targeted with phishing and cross-site scripting attacks. If a keylogger can be installed on a home worker’s PC even though the PC may not hold any data of any value, credentials for an office system may be determined. The threat posed by remote workers, though, is not the focus of this study.

1.3.1.Exfiltration using DNS aka DNS tunnelling

DNS as a protocol is often allowed outbound even though DNS queries on a network should be resolved by internal DNS servers. Although DNS queries use UDP for speed the communication is 2-way in that a DNS response is expected. The DNS protocol only allows packets of 512 bytes, so to transfer any amount of data many queries need to be sent in the form of multiple packets to the same parent domain.

A DNS query will always find its way to the authoritative DNS server for the domain queried, see Fig. 1.1. The endpoint of the attack is therefore a server acting as an authoritative DNS server. DNS tunnelling is therefore a covert way of exfiltrating data and several toolkits are available with which to do this. To encode the communication, Base32/Base64 Binary encoding or Hex encoding is often used. The responses can either be CNAME (limited to 63 characters) or TXT (limited to 220 characters). EDNS can also be used to increase the payload.

Fig. 1.1.Outbound DNS request followed by response.

1.3.2.DNS tunnelling tools

There are several tools available to effect DNS tunnelling. They are:

•DeNiSe — This is a Python script for DNS tunnelling.

•Dns2tcp — This exfiltrates data to an authoritative DNS server using UDP port 53.

•Dnscat2 (Dnscat, 2018) — This tool is specifically designed with Command and Control attacks in mind and is available as Windows and Linux binaries.

•Iodine — Iodine is a more recent tool that has client and server components. A VPN tunnel is effectively set up between the client and server using a different IP range to the physical IP addresses (Iodine, 2014).

•Meterpreter DNS Tunnel (K-Max, 2018) — Uses Kali as the attacking tool and a small payload on the compromised workstation.

Improvements to these existing tools are discussed by Revelli and Leidecker (2009).

Using varied name server queries and varied TXT responses, various tools have been developed, which has led to the development of NSTX (Name Server Transfer Protocol), another technique for exploiting DNS.

The tools Iodine and DNScat2, which are available for DNS tunnelling, require local administrative rights to install, and DNScat2 is detected by Sophos and AVG. Because having administrative rights on a workstation is not possible on a secured network, these tools are theoretically not a threat; however, this does not mean that the vulnerability is removed, as a new method using PowerShell could still work. A recent example of a DNS exfiltration tool is DNSExfiltrator (DNSExfiltrator, 2018), which has a JavaScript client that could be triggered by a cross-site script or rogue link.

1.3.3.DNS tunnelling detection

According to Zimba and Chishimba (2017) one of the greatest challenges in detecting DNS tunnelling is that most firewalls and IDS devices do not inspect DNS traffic. Mehmet and Ince (2016) highlight that if a workstation’s configured DNS servers cannot resolve external DNS, DNScat2 can be configured to exfiltrate data using any DNS cache server that a workstation can communicate with.

DNS tunnels can be detected based on the entropy of requested hostnames (Butler and Grady, 2011). The number of DNS queries of a hostname for a given domain could also be an indicator.

Logging of DNS requests is therefore important as this provides evidence of DNS exfiltration and of the location where data is being exfiltrated to. An examination of the ownership of a domain name may provide some evidence of the attacker’s identity should they have been careless enough not to use fake details. The obvious arguments against DNS logging are the sheer size of the logs that would be produced, and that these logs would need to be archived and managed.

Although DNS tunnelling might look complicated it is much safer an option for an attacker as DNS requests are less likely to be logged compared with HTTP/HTTPS requests which would be logged by a web proxy or outgoing SMTP email, which in turn would be logged by an email gateway.

DNS tunnelling is interesting in that although DNS is a layer 7 protocol, the object of DNS tunneling is to establish TCP communication (which would be layer 3 — the network layer) over DNS.

Netflow’s FlowPro Defender is a tool that can be used to detect DNS tunnelling (Scott, 2016).

DNS logging allows one the opportunity of detecting requests to dynamic DNS hosts. Evidence of DNS tunnelling will be found in DNS Cache server logs. The requests will make use of the maximum DNS packet size which is 253 characters, with a maximum of 63 characters per label. This is defined in RFC1035 (Mockapetris, 1987) as x.y.z where y.z is a parent domain and x is (255 — length (y.z) – 63 – 63 – 63) characters (Dooley and Rooney, 2017).

DNS URLs over 52 characters are not normal, so in simple terms the first sign of something not being right is a long DNS frame (Guy, 2009). The next giveaway is the entropy of the first label. If a label is the first label of a DNS tunnel, it would be expected to be encoded with base32 giving a higher entropy (Butler and Grady, 2011).

DNSSEC may prevent DNS cache servers from DNS poisoning. However, as DNS exfiltration techniques use valid DNS packets, DNSSEC does little to prevent DNS tunneling. The reason for this is that DNSSEC is designed as a mechanism for a browser to check with a domain registrar that DNS records being returned by DNS Cache servers are consistent with the registrar’s signature for those records. In other words, a rogue domain used for DNS exfiltration could still be protected by DNSSEC.

1.3.4.Malware using DNS tunnelling

A new trend is malware using DNS to send C&C commands (Khandelwal, 2017). DNSMessenger is an example of a Remote Access Trojan (RAT) that uses DNS queries to launch malicious PowerShell commands on compromised computers. Examples have been detected in sophisticated attacks launched from a VBA macro embedded in a Word document, which is used to execute a PowerShell script (Brumaghin and Grady, 2017). DNSMessenger is fileless as it does not write files to the targeted system, but uses DNS TXT messages to fetch PowerShell commands stored remotely as DNS TXT records (Khandelwal, 2017). The method modifies the Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) database to maintain persistence after reboots.

1.4.The Threat Posed by Web Storage and Web Exfiltration

Web-based exfiltration methods can either be covert or overt. Data can be transferred in the background using the web-based protocols HTTP or HTTPS, which use an organisation’s proxy server, or by a rogue employee to a web storage account such as Dropbox, OneDrive, SpiderOak, etc. Microsoft OneDrive, Dropbox and SpiderOak are all examples of commonly used web storage accounts. Dropbox can be used with or without an agent, however, in order to use the agent, further TCP ports must be configured on a firewall, so using Dropbox in this mode would not be possible on a secure network. The OneDrive App is often installed with Microsoft Office and the App works quite happily over a web proxy. SpiderOak provides encrypted web storage and so is an example of a business system that could be exploited by an attacker who would be able to conceal the data stolen.

The threat of employees transferring data to web storage accounts is very real. OneDrive is ubiquitously installed on workstations and can easily be configured by users to steal data, then to be removed from a system. It is interesting to note that OneDrive is unusual as an application in that it does not require local administrative rights to install and often installs itself when Office is upgraded as access rights are automatically elevated by the operating system to install updates. OneDrive is also installed by default on many new machines. Microsoft OneDrive for Business is an application which is often unintentionally installed on systems when Microsoft Office is installed. Assuming OneDrive is installed on a workstation, all a user or an attacker needs to do is temporarily configure it to use a Microsoft account. Once data has been taken, OneDrive can then be reconfigured, leaving no obvious trace that it has been used to exfiltrate data.

Tracking browsing is difficult as one webpage might reference several others for content. Looking at proxy server logs can also be confusing as references to other sites can often imply that a user has knowingly navigated to these referenced sites.

Not surprisingly, removing general web browsing from networks is becoming more common. Proxy servers can be set to allow access to only the banking sites and business sites needed. This might sound extreme but is not as impractical as it sounds. If access is removed totally, any forms that need to be completed online can be done by machines in a DMZ, and the completed forms transferred up to internal systems by email or hot folders. This model is effectively that of cloud computing where internet access from the cloud is restricted but a user can access the web directly from the desktop. Done properly this is like the age-old model used by the military called Bell-LaPadula where information can be transferred up to more secure areas but not down.

1.4.1.ICMP tunnelling

Several utilities are available for establishing ICMP tunnels. The most popular tool is ptunnel (Stodal, 2005). The main reason for these utilities is to allow a notebook user to bypass a proxy server on a public WIFI system. Despite the use of these, a good firewall should detect this traffic; however, to remove the vulnerability, the organisation’s firewall rules should not allow users to send the Ping message from workstations.

ICMP tunnelling tools were developed to provide a means to bypass a proxy server by creating an ICMP tunnel to an external web proxy server. However, it is easy to see how ICMP tunnelling can be exploited in a similar way to DNS tunnelling to create a covert channel by which data could be exfiltrated.

1.4.2.NTP tunnelling

Liska (2016) highlights that NTP is an old protocol with certain vulnerabilities in its design. NTP uses UDP port 123 and is required by servers to synchronise time. Workstations generally synchronise with domain controllers as part of a global policy. NTP or UDP 123 outbound is therefore not required from a workstation, however it can be used to generate several attacks internally and as an exfiltration method from a server configured as the network’s internal time server. Hyper-V replication requires that time is synchronised on a network to within 5 minutes, else replication stops. Microsoft’s Kerberos implementation requires time not to drift too much else machines have problems accessing network resources. Therefore, disrupting time on a network has serious consequences. Because an NTP query to the internet requires a response, NTP could also be used to establish a tunnel in a way similar to DNS tunnelling. The firewall rule allowing NTP outbound should therefore be restricted to genuine NTP time servers only. CVE-2015-7871 is a vulnerability that allows a server to accept a forged NTP packet from temporary peers (Liska, 2016). Safebreach, in their 2017 Security report, highlights that NTP is a sneaky method that hackers use to exfiltrate data (Safebreach, 2018).

1.4.3.The threat posed by email

Tracking email is quite straightforward, as each email generally has one source and one recipient. So, if email is exfiltrated by email, seeing what has happened is straightforward assuming an email gateway such as the Trustwave Secure Email Gateway or Mimecast has been used. Any rogue insider with a little knowledge would be aware that using email as a method to exfiltrate data is likely to leave a trail.

1.4.4.Steganography

This is the practice of hiding a message within a picture. The most popular method is to use the least significant bit of a pixel to hide data, as changing this causes no visible change to the appearance of a picture. Steghide, Stegosuite, Jsteg, Openpuff, JPHide and JPSeek are just some of the tools available with which to do this (Hegarty, 2018). Another technique is to merely append code to the end of a file; however, this is more likely to get detected.

Several leaks have used steganographic means to exfiltrate data; however, looking at this from a practical perspective, an attacker needs to find image files on a system in which sensitive data can be hidden. If a large amount of data is to be stolen, then it goes without saying that the amount of data to be exfiltrated using steganographic means will become significant, causing a bottleneck for the attacker. The volume of network traffic generated by using this method would provide easily detectible evidence, especially for any traffic monitoring systems such as Darktrace or Bro. An attacker would also need to be transmitting different pictures for the transfer not to look odd. The automation of the process of sending out data via varying pictures so that the hidden data can easily be extracted is perhaps a bit unlikely, though this method is not to be overlooked as a way of exfiltrating small amounts of data. The main threat from steganography is as an attack vector to deliver payload hidden in a picture. eBay and Facebook now re-render images uploaded to their platforms, which corrupts any steganographic content. Software tools like Stegohunt have been developed to detect the presence of hidden data and payloads in images (Whetstone, 2018), though real-time detection using antivirus programs is not standard.

1.4.5.Dealing with a cyber attack

After an incident, the key element that one looks at is logs. Logs hold tangible evidence of events. After an incident, a timeline must be drawn up showing what happened where and when. If clocks are not synchronised, this becomes not only very difficult but extremely confusing and provides ammunition for contesting any breach report. The time synchronisation of a system to a single reference time source is a requirement of ISO27001:2013(A.12.4.4).

Response plans need to be in place to address likely risks and recovery plans need to be designed to meet organisational recovery objectives in the event of system interruption or failure. Recovery plans need to be tested according to the “Plan, Do, Check” model of continual improvement described in BS 22301 (2014).

Whilst systems can be made resilient by deploying virtual servers on clusters using storage array networks and implementing server replication, the threat from ransomware is that unauthorised changes to data are also replicated to replica servers. For this reason, offline backups are vital. The downside of offline backups is the time taken to restore them and the loss of any data that may have been added or changed since the backup was taken. It is important where recovery time objectives are low to create an environment whereby as many risks as possible to system uptime are eradicated.

Should an incident occur, affected systems must be isolated immediately. The measures deployed will depend on budget and the organisation’s risk appetite.

1.5.Remediation of Security Breaches

In theory one has a CERT (Cyber Emergency Response Team) or a BERT (Business Emergency Response Team) on standby should an incident occur. A BERT is an inhouse version of a CERT, so would be familiar with company procedures and will have no conflicts of interest in terms of the confidentiality of the data or services being restored. A CERT, however, being a community response, poses lots of issues in terms of GDPR processor agreements, confidentiality etc.

Should external assistance be part of the recovery plan then a CERT will need to comply with the company’s vetting policy and suitable NDAs will need to be signed. Though a company might not see Computer Forensics as its business, inevitably HR will have to hire for a Computer Forensics department when internal investigations are required. When this happens, it is important to follow the advice of the UK Association of Chief Police Officers and the guidance provided by ENISA (ACPO, 2012). In Computer Forensics, there are four basic rules (Schou and Hernandez, 2014).

1.Investigators must not take on work that is beyond their skill.

2.A log must be kept of how the evidence is preserved from point of collection to court. This is called a Chain of Custody.

3.Evidence must not be degraded. This is called Preservation.

4.Every step of an investigation must be recorded.

Should personal data be put at risk as a resultant incident then the organisation’s GDPR breach reporting procedures will need to be followed and the appropriate supervisory authority notified without undue delay, and not later than 72 hours after the organisation becomes aware of the breach. Article 33 of the GDPR also requires that if the breach is likely to result in a high risk of certain individuals’ rights and freedoms being adversely affected, those individuals must be informed without undue delay, and that the cause of the breach must be identified, and that measures must be put in place to contain the breach and prevent any repetition of the incident. Seeking the advice of the Information Commissioner’s Office when reporting a breach to confirm the response is correct is accepted as expected practice.

Event logs are crucial for determining the cause of a breach. ISO27001 specifies that logs should be maintained for months, as does COBIT 5. Logs can be unmanageable and even a small organisation with a few virtual servers will produce many logs. A SIEM (System Information Event Management) solution that collates logs solves this problem. Splunk goes further and is a SIEM solution that analyses logs in real time for unusual behaviour (Splunk, 2018).

1.5.1.Detecting attacks using honeypots

Honeypots are a terrific way of detecting that something is not right on a network. The idea is that should an attacker get in then the first thing they would want to do is to scan the network for vulnerabilities. This would normally be a scan of all the IP addresses in the local area network’s IP range and either all the ports or the most likely ports which the attacker can use to hop onto a server. A honeypot will sit on one IP address on the network and will be listening on all ports. Should another device try to connect to the honeypot, an alarm will be triggered and an alert will be sent. Thinkst Canary is a honeypot that can simulate a Windows server or a Web server, and is designed to entice an attacker to investigate further before triggering an alert (Thinkst Canary, 2018).

1.5.2.Detecting attacks by network monitoring

Darktrace and Snort, which monitor network traffic, are great tools with which to detect anomalies. Traffic monitoring is expensive, though, as the idea of traffic monitoring is to detect anything abnormal on a network. In practice, the setting up of new workstations where large amounts of programs and data move round the network and even Windows updates are good examples of false positives that can trigger an alert, so this method is not without its drawbacks.

1.6.Detection of Security Breaches — Overview

One of the issues in comparing security products is that there is no comprehensive dataset to be used for data exfiltration testing, and no generic framework for testing. This is an issue highlighted by Ullah et al. (2017).

Al-Bataineh and White (2017) describe how botnets can be used to exfiltrate data using encrypted channels. Interestingly they make the point that rather than providing a problem, encryption can give the attacker away, as a large transfer using encryption could be identified as an anomaly. Zeus is the most common botnet which allows an attacker to manage the botnet remotely to log key strokes and take screen shots. It can even add fields to forms to enable the collection of more information than a form would normally need, and if applied to a banking site might even ask for a social security number or a credit card PIN. Al-Bataineh and White observed that HTTP traffic exchanged by botnets has normal headers; however, the content of POST responses is often random which could assist with detection. Although encryption hides what an attacker is doing, Al-Bataineh and White propose that one should “consider encryption as an opportunity for detection rather than a limitation because if encryption is detected where it is not expected it should be considered an anomaly”.

In an encrypted message the frequency of a byte in a message should be the same for every byte. This is known as Shannon’s Entropy. To maintain throughput when inspecting traffic flows, a manufacturer may decide, having identified a file type upon examining the start of a file, that it is not necessary to examine the rest of the data stream (Shannon and Weaver, 1949).

Deep packet inspection (DPI) of HTTPS packets is another technique that is emerging on some firewalls. This works by decrypting encrypted channels at a firewall then re-encrypting them before they reach the user.

On anything but a small corporate network a proxy server would be expected. This is now a requirement in PCI DSS questionnaire C and the UK Cyber Essentials scheme. Proxy servers are designed to inspect and log data downloaded but not necessarily to detect data uploaded so it is important to ascertain how good they are at detecting and recording data being uploaded. From an attacker’s perspective exfiltrating data using web-based services might appear a risky strategy because requests are likely to be logged but even if access to websites and users and downloads may be logged it does not follow that data being uploaded is being logged.

Anomaly detection can either be host-based or network-based, the first looking for anomalies on the host, the latter looking for anomalies in network traffic. An example of suspicious network traffic would be web use where the upload traffic volume is higher than the download volume. An example of a host-based anomaly could be high levels of network traffic at an unusual time of day (e.g. at night) (Darktrace, 2018).

1.6.1.Black hat, white hat and grey hat hacking

To check whether vulnerabilities can be exploited, ethical hackers or penetration testers are often employed. They then try to find and exploit vulnerabilities on the basis of some knowledge (grey hat), no knowledge (black hat) or a lot of knowledge (white hat) of the system being tested. It is important that a reputable company is used for this, and, when systems are being tested, that system administrators are on hand should any services hang as a result. Attempting to hack a system without authorisation is a criminal offence, so penetration testing companies must be certain that they have the proper authorisation and that any undesirable consequences are understood before attempting to see if any vulnerabilities can be exploited.

1.6.2.Open-sourcing of security tools

Many security tools are available open source for Linux. Bro is another tool for network analysis and security monitoring (Bro, 2018). Snort is an open source intrusion prevention system capable of real-time traffic analysis and packet logging. Pfsense is an increasingly popular open source firewall (Pfsense, 2018).

1.7.Methods and Models for Security and Privacy

From Ullah et al. (2017) it is apparent that many of the methods proposed in academic studies for detecting and preventing data loss have not been trialed by real companies and remain academic ideas and that the practicalities of implementing some of the ideas have been overlooked.

The data classification model chosen will depend on the types of data an organisation holds. For many organisations this is just confidential, personal data, and unclassified data. In a military context, top secret data would be on a need-to-know basis, so a higher-ranking officer might not have access to some data that lower ranks working on projects might have. “Need to Know” or “Least Privilege” are security practices that are common in many organisations.

Document management systems like iManage (iManage, 2018) and Laserfiche are good ways to protect documents as, with these systems, documents are stored in a repository rather than on file shares, thus adding another layer of security. Further access permissions are then set with the document management system providing a further layer of protection.

1.7.1.Methods for security reengineering

Email is the lifeblood of many organisations, however when it comes to agreeing to contracts with other parties it is soon seen how inefficient it becomes. Multiple versions of draft documents which are stored by all parties do not just clog up email systems but file storage and message archives too. Several products that make this experience better are portal-based. Some also provide the ability to compare documents online and this means that the whole collaborative experience can be achieved online. Examples of this are Objective-Connect, iDeals data rooms and Workshare. SharePoint can also be configured to provide this functionality.

Products like iDeals, Workshare, and Objective-Connect provide secure online virtual data rooms where companies can share documents with other parties. These systems provide a more efficient way for companies to collaborate when compared to email. The use of portals has become common for large companies, councils and universities, removing the need to send large attachments by email. Some of the products available to provide this functionality are Objective Connect (Objective, 2017), which allows users to share and version documents with others in its portal, iDeals which features document sharing with very restrictive viewing, and DeltaView’s Workshare which provides document comparison within its portal.

Blackberry UEM is an alternative approach to providing mobile access to an Exchange Server. This is a full MDM solution which can provide connectivity with mobile devices and devices running Blackberry’s iOS or Android app. It uses outbound ports only, thus eliminating the threats that go with having inbound ports configured (Blackberry, 2018).

1.7.2.Privacy-enhancing technologies and trustworthy information systems

A common technique is to tag documents with keywords, then use an AV tool such as ClamAV to generate signatures. The signature can then be added to a proxy server such as Squid to block these from leaving the organization (Rashid et al., 2017).

Boldon James provides tools to add metadata tags to documents (Boldon James, 2018). These can work with Data Loss Prevention systems such as Forcepoint, Intel Security and Symantec DLP.

Tukan’s GREENmod (TukanIT, 2018) is another tool. This integrates with McAfee Threat Intelligence Exchange/Data eXchange Layer (TIE/DXL), and McAfee DLP (McAfee, 2017), also to prevent data exfiltration.

Safetica is an example of a Data Leak Prevention product which deploys agents on workstations (Safetica Endpoint Client) which communicate with a Safetica Management Server. This is an example of perhaps what will be a suite of new products to protect against data loss. Data can be tagged depending on folder location or file type and using DLP rules, which look at tags and file contents. Sensitive data can be prevented from being attached to emails or transferred to web storage, and even screenshots of sensitive data can be prevented. Safetica also provides the ability to see an overview of all web browsing, all sent email, all file activity and all printing by a user.

1.8.What Kinds of Products Are There to Prevent Data Theft?

The approaches to detecting and preventing data exfiltration fall into 5 categories:

1.Block data being exfiltrated at a firewall. Several firewall manufacturers now offer a DLP bolt-on which uses deep packet inspection to provide protection against data loss. The protection is based on rules that have been set to detect phrases and number patterns.

2.Use an agent that applies centrally managed policies and blocks leaks at the endpoint. This approach enables a great deal of flexibility in terms of integration with Active Directory, file tagging, reporting and alerting a user that they are doing something which is not permitted. Safetica is an example of a system that deploys a workstation agent.

3.Use of a proxy server that has built-in data-loss detection and prevention capabilities. The Trustwave Secure Web Gateway (SWG) is a good example of this.

4.Next generation firewalls that are both firewall and web proxies.

5.Traffic monitoring. Based on an analysis of normal network traffic, AI is used to detect abnormal network traffic. This is the principle used by Darktrace.

We will discuss these three approaches and some of the products using these approaches, and test them accordingly.

1.9.Detect and Block Using a Firewall

It is important to configure firewalls in the right arrangement from day one as the architecture of a network is hard to change later without service disruption and risk.

It is interesting to note that the separation of the internal network from the DMZ and the internet by 2 firewalls, as in Fig. 1.2, is now a requirement by some banks under PCI DSS questionnaire D. The three-legged firewall, as in Fig. 1.3, which has been a cost-saving option for smaller companies for several years, is therefore falling foul of security standards. If multiple firewalls are used, a DLP solution would normally be required on the internal firewall only.

Quality switches like the CISCO SG500 series now have access control lists either based on a MAC address or an IP address. These switches are effectively firewalls. Complex rules can now be set on many network switches and unused ports can be shut down. ‘Sticky Macs’ is a feature whereby a switch learns and remembers connected MAC addresses and should an MAC address violation occur the affected port can be automatically shut down.

Fig. 1.2. Traditional network diagram.

Fig. 1.3.The three-legged firewall.

1.9.1.Detect and block using an agent or app at the endpoint

Safetica and Infoblox are full data loss prevention solutions which defend against planned or accidental data leaks and malicious insider actions by deploying a centrally managed agent on workstations. By using an agent on each workstation documents are tagged according to sensitivity which then allows access controls determining whether the documents may be copied, printed or emailed. Safetica can also prevent screen shots or clips of sensitive documents (Safetica, 2018; Infoblox, 2018).

McAfee DLP is a utility that can scan, identify and classify data without user intervention. Policies can be defined around how it alerts users to policy violations (MacAfee, 2017). The attraction here is not having to classify data every time data is saved.

Symantec DLP is another utility that can scan and automatically detect sensitive documents and images. Network Prevent for Web can be deployed at network egress points and integrates with proxy servers using the Internet Content Application Protocol (ICAP, 2018). Symantec DLP can monitor the use of sensitive data and goes as far as digitally shredding documents (Symantec, 2018). McAfee, Sophos, Trend Micro, Kaspersky, and Symantec all follow the ICAP standard. They all provide real-time content filtering, though it is not necessarily implemented in any of their products. It must be noted that the ICAP protocol and feeds are also legitimately used for advertising as well as virus checking and language translation (ICAP 2018).

SonicWall Capture Client is a workstation agent designed to detect ransomware by Sentinel One. Should an attack happen it can roll back the attack (SonicWall, 2017).

1.9.2.Detect and block using a proxy

Trustwave Secure Web Gateway (SWG) is Trustwave’s ‘Zero-Malware’ web-proxy solution (Trustwave, n.d.). Because the secure web gateway uses its own DNS settings, a gateway firewall can be configured such that DNS outbound on UDP port 53 is only possible from the Secure Web Gateway device.

1.9.3.Detect and block using a next-generation firewall

Sophos XG UTMs and Zyxel USG UTMs are examples of all-in-one firewalls, web proxy, and network monitoring solutions. These are ideal for very small organisations.

1.9.4.Detect and alert using network traffic analysis

Darktrace and Snort are network-based anomaly detection systems which identify unusual network traffic. These were discussed in Section 1.5.2.

1.9.5.Detecting sensitive data

Many of the tools that are designed to assist with data classification are designed with large companies in mind. An example is Spirion (formerly IdentityFinder) which is a tool that can be used to search file shares for sensitive data (Spirion, 2018).

Unlike traditional security systems (e.g. IDS, IPS and firewalls), which are supposed to act when an attacker enters the enterprise, data exfiltration countermeasures are expected to work when an attacker is on the way out with sensitive data (Ullah et al., 2017). Firewalls are generally designed to keep attackers from getting in, not from getting out when they are inside. This is very similar to what Houdini did; he exploited the fact that locks at the time were designed to prevent people from entering areas, not from getting out of them.

GlobalVelocity (GlobalVelocity, n.d.) is a DLP solution for protecting data in the cloud. The challenge for companies using cloud providers is not knowing the level of protection in place and having limited control over how DLP products might be configured.

Microsoft Intune is an example of a cloud-based DLP solution whereby the configuration is done by the company whose systems are being hosted rather than by the cloud provider. The Office365 Enhanced Protection and Mobility Suite offers several security mechanisms to protect data. Rules can be set up in Office365 to detect the exfiltration of credit card data and social security and national insurance numbers. The DLP rules can be set for all country formats or specific countries, thus catering for various formats of national insurance numbers. However, setting countries unnecessarily in the rules could obviously increase the rate of false positives.

1.10.Recommendations to Protect Against Data Theft

The following recommendations should be considered to protect against data theft:

•Uninstall Microsoft OneDrive using a group policy (GPO) if it is not required in an organization.

•Use a proxy server that can block web storage websites.

•Instant messaging systems should be blocked by the organisation’s web proxy.

•Consider blocking Ping (ICMP) and NTP outbound from workstations.

•Companies should consider a default deny on a proxy server for website browsing and only websites needed for business purposes should be added as needed.

•Primary and secondary internal DNS servers should not be configured to resolve external DNS names, as good web proxy servers can be configured to use external DNS cache servers. This not only improves security, it also reduces the load on the internal DNS servers. For WSUS and AV to get updates, a dedicated DNS server should be used.

•Limiting the size of email attachments and the number of attachments that can be attached to an email are practical steps to restrict the amount of data that can be stolen by email.

Supply chain vulnerabilities must also be considered. To quote the National Cyber Security Centre’s annual report:

“2017 saw some significant examples of supply chain attacks, including the compromise of a large number of managed service providers (MSPs), enabling access to commercially sensitive data from them and their clients. At least two software companies had their products (MeDoc and CCleaner) compromised at source, resulting in their customers being infected with malware when downloading the software/updates.” (NCSC, 2018)

Minimizing the amount of sensitive information that an organisation holds clearly minimizes any impact from a data leak. This principle is at the heart of information governance and GDPR strategies with respect to personal data. The same principle must apply to all confidential and sensitive information, that regardless of the measures that are put in place to protect data, unnecessary data should not be collected as this increases the impact of any breach.

The deployment of end-to-end encryption systems such as GalaxKey or WhatsApp on a system makes it very difficult for monitoring systems to identify data in an email or text message as the monitoring system will have no way of decrypting the data it is trying to monitor. However, the use of these systems for specific occasions where a high level of confidentiality is required makes perfect sense.

To quote Rashid et al.: “Due to the diversity of attack vectors no single security control provides protection against all of these vectors. Multiple detection mechanisms must be used together in a multi-layered approach” (Rashid et al., 2017). The result is often referred to as defence in depth, but as any practitioner knows, this leads to unintended conflicts between products. Antivirus updates can be blocked by firewalls and one-time links which are often used for password resets are claimed by proxy servers, to name just a couple of the possible issues. Setting exclusions and resolving conflicts has become a regular part of an IT system manager’s day.

One interesting approach to reducing the impact of data leaks is the concept of Zero Trust, where everything is untrusted (Vijayan, 2018). The concept is that any threat is limited to the data on one desktop; however, this means that the reporting and monitoring of devices becomes difficult. Microsoft has addressed this issue for a user of Office365 with the Enterprise Security and Mobility suite, which does cater for this, as Microsoft Intune registers and validates that connecting devices are patched and safe to connect to. For companies not using Office365, Centrify provides a similar Zero Trust framework (Centrify, 2018). In an office environment where all services are cloud services, the use of Zero Core clients that have a Citrix or terminal server that is imbedded in firmware is a strategy that removes the threat from viruses at the endpoints.

Due to the plethora of approaches there is no standard implementation, meaning staff with experience in one organization cannot transfer their knowledge procedures to another company, as the systems, methods and procedures in addressing the security of sensitive data will differ. This poses real challenges for companies that rely on contract staff.

1.11.The Future — STIX, TAXII and Cyber Threat Intelligence

To aid the sharing of the security information protocols that have been developed, the computer language known as Structured Threat Information Expression (STIX, 2018) and the protocol known as Trusted Automated Exchange of Intelligence Information (TAXII, 2018) are designed to share CTI (Cyber Threat Intelligence) information. One would expect that a good firewall with DLP would interface with external live CTI databases and that it would automatically update itself using these databases.

Data Classification system vendors need to integrate their systems with gateway firewalls and web proxies to protect against data leakage. With so many solutions available it is important that products adopt the ICAP (ICAP, 2018) standard for transferring information.

1.12.Conclusion on How to Guard Against Attacks and Prevent Data Theft

Although the above technical exploits are perhaps emerging threats, an analysis of high profile historic exploits has shown that, generally, less sophisticated methods have caused many of the greatest leaks. It is also apparent that security standards like PCI DSS have yet to address some of the emerging methods that can be used for data exfiltration. This will no doubt happen as the standards continue to evolve. In the breaches reviewed, the auditing of systems has often not been as robust as it should have been, as is seen in the cases where patches and SQL injection were the causes of leaks. Other breaches have involved deception from insiders. Since 2017, however, it is apparent that attacks are getting more sophisticated. Based on the attack vectors discussed, security auditing will need to become more robust, standards will need to evolve faster, and the assessment of emerging risks will need to be a regular item on a corporate board’s agenda.

Packet inspection creates a huge overhead on a firewall’s performance; however, if firewalls are going to be fit for purpose they will need to do more. With so-called next-generation firewalls, manufacturers are rising to the challenge. This is perhaps evident in the recent fast-rising costs of the latest next-generation firewalls, which have increasingly faster processors. Firewalls have sophisticated features that take time to develop and, due to the long testing processes required, this unfortunately means that the detection methods deployed are not necessarily aligned with the detection of emerging threats.

Companies need to assess the risks of storing data on mobiles and desktops. This data can be exfiltrated using apps that may be able to read data on the devices. Security standards will need to become much more adaptive to changes in the usage of technology. Firms that claim compliance should be required to regularly requalify. Banks and other payment providers have required retailers to reassess their PCI DSS compliance on an annual basis, and companies that do not comply have fines applied to their credit card accounts which are automatically paid from a retailer’s bank account. The fines are relatively small but are automatically applied as a way of making sure firms address their need to be compliant. The UK’s Cyber Essentials scheme may need to follow similar strategies.

This reflects how quickly the use of technology changes and how slowly several security standards have evolved to deal with emerging threats. It is notable that the PCI DSS has reacted quickly to change with annual updates, unlike the ISO27001 standard that has only had 3 revisions since 2013. As stated previously, it is surprising that ISO27001:2013 does not mention data loss prevention other than the physical measures taken to prevent data loss which are detailed in Section A.11.2. However, one could argue that ISO27001, COBIT 5 and NIST embrace the need for rapid change in their concept of risk, and that they emphasise an organisation’s responsibility to assess risks, mitigate risks, and remove risks. ISO27001 Section A.12.6.1 states “Information about technical vulnerabilities of information systems being used shall be obtained in a timely fashion, the organization’s exposure to such vulnerabilities evaluated and appropriate measures taken to address the associated risk.” ISO 27005:2011 12.1 highlights the responsibility of an organisation to re-assess risks based on “new threats that could be active both outside and inside the organisation and that have not been assessed.” Risk managers must therefore research and assess the risks from emerging threats. These threats may not only apply to a company’s systems but may also have adverse effects on the rights and freedom of others.

Sadly, security standards have often failed to remove the threat from insiders. It is important that employees are vetted and understand the motivations for the implementation of systems that monitor their behavior. IT departments must work closely with management and HR departments to not only monitor staff but also to develop a positive culture in an organisation whereby information security is the concern of every employee. Culture, and the ability of companies to implement new policies and get staff to grasp the importance of adhering to them, are essential to improving security and preventing data loss.

Web exfiltration is by far the greatest threat. DNS exfiltration is possible but can be dealt with by not allowing a workstation to resolve external DNS URLs. NTP and ICMP are not required outbound from a workstation so these ports do not need to be enabled though a firewall from a workstation.
