Chapter 2

Management of a Cyber Attack

Thomas Welsh

Northumbria University London, UK
twelsh37@gmail.com

ABSTRACT

This article will look at the ways an organisation can prepare for, deal with and then recover from a cyber attack against it. There are multiple possible scenarios that can be attributed to a cyber attack. This paper looks at the creation of security policies, cyber incident response plans and organizational risk and cyber insurance.

Keywords: cyber attack, management, cyber warfare, IDS, firewall, governance policy, security policy, cyber incident response, risk, cyber insurance

2.1.Introduction

We live in interesting times. Almost daily, we see reports or news of yet another cyber attack. The stories of breaches come out so regularly nowadays that cyber security issues are getting a lot of visibility in the boardrooms up and down the country (Rothrock, Kaplan and Van Der Oord, 2018).

To give a flavour of what has been happening over the past year or so I have included four noticeable breaches that made the mainstream news in the United Kingdom. These are by no means the biggest or the most destructive of the breaches that have occured over the past few years. This is just a taste of what we will discuss in this chapter.

Morrisons: In 2017, Morrisons, the UK Supermarket chain, was sued by current and former employees after a member of staff stole data on over 100,000 employees. The member of staff in question was fired and subsequently went to jail for 8 years. (BBC News, 2017)

Tesco Bank: In 2016, Tesco Bank, the online finance arm of the Tesco Supermarket chain, admitted that over 40,000 accounts of its customers had been accessed. 9,000 of those accounts had money removed before Tesco Bank froze the online transactions ( Jill Treanor and Jones, 2016).

BA: In 2018, BA announced that it had been hacked and that its web site and mobile applications had been breached. The cyber criminals got away with financial information on over 380,000 of BA’s customers. BA are looking at fines from the regulator, the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO), in the region of £500 million (Calder, 2018).

Facebook: In 2018, Facebook was fined £500,000 by the ICO. This was for their part in the Cambridge Analytica scandal. The fine was for two breaches of the Data Protection Act. The ICO concluded that Facebook failed to safeguard its users’ information and that it failed to be transparent about how that data was harvested by others (Hern and Pegg, 2018).

If you have been paying attention to the security news over the past couple of years you will notice that I have not included the major ransomware outbreaks like Wannacry and NotPetya or any breaches of Industrial Control Systems like the Ukrainian power plants (Park, Summers and Walstrom, 2017).

This article will focus on a practitioners’ view of cyber security. Specifically, it addresses the management of a cyber attack.

In Section 2.1, the introduction, we run through some statistics regarding cyber attacks and cyber crime. We define what we mean by a cyber attack.

Section 2.2 looks at security incident response and covers areas such as security policies and cyber incident response, then walks the reader through an example of how to handle a ransomware incident using a runbook.

Section 2.3 examines organisational risk and the use of tools like cyber insurance to mitigate some of these risks. There are tables in this section that look at the insurance marketplace of 2017 and show the state of the cyber insurance playing field. GDPR fines and their insurability are also discussed.

Section 2.4 is the conclusion and is a brief wrap-up of the chapter.

2.1.1.What is a cyber attack?

Depending on which information sources you consult, you can find various definitions of a cyber attack. In the military, a cyber attack may present itself completely differently from a cyber attack against a civilian organisation. Hathaway et al. (2012) state that there can be multiple definitions of a cyber attack depending on your viewpoint.

Most of these definitions fall into a few categories.

•Cyber attacks — An entity takes an action that impairs the function of a computer or computer network

•Cyber crime — An action that is carried out by non-state entities, executed from a computer system, that breaks criminal law

•Cyber warfare — A cyberattack that damages property or results in physical injury that is similar to normal warfare

If one was to examine each of the above definitions for a cyber attack, the meaning of the term could be distilled down to the following: a cyber attack is an unauthorised action carried out with the goal of subverting a security control or policy. This is in keeping with Hathaway et al.’s (2012) definitions.

Examples of these kinds of attacks are:

•An adversary launches a Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) attack against an organisation’s website. The outcome of this is that the organisation’s website is no longer available. The impact of this could be a loss of revenue that would have been generated in sales. Reputational damage could be one other impact of such an attack. It can be an embarrassment for a major organisation to lose control of its website, and it can be a breach of regulation or legislation for a regulated business to lose control of its website.

•A database is compromised, and the data in it is changed. This can lead to the loss of integrity of the data held in the database. This attack can be caused by the actions of an insider. The insider in question may be someone manipulating pricing for financial gain, a disgruntled employee, an errant process or database call, etc.

•A targeted attack is made against a military objective with the aim of evaluating the defenders’ response to such an attack. Multiple such incursions into a network/device can be used to footprint the organisation and from this, insights into how a defender may react to specific sets of circumstances may be gleaned.

2.1.2.Some cyber attack statistics

If you look at a newspaper today, you can probably find at least one article pointing to the rise in cyber attacks globally. Table 2.1, taken from Lewis (2018), shows the estimated daily activity for several different types of cyber crime.

As you can see there are significant numbers of threats found each day. Some of the malicious scans can be attributed to things like Shodan, Google bots or other automatic scanning software. The large amount of phishing and ransomware activity seen daily is more interesting.

Table 2.1.Estimated daily cyber crime activity (Lewis, 2018).

Table 2.2.Regional distribution of cyber crime in 2017 (Lewis, 2018).

The cost of cyber crime is not insignificant. Lewis (2018) breaks the estimated costs down in the “Economic Impact of Cyber Crime — No Slowing Down” report. The results of this report are shown in Table 2.2.

The costs indicated in Table 2.2 for the world lie in the range of $445 to $608 billion dollars. This is a huge amount of money and clearly indicates that cyber crime does indeed pay.

Organisations trying to thwart this kind of ongoing onslaught need to invest heavily in cyber defences. These defences should be a combination of physical, technical and policy-based controls. Examples of these controls could be, but are not limited to, the ones on the following list:

•Access control systems

•Firewalls/intrusion detection systems (IDSs)

•Policy documents, e.g. acceptable use policies

•Awareness training

Without controls in place it can be very hard to gain any security traction in an organisation. A security practitioner needs to know what the organisational security stance looks like before they can put in place a relevant security plan. With a plan you can gauge your security maturity against a set of standards. Some examples of these standards follow:

•UK Cyber Essentials/Cyber Essentials Plus

•CIS Top 20

•ISO27000/27001

Adhering to a security standard also allows an organisation to gauge itself against its peers in their industry. This can sometimes be good as it allows you to see how well you are doing against the competition. It should be remembered, though, that each company is different and they all have their own unique challenges.

2.2.Security Incident Response from an Organisation’s Viewpoint

Whenever an organisation comes under sustained or targeted cyber attack, it is the responsibility of the security team, working in conjunction with other operational or business teams, to mitigate the attack to the best of their abilities. Sometimes this will entail little input from other teams in the organisation; sometimes it may entail operational teams in the business working with other external thirdparty companies/agencies.

To enable the security team, and the organisation in general, to deal with cyber attacks successfully, there should be effective policies, procedures and guidelines in place that enable the employees in an organisation to be aware of what a cyber security incident is and what their actions should be when they detect a breach of policy or observe a suspicious event.

Procedures put in place by a security team are there to enable the security team or an operational team to better handle specific types of cyber attack, be they phishing campaigns against specific individuals in an organisation or virus/ransomware outbreaks right through to Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) attacks against an organisation’s internet-facing services.

This section will concern itself with policies and procedures that should be in place in an organisation that will enable it to react to and manage to a logical conclusion a cyber attack aimed at an organisation.

2.2.1.Creating effective security policies

Security policies are at the heart of an organisation’s security posture. Having effective and pertinent security policies defined for an organisation is the first port of call for any new security department.

Policies are in themselves security controls. A breach in a security policy by an employee could trigger a human-resources (HR) incident whereby the employee may have to take part in some sort of HR review process. In the worst-case scenarios, a breach of a security policy could lead to the termination of an employee.

Whenever a new employee starts with an organisation, as part of the induction process into the organisation, the new employee should acknowledge that they have read the relevant policies applicable to them. This then puts the onus on the employee to adhere to the policy and report breaches of the policy to the relevant party.

Security policies should be based on a standard template for the organisation. This ensures consistency of approach from the company and is also a good practice from an auditors’ point of view. If an auditor were to look at 20–30 policies from a company and they all had different layouts, then this may suggest to the auditor that there is no “joined up plan” in respect to the company’s policies. Conversely, if an auditor were to look at 20 policies and see that they all maintained a standard layout with a consistent approach, then that makes it easier for the auditor to audit and it also makes it much easier for an employee wishing to get to the heart of the policy statement itself.

2.2.1.1.Format and layout of a policy

The thought of creating a policy from scratch can be quite daunting. It was for the author when he had to create a new policy for the first time. What he soon realised though is that there are a lot of reference policies available freely on the internet. Though these may not fit your organization exactly as you would like, reading other policies gives you a general overview of what a policy is, and what it comprises. SANS Institute, for example, have multiple security policy templates. You just need to fill in the organisation’s name and you will have a working policy.

When creating policies from another person’s/organisation’s policy, it is important that you consider the wording of the policy. Does it “fit” with what you want your policy to say? If not, what can be changed to make it more applicable?

The wording of a policy is also important. The writer of the policy does not need to be a wordsmith, but word usage in policy is important. The word “SHOULD” is ambiguous in policy. You are telling someone that they should do something, but that it’s ok if they don’t. Replacing “SHOULD” with “MUST” changes the reading of the sentence and its applicability.

Consider the following control statement:

All company assets SHOULD be patched on a regular basis.

Reading this statement, the reader can take away two meanings. The first of these is that it is not mandatory that systems are patched regularly, and the second of these is that all assets are patched regularly.

If we rewrite the control statement as follows, it is much clearer:

All company assets MUST be patched on a regular basis.

Reading this, the only thing a reader can take away is that all systems MUST be patched regularly. You could argue that regularly is also ambiguous as it could mean weekly or annually since both are regular. Other wording in the policy could help you get around this ambiguity.

Brander (1997) in his RFC 2119 “Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels” sets out to define the use of the above keywords and several others as they should be used in RFC documents. Such clarity is sometimes achievable in a good policy and it assists both the reader and the writer in the definition of the policy. The RFC states:

“The key words “MUST”, “MUST NOT”, “REQUIRED”, “SHALL”, “SHALL NOT”, “SHOULD”, “SHOULD NOT”, “RECOMMENDED”, “MAY”, and “OPTIONAL” in this document are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119”

A good policy document is as succinct as it can possibly be, but it should at least incorporate the following sections.

2.2.1.2.Preparing a security policy

The actual writing of a security policy is relatively simple when you have pulled together the layout and content of what you wish to incorporate in the policy.

As a “rule of thumb”, you should have sections similar to the sections denoted in Table 2.3.

Always aim to write a policy in as succinct a manner as possible. Being too “wordy” can often complicate the policy and allows ambiguity and interpretation to slip into the wording. This is not a good thing as it can derail the policy.

The policy statement tells the reader what is defined in the policy. Table 2.4 is a section of a WIFI acceptable-use policy that the author wrote. Using the SANS (2014) Wireless Communications policy as a starting point the author created the security policy control statements in Table 2.4.

After the policy statement had been written, it was then run through the legal team to ensure it complied with local laws and regulations. Bear in mind that if you are an international company then it may require several revisions to have an overarching policy that is compliant with all regions in which the organisation conducts business. It may be necessary to have an overarching policy and then certain region-specific mini policies to cope with local laws and regulations.

As can be seen from Table 2.4, there are 6 policy control statements. Each one is well bounded with what control it is putting in place. This will assist the Security Team in monitoring the policy for compliance and will assist the business in dealing with breaches of the policy.

Table 2.3.The main sections of a policy document.

Section

Contents

Versioning/Document Control

This section records the following.

The policy owner

Who approved the policy

How often it is reviewed

Next review date

Review Schedule

This section lays out what would trigger a review of the policy

Overview

What the policy is aiming to cover

Objective

What the objective of the policy is

Scope

The scope of the policy and any limits put on it

Policy

This section lays out the policy statements

Compliance with policy/Handling exceptions to policy

This section is used to inform users of how policy compliance will be measured, how to deal with an Exception to Policy (ETP), and how to deal with breaches to policy.

Table 2.4.An example of control statements in a security policy.

Security Policy Control Statements

“The Company” provides free WIFI access to the internet for employees, contractors and visitors to the “The Company’” business premises.

Employees, contractors and visitors must not use the “The Company” WIFI connection to:

Upload, download, use or reuse any material which violates any applicable copyright laws or which violates the rights of any individual or entity;

Access defamatory, obscene, indecent, abusive, offensive, harassing, violent, hateful, inflammatory, or otherwise inappropriate material or content;

Visit sites that could be deemed inappropriate, offensive, pornographic, or that contain material of an obscene nature;

Use peer-to-peer software on their own personal devices, for the collection or dissemination of copyrighted material for which they are not the copyright holder;

Attempt to bypass any security controls put in place to monitor or restrict access to the “The Company” WIFI; and

Introduce any viruses, trojan horses, worms, logic bombs, or other software or material which is malicious or technologically harmful.

Table 2.5.Liability clause.

Liability Clause

“The Company” is not responsible for the accuracy, validity, legality or usefulness of information available, or any viruses and software designed to damage equipment and networks, which you may encounter while connected to “The Company” WIFI

“The Company” is not responsible for damage caused by connecting personal devices to the “The Company” WIFI.

“The Company” is not responsible for any use or transactions carried out using the “The Company” WIFI service. Responsibility for the security of such transactions rests with the user and “The Company” cannot accept responsibility or liability for any loss or damages arising from such use of its WIFI services.

Table 2.5 is the final part of the policy and defines what the company is not responsible for on the WIFI policy. Specifically, the policy states that it is not responsible for incorrect information, damage to property attached to the WIFI network and for the security of any connections carried out over the WIFI network.

2.2.1.3.Exceptions to policy

An Exception to Policy (ETP) should not be confused with a policy breach.

A policy breach is when a security incident has occurred that has broken one of the policy statements. An ETP is an outlier in an organisation who is not able to comply with a policy statement at a particular time. This may be for technical, business, or financial reasons.

Exceptions to Policy should be logged somewhere in an organisation and should be reviewed on a regular basis to see if the ETP has been rectified or if an extension to the ETP is required. It would be prudent for the person/people reviewing the ETPs to do this on at least a 6-monthly basis. Any longer and the ETP almost becomes irrelevant, as the ETP, instead of being an Exception to Policy, is supporting a policy breach.

Security policies are an important part of the security practitioner’s toolset. Well-maintained and well-reviewed policies help a company to protect its information assets as well as the organisation as a whole.

2.2.2.Cyber incident response plan

The Cyber Incident Response Plan (CIRP) is the “go to” document in a business arsenal that defines how a cyber incident is handled.

2.2.2.1.Security procedures

Having defined a robust policy document, the next task for security practitioners is to lay out the procedures to be followed when handling a security incident.

Procedures differ from policy in that they are the methods by which breaches of policy can be followed up. These are well-defined and include such things as:

•When a procedure should be instigated.

•Who will control information flow whilst the procedure is being executed.

•What tasks need to be completed at the end of an incident.

•Any other follow-up tasks.

There is no such thing as an overarching procedure that governs all others. Procedures backed up by policy are fluid documents. They mature over time and are never really finished. They are often referred to in business circles as “living documents”

When defining procedures, it is advisable to have a methodology already planned. This methodology will lay out the different phases of the procedure and allow the writer to assign tasks to the specific phase. Figure 2.1 shows the phases of an incident response process. This process may not fit every procedure or playbook but it does give a high level view of the procedures that will be defined.

Fig. 2.1. High level incident response process.

Fig. 2.2. Ransomware incident response process.

Each of these phases logically flows into the next and this provides for a structured process. This process, however, is fluid. It may be necessary to modify the process so that it fits with a particular security incident playbook. For instance, upon discovery of a data breach under the European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) you must inform the regulator, which is the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) if you are in the United Kingdom, of the breach within 72 hours of the breach occurring (Marotta et al., 2017). Note that the 72 hours is linear and does not honour working hours. If you discover a breach or a reportable event at 12pm on a Thursday, you are duty bound by the auspices of the GDPR to report the breach or reportable event to the regulator by 12PM on the Saturday.

Figure 2.2 shows the process defined in Fig. 2.1, modified to fit a ransomware playbook.

The individual phases in the ransomware process which are defined in Fig. 2.2 will now be discussed.

2.2.2.2.Identification

When a device is initially infected with ransomware there are several potential Indicators of Compromise (IOCs)

•If the user was completely unaware, then the first indicator a user would receive would be a message telling them that their files had been encrypted and that in order to recover their files a ransom would need to be paid.

•If a user is more familiar with the work patterns of their computer then they may in the first instance notice that the computer is more sluggish than usual. This is because the ransomware is consuming CPU cycles and disk IO bandwidth encrypting the user’s data.

When the user has identified that they have been a victim of ransomware then they will escalate the incident to the respective incident handling process.

Initially, when the incident responders conduct their triage of the computer, they should note the ransomware details and any ransomware payment demands. The incident responders should note which resources have been affected by the ransomware and whether any shared resources were affected, e.g. corporate file shares.

2.2.2.3.Initial containment

It is important to treat a potential ransomware incident with the gravity it deserves. Ransomware can pose a significant risk to normal business operations. Take a look at the news and press articles surrounding the WannaCry ransomware outbreak and how it disrupted the National Health Service (NHS) in the UK. The NHS was severely crippled due to the scale of this outbreak.

Ransomware poses a substantial risk to an organisation’s normal operations. In the event of a ransomware outbreak, the initial response should be swift and sharp. This will help limit the effects of the outbreak and help prevent further impact to the normal business operations of the company.

Where containment efforts may lead to the interruption of normal business operations, the business owners of that process should be involved in the decision process.

2.2.2.4.Notification

The initial notification of an incident is usually one of the shortest phases of the whole incident response process, although there should be ongoing notification throughout the lifecycle of the incident.

Without a doubt, ransomware will have an effect on normal business operations. To this end there will be multiple notifications that may need to be sent out to both internal and external third parties.

Employees need to understand what has happened and what is being done about it.

External parties may include the regulator, law enforcement, insurance companies if the company has cyber insurance, and any other regulatory or legislative body that local regulations mandate should be informed.

2.2.2.5.Analysis

The majority of ransomware breaches normally originate from a user clicking on a link in a malicious email, or from a drive-by download on a user’s computer. It is of the utmost importance that this evidence is captured so that a root cause analysis can be carried out to identify the malicious file. This evidence will be on the initially infected computer that executed the ransomware program. It will not be on file shares encrypted by the ransomware. The collection and preservation of this evidence is paramount.

Once a particular user’s computer has been identified as the initial infection point, this computer should be isolated from the network. The easiest way to do this is to remove its network connection. The computer should not be powered down until a memory dump has been taken. This ensures that whatever malicious code was being executed can be captured in memory.

If the normal business operation is to then format/rebuild the computer, a disk image of the hard disk/disks should be taken. Bear in mind that if full disk encryption is used then the decryption keys for the disk should also be saved. It is ultimately preferable to keep the whole machine quarantined until the investigation is over. If this is not possible, then the hard disk should be retained, as this is also a better chain of evidence than a disk image taken by an employee. The running of anti-virus scans prior to disk imaging should be prevented as this can taint the evidence.

Analysis is used to confirm the initial infection vectors and to confirm what the capabilities of the ransomware are. With this information it may be possible to identify the ransomware type/family. All diskbased analysis should be taken on a disk image and not on the original disk itself. This will protect the integrity of the evidence.

Analysis of the malware may require third party support from incident responders if there is no in-house expertise in malware analysis.

2.2.2.6.Containment

Although there are similarities between the containment and initial containment stages the main differentiator is the criticality. The initial containment actions are reactionary and possibly temporary in nature. They are put in place to contain the initial outbreak. In the containment phase the actions are carried out in a planned and methodical manner. They are implemented to manage the full scope of the incident.

When the initial infection vector is identified, further containment actions will need to be carried out. If IOCs are identified as URLs, IP addresses, email addresses, etc., then blocks/alerts can be put in place to inform the incident responders of further infections on the organisation’s infrastructure. These blocks/alerts help mitigate the threat and prevent it from reoccurring. It should be borne in mind that malware authors change up their malware regularly and that an IOC for the current outbreak may not work for a future outbreak.

If any further IOCs are discovered on the organisation’s infrastructure, then these systems should be isolated from the network, and memory and disk images taken to preserve evidence.

2.2.2.7.Eradication

During the eradication phase, the organisation removes the threats and elements identified as part of the contamination from its infrastructure. Having contained the infection, eradication follows closely behind.

The eradication phase is when the organisation removes all indications of the infection from its systems and the systems are put back into service. It is hoped that systems placed back in service have had service restored to a state similar to the state before the ransomware was detected.

2.2.2.8.Recovery

The recovery phase is when the organisation’s systems return to normal operations. In this phase it is assumed that the ransomware threat has been neutralised to such an extent that no further impact of the ransomware can occur.

The recovery phase can only commence when all containment and eradication actions have been completed. This should have included blocking the attackers’ website and patching or mitigating the vulnerable software or services on the organisation’s infrastructure. During this phase, files may be retrieved from backup and the rebuilding of computers from verified known good media may have commenced.

In the event that some parts of the business may require some files or information retrieved as a matter of priority, further steps must be taken. Even before all the eradication steps have been completed, it is of the utmost importance that these restored resources are properly secured from re-infection. The organisation should limit what files can be restored to reduce the work needed. Files restored should have the least amount of access privileges possible in order to enable operation but prevent re-infection. It is not unheard of for restored files to be re-encrypted when a successful containment and eradication process fails.

2.2.2.9.Post-incident actions

Having reached a state of normalcy after the ransomware infection it is imperative that the organisation carry out a post-incident review (PIR). The PIR is carried out to ensure that all lessons learned are captured and fed back into the process. The ultimate aim is to ensure that similar incidents do not occur again, and if they do, then any previous incident experience is captured and distilled down into knowledge which is captured in the organisation’s appropriate playbooks.

In the PIR meeting all the parties that were involved in the incident should have representation. It is important to have this meeting chaired by a person of sufficient authority that can guide the meeting along. PIR meetings are not a forum to deride other teams for their performance or lack thereof. This is not constructive but will put them on the defensive and will therefore prevent valuable lessons from being documented from the previous incident.

The PIR should consider what went well and what went badly. It should identify areas of improvement and minute any actions to be reported back to the review in a timely manner. Areas to consider may include any of the following:

•Policies

•Patch Management

•Vulnerability Monitoring

•Alerting

•Firewalls and blocking software

•Employee training

•Preparatory tasks that may help in the future

Finally, organisations need to ensure they have sent out any additional notifications that are required both internally and externally. Nothing enrages employees more than lack of communication. If you do not put out notifications to update the organisation’s employees, then they will fill this communication void with hearsay and conjecture. This can ultimately derail all the good work carried out by the incident responders. Organisations and individuals also have to bear in mind their reporting requirements in relation to any relevant legislation and regulation that their organisations may work under.

2.3.Business Risk and Cyber Insurance — Its Place in Your Cyber Response Toolkit

It seems like almost every day we hear about a new system that has been exploited or a news story on how some organisation has had a data breach (BBC, 2017; BBC, 2018). As more and more of these breaches and exploits become available, more boards of companies are beginning to wake up to the risks posed to their organisations.

The management of an organization can no longer ignore these threats. On their part, governments and regulators have set up new laws and regulation to try and create a consistent framework and consistent breach reporting mechanisms across regions. In fact it could be argued that the relatively new European Union General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is already shaking up certain parts of business risk. Albrecht (2016) posits that businesses were already pointing to GDPR as a major risk and that it was being looked at as a key management task for an organisation.

Not all organisations are taking the responsibility for GDPR regulation as seriously as others. Addis and Kutar (2018) point out that a large number of organisations may not have been compliant with the GDPR regulation by the time it was implemented in May 2018. In fact, if you look around you will see that larger organisations have implemented GDPR programs in their organisations and are actively pursuing them. Conversely, a lot of smaller companies are not aware of their responsibilities under GDPR and are woefully unprepared for any actions that may be taken against them (Addis and Kutar, 2018).

One recent article by Page, Kaur and Waters (2017) looks at directors’ liability and the growing concern as to what it means in the industry. The authors point out that cyber attacks and data loss are two of the biggest concerns facing companies. Because of regulation in certain sectors of industry directors are having more and more regulation and legislation heaped on them. Directors now must look at ways to mitigate this risk against their personal liability whilst discharging their duties efficiently.

2.3.1.What is risk management?

Marotta et al. (2017) state that “Risk is the possibility of suffering a loss or harm”. Looking at this statement we can divine that risk is the outcome of several factors.

•Incident — The occurrence of a risk

•Threat — A cause of the risk

•Vulnerability — A weakness that can be exploited to create an incident

•Impact — The direct and indirect consequences of the actions of a threat on a vulnerability

The management of the above four items is called risk management. It is all about identifying risks in an organisation and then putting plans in place to handle or mitigate risks.

Risk management is made up of two distinct parts.

•Risk identification — Involves listing the elements of risk: threats, vulnerabilities and impact.

•Risk analysis — Involves carrying out the analysis of risks, focusing on the probability of a risk happening and the impact that risk would have on the organisation.

The World Economic Forum defines the above as a simple calculation.

Risk = probability × impact

Having carried out your risk analysis you can then move on to define a risk treatment. This allows you to define the measures you wish to implement to handle the identified risks (Taylor et al., 2016).

There are only four ways to handle risk.

•Accept — A company may accept the risk of an outcome happening if there is deemed to be a low likelihood of the risk materialising.

•Reduce — A company may put controls in place to reduce the impact or likelihood of a risk materialising.

•Transfer/Share — This is where an organisation may look to transfer the risk to another party, e.g. buying insurance policies to cover the risk.

•Avoid — Some risks are just not worth taking on and a business may choose to avoid them, e.g. choosing not to entering a new market where the risks are not fully understood.

The next section of this chapter discusses how you could transfer/share the risk with a third party in the form of a cyber insurance policy.

2.3.2Cyber insurance

It could be said that cyber insurance first started to appear around the 1970s. A company could purchase insurance to cover them for computer crime (Marotta et al., 2017). From those early days specialist insurance has sprung up to assist companies in attempting to mitigate the risk of a cyber event. Property and liability insurance policies will not, in general, cover a cyber event (Biener, Eling and Wirfs, 2015).

When an organisation looks to procure a cyber insurance policy it is useful to have some terms of reference to put to the insurance organisations. This allows the organisation to easily judge each company on the same basis. A useful term of reference could be using the same taxonomy for the discussions with the insurers, so that the organisation is discussing similar products on a similar footing.

Table 2.6 lays out a taxonomy of operational cyber security risks. It was developed by Cebula, Young and Popeck (2014). This is version two of the taxonomy and it was updated from the original, dated 2010.

As can be seen, Table 2.6 lays out four classes, each with its own sub-categories. These sub-categories each have elements that apply to that class. The table can be used to do a detailed risk analysis of actions inside each of the classes. Cebula, Young and Popeck (2014) point out that a risk in one category can possibly create a risk in other categories. An example of such is below.

“…a software failure due to improper security settings could be caused by any of the elements of inadvertent or deliberate actions of people” (Cebula, Young and Popeck, 2014).

As mentioned previously, GDPR is a boardroom issue in companies that are aware of it. One of the major risks of GDPR are the fines the regulator can impose. In the United Kingdom prior to GDPR the maximum fine the Information Commissioner’s Office could hand out to a company was £500,000 (Information Commisioner’s Office, 1998). Now with the GDPR being in effect the fines are much heavier. A breach of the GDPR could leave an organisation liable for a fine of €20 million or 4% of global turnover, whichever is greatest (Marsh, 2016).

Table 2.6.Categories of cyber risk, derived from Cebula, Young and Popeck (2014).

Category

Description

Elements

Actions of People

1.1 Inadvertent

Unintentional actions taken without malicious or harmful intent

Mistakes, errors, omissions

1.2 Deliberate

Actions taken intentionally and with intent to do harm

Fraud, sabotage, theft and vandalism

1.3 Inaction

Systems and Technology Failures

One of the major sticking points of cyber insurance is that the coverage of regulatory fines is a grey area. Aon and DLA Piper (2018) and Marsh (2018) both agree that your insurability for GDPR fines is really dependent on where you are located in Europe (Fig. 2.3). Basically, if you are in a highly regulated environment then you will be unlikely to get insurance to cover GDPR fines without any stipulations on a policy.

Now that we have covered the insurability of GDPR fines it will be worth looking at what other risks can be covered by a cyber insurance policy.

Fig. 2.3.Insurability by country, Aon and DLA Piper (2018).

Typically, an organisation will have a level of risk they are willing to accept. This is usually set by senior management and will be cascaded down through functions like operational risk or a risk management function. Sometimes these functions are carried out by a single person, sometimes by teams, depending on the size of the organisation.

Table 2.7 by Marotta et al. (2017) shows a quick view of what levels of cover an insurance company may be willing to provide. It should be noted that when dealing with insurance companies the organisation may be better suited to using an insurance broker who has experience in the area of cyber risk and cyber insurance (Shackelford, 2012).

As Shackelford (2012) points out, organisations should not rely completely on cyber insurance policies to mitigate their cyber risk.

Table 2.7.Coverage of several existing insurance policies derived from Marotta et al. (2017).

Kopp, Kaffenberger and Wilson (2017), in their working paper for the International Monetary Fund, point out that 90% of the costs of a cyber incident can be attributed to indirect factors.

This is broken down into four phases with examples of both direct and indirect costs shown in Table 2.8.

The four phases can be broken down as the following:

•Prevention — These are the normal day-to-day running costs of a business taking care of its regulatory and business requirements.

Table 2.8.Costs of cyber events (Kopp, Kaffenberger and Wilson, 2017).

Phase

Direct Costs

Indirect Costs

Prevention (continuous)

Opportunity cost

Increased funding costs

Redesign of business processes and systems

Rebuilding relationships, reputation and brand value

Investment in better security systems and preparedness capabilities

•Reaction — This is when the initial breach takes place and how the company reacts to it. This could entail incident response, forensics, and communications to both internal and external parties.

•Impact Management — This is when an organisation checks on its security controls and infrastructure configurations. It is about managing the direct impact of a breach.

•Business Recovery and Remediation — These are the costs of repairing the breach and putting in controls that will assist in preventing a similar breach in future. As part of this phase the organisation should start to rebuild reputation and customer goodwill.

An effective and well understood cyber strategy should underpin any organisation no matter how big or small they are. Cyber security is the melding of people, process and technology, sometimes termed the Three Pillars of Cyber Security (IT Governance, 2018).

2.4.Conclusion

As can be seen from this paper, to be in a position to manage a cyber attack effectively takes time and resources.

From the introduction to this article, we explained the definition of a cyber attack and how this can change depending on the viewpoint of the practitioner. We distilled these meanings down to a single definition that in our opinion covers all three areas.

Looking at the statistics of cyber attacks we can see that the cost and frequency of attacks are continuing to grow, and that cyber attackers are here for the long haul.

We discussed how to create security policies which can be put in place to manage the expectations of users using tailored policy control statements. Running through policies brought us naturally to cyber incident response plans.

We walked through a ransomware runbook and saw how, using our cyber incident response framework, we can work through an incident to reach a logical conclusion. We also carried out post-incident actions. This is when we can use what we have learned in the investigation to update our controls so they are always improving.

Looking at business risk, we covered some of the language used in the risk arena. This took us on to the section on cyber insurance. It can be said that there really is no single policy that will address the risks borne by every organization. Not everything can be insured. We pointed out that for some companies cyber insurance will not indemnify an organisation against regulatory breaches or fines. This is an important point as GDPR fines of €20 million or 4% of global turnover far outstrip the maximum fine of £500,000 under the UK’s Data Protection Act 1998.

Preparing for and defending against cyber attacks at an organisational level is a complicated task. Hopefully some of the information in this article will be useful to other practitioners in the field.
