Chapter 3

Practical Cyber Security for Digital Trains

George Copeland

Northumbria University London, UK
george.copeland@outlook.com

ABSTRACT

On-train networks have moved from being a set of isolated engineering solutions to becoming integrated cyber-physical systems, creating ‘Digital Trains’. The interconnectivity between Digital Train systems is generally driven by operational efficiency and cost rather than security. It is asserted that the architectural standards which define on-train networks have not kept pace with the developments in the industry or with cyber security, and that the combination of ICT and ICS networks introduces potential risks that are not fully understood by decision makers. Inclusion of both the Digital Railway and Digital Trains in the scope of Critical National Infrastructure CPNI (2108) and therefore the NIS Directive (Directive (EU) (2016/1148) should help in this respect but that may not be soon enough to prevent an incident. Following these recently introduced regulatory requirements, consideration is required as to which is the most appropriate security standard with which to provide appropriate assurance given the mix of technologies.

Keywords: digital train, digital railway, critical national infrastructure, NIS, IACS, cyber-physical

3.1.Introduction

The current drive for digitisation in automation and control is often referred to as ‘Industry 4.0’, or the fourth industrial revolution. “While Industry 3.0 focused on the automation of single machines and processes, Industry 4.0 focuses on the end-to-end digitisation of all physical assets and integration into digital ecosystems with value chain partners” (PWC, 2016). In the UK, the railway is part of the transition to digitalisation, but because of the way that it is currently structured, the approach has been fragmented and disparate, not least between Digital Trains and the Digital Railway. In the UK, trains are owned by Rolling Stock Leasing Companies (ROSCOs), and operated by Train Operating Companies (TOCs), mostly delivering fixed term franchise agreements let by DfT. TOCs generally include major investments, including train upgrades and purchases, in their franchise bids, returning assets to the ROSCOs at the end of the franchise. The trains run on the infrastructure provided by Network Rail, which is a nationalised organisation. Digital Trains are one of the major investments being made by TOCs, and the Digital Railway is being developed by Network Rail without much synergy. This is not the only reason for current concerns about how the railway is operating but has contributed towards the need for a “review to look at the structure of the whole rail industry, including increasing integration between track and train” (DfT, 2018). This research focuses on Digital Train development with a view to defining a practical way to deal with the “new operational risk for smart manufacturers and digital supply networks: cyber” (Deloitte, 2017).

On-board train networks have moved from being a set of isolated engineering solutions to becoming integrated cyber-physical systems. The extent of on-board systems ranges from the provision of public wifi to operational controls, creating a ‘multi-agent’ architecture, described by Yagdereli et al. (2015) as comprising multiple sub-systems or being systems of systems. Although it is recognised that segregation is desirable the interconnectivity between on-board systems is often driven by operational efficiency and cost rather than security. It is asserted that the standards which define on-train networks have not kept pace with the developments in the industry or with cyber security and the potential risks are not fully understood by decision makers. In the UK the inclusion of the railway in the scope of Critical National Infrastructure CPNI (2108) and therefore the NIS Directive (Directive (EU) (2016/1148) may help in this respect but early indications appear to set compliance at a low level.

The Digital Railway includes the infrastructure used to support railway signalling and other safety systems. In the UK this is managed by Network Rail. The Digital Railway’s footprint on trains is largely confined to the driver’s cab where it delivers safety systems designed to alert the driver to unexpected events and in some cases override train controls to stop the train. These systems currently include ATP (Automatic train protection), AWS (Automatic warning system) and TPWS (Train protection and warning system). All of these systems are delivered through a dedicated communications network called GSM-R (Global System for Mobile communications — Railway). Network Rail is in the process of delivering a strategy to upgrade the Digital Railway, deploying systems that provide in-cab signalling, traffic management and a connected driver advisory system. This will use the same (and upgraded) GSM-R to implement the following: ETCS (European Train Control System) to allow trains to run closer together and to travel at their best speeds while maintaining safe braking distances, CDAS (Connected Driver Advisory Systems) and ATO (Automatic Train Operation) which provide decision support to drivers in the cab so that they have the information they need at the right time to boost performance and safety, and TM (Traffic Management) to optimise performance as trains flow across the network, maximising the throughput that existing track can support and adapting in real-time as network conditions change to aid rapid recovery (NR, 2018). ETCS is an advanced form of ATP and the combination of ETCS and GSM-R is referred to as ERTMS (European Railway Traffic Management System) (EU, 2018).

Digital Train includes the remaining on-board systems that deliver services such as RCM (remote condition monitoring), PIS (passenger information systems), SRS (seat reservation systems) and public wifi. These systems do not have access to GSM-R and use a separate MCG (Mobile Communications Gateway) to enable internet access using data sims procured from commercial MNOs (Mobile Network Operators).

From a rolling stock perspective, the Digital Railway includes the Train Control Systems that are safety-critical, whereas Digital Train includes Train Management Systems, which may be operational or business-critical and are less regulated. Ideally the Digital Railway and Digital Train systems remain segregated, but for operational efficiency and cost management new trains are being delivered with more and more systems being interconnected.

Train Communications Networks (TCN) were originally based on industrial field-buses. They lacked performance and were not designed for trains. As there was no standard, proprietary designs emerged which resulted in a lack of interoperability between vehicles. Schafers and Hans (2000) describe the development of IEC 61375-1 and its publication as an international standard in October 1999. The initial standard included only a Multifunctional Vehicle Bus (MVB) which connects equipment on and between vehicles and a Wire Train Bus (WTB) which interconnects vehicles via jumper cables or automatic couplers.

The IEC 61375 standard, as shown in Fig. 3.1, has since been supplemented to elaborate on the protocols for the bus networks and:

i.in 2012 to add the CAN-Open protocol based on ISO 11898 much like that used in road vehicles, and

ii.in 2015 to add the Ethernet Train Backbone (ETB) and introduction of the concept of an Ethernet Consist Network (ECN)

Fig. 3.1.IEC 61375 architecture.

The components of IEC 61375 are shown below in Fig. 3.2:

Fig. 3.2.IEC 61375 series of standards.

An ECN is the network that serves a single Consist: “A Consist can be a train set or unit, a rake of coaches, it is a single vehicle or a group of vehicles which are not separated during normal operation. A Consist contains one, several or no Consist networks,” IEC 61375-2-6:2016 (Draft). This is illustrated in Fig. 3.3.

Using an ETB to connect the train means that communication between ECNs can exploit ethernet performance, currently up to 10 Gb/s (10000BASE-T). An example is shown in Fig. 3.4 below. This enables greater flexibility in train reconfiguration. To avoid IP conflicts, whenever two or more Consists are reformed to make a train there is a process of Inauguration, which gives all nodes of the ETB their IP address and controls how they relate to all the other nodes on the same backbone.

The draft IEC 61375-2-6:2016 is entitled ‘On-board to ground communication’. This document introduces a Mobile Connectivity Gateway (MCG) onto the ETB to enable connectivity to shore-based systems.

Fig. 3.3.Train consists.

Fig. 3.4.Consist networks.

The introduction of an Ethernet network onto the train and its use to interconnect the MVB, WTB and CAN-bus transforms the network into a LAN, and the connectivity provided by the MCG gives the LAN a WAN connection. The IEC 61375 standard offers little cyber security direction; only the as yet unpublished IEC 61375-2-6 refers to IEC 62443 for guidance on risk assessment and mitigation.

As well as its multi-agent nature there are a number of characteristics that make the Digital Train LAN/WAN distinctive:

i)WAN connectivity is usually via 4G which is unreliable across the railway network;

ii)There are approximately 20,000 passenger vehicles distributed across the country according to DfT (2017);

iii)Each train generally has 1 or 2 company representatives on-board, and maybe several hundred customers, some of whom are using the on-board network to access the internet; and

iv)Trains move, sometimes at high speed.

This is not the same cyber security problem, with the same risks, that exists with land-based networks.

Ethernet Backbones have been included in the new train design and build since the IEC 61375 standard was extended in 2015 to include the ETB, but with public WiFi having become a hygiene factor in the customer experience, and with governmental influence on the rail industry, legacy fleets are also being fitted with ‘Ethernet Backbones’ and an MCG to provide internet connectivity to deliver public WiFi and ‘Infotainment’. Where this network is used only for public services there is no issue but once the network is available the temptation for train engineers to use it to connect other systems is difficult to resist. Although some industry bodies have published guidelines, there are few firm design principles, and any that there are have been constrained through limitations on power, space and cost when retrofitting aged vehicles.

Referring to retrofitted systems, RSSB (2016) alludes to the problems that have arisen due to the ad hoc nature of on-board network implementation and attributes these to the poor standard of network awareness and uncoordinated commercial influences. RSSB advocated separate train networks but recognises the drivers towards integration and warns that “the integrity needs to be robust and provided with security and privacy controls”. To elaborate, connectivity to on-board systems started with individual system upgrades introducing 4G receivers for a single device. This enables systems such as seat reservations displays to be updated remotely. Similarly, some condition-based monitoring systems were updated to enable data to be offloaded, again using a 4G connection. It was the introduction of public wifi on trains that prompted the retrofitting of ETBs, albeit with a simpler architecture than that defined in IEC 61375. It was recognised in some quarters that network segregation and security controls were a necessary consideration and early publications such as Tonks (2016) raised awareness regarding the emerging requirements.

Fig. 3.5.Basic retrofit architecture.

The need to segregate networks was initially envisaged as a physical exercise and dual backbone designs were originally proposed but the cost of duplicating switches, the lack of on-board space to accommodate additional equipment and in many cases the lack of sufficient power has guided suppliers towards single backbones such as the one shown in Fig. 3.5 above, reproduced from Duffy (2018), which shows a typical implementation solely to provide public wifi.

From the same source, Duffy (2018), a more complex design to accommodate a wider range of connected on-board systems is shown in Fig. 3.6 below.

Neither the 61375 standard nor the solutions advertised by the rail supply chain make much reference to cyber security, yet it is clear that such advances in integrated solutions have an impact on both threats and vulnerabilities. Previously, all on-board systems stood alone and required specialist knowledge to access, but largescale integration expands the attack surface available. The use of ethernet as a link layer protocol extends the source of threats as it brings the means to attack it into the capability of a far wider group of actors. In the corporate world it would be inconceivable to allow such a scenario to be unprotected and yet industries such as rail have been slow to react, with requirements generally being driven by regulation rather than corporate risk management.

Fig. 3.6.Complex retrofit architecture.

3.2.In Search of Solutions

Many international standards are adopted by peer organisations around the world and renamed to identify the local standard authority’s approval. For instance, ISO 27001 is also known as BS EN ISO/IEC 27001 in the UK and AS/NZS ISO/IEC 27001 in Australasia. In Germany the DIN (Deutsches Institut für Normung e.V. (German Institute for Standardization) organisation has published DIN EN ISO/IEC 27001 and so on around the world. Standard referencing requires that standards are cited as ‘authorising organisation and year’, e.g. 27001 would be cited as BSI (2013), but BSI published many standards in that year, including other standards referenced in this document. For that reason, and for readability, this document will use the basic nomenclature, without any prefix, when referring to a standard and will include the nomenclature where it is cited. The reference will identify a BSI standard if one is available or will refer to the standard originator, e.g. IEC, if there is not, which will also clarify which version of the standard is being used, e.g. 27001 will be cited as (BSI, 2013) 27001 and referred to as 27001 and IEC 62443-1-1 which at the time of writing has yet to be included in BSI’s library, will be cited as (IEC, 2009) 62443-1-1 and referred to as 62443-1-1.

There are multiple sources of guidance to industry from both government and non-partisan industry organisations including NCSC (National Cyber Security Centre), DfT (Department for Transport), DCMS (Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport), HSE (Health and Safety Executive), RDG (Rail Delivery Group) and RSSB (Rail Safety and Standards Board).

RDG (2017), the Rail Cyber Security Strategy, is published by the Rail Delivery Group, which is an industry body designed to represent the interests of the rail Train Operating Companies (TOCs). The document references various standards, including (BSI, 2013) 27001 and the NIST Cyber security Framework (NIST, 2018) although in 2017 it referenced the 2017 version, which in turn references (BSI, 2011) 62443 (but as the ISA version dated 2009) and other security standards.

In the UK, ‘Transport’ is part of the critical national infrastructure (CPNI, 2018). The government has identified DfT as the ‘Competent Authority’ for Transport and DfT have included TOCs under the sub-sector ‘Rail Transport’ (DfT, 2018) in the scope of the NIS Directive, (Directive (EU), 2016/1148). It therefore follows that the sensible option is to follow standards that will deliver the most cost-effective route to NIS compliance. NCSC (2018a) gives some guidance on this, also helpfully pointing towards both the 27000 and 62443 series of standards.

Whichever is the most appropriate security standard for this environment is far from clear. The diagram shown in Fig. 3.7 below shows some of the material that is available to the industry and how they interact.

As Fig. 3.7 shows, there is plenty of guidance relating to IACS and also to trains in particular but it is generally vague and simply offers possibilities. This is not just a problem in the rail industry. For example Leszczyna (2018) in a survey of standards appropriate to smart grids observed “the situation that operators may find it difficult to orientate themselves in this plethora of literature”.

Fig. 3.7.Industry guidance.

The common theme of industry guidance documents is that they recommend the development of a management system driven by one of the requirement standards relating to cyber security. NIST (2018) is very helpful in this respect as it includes references to a variety of standards that satisfy the requirements of each subcategory in the framework it defines. This is possibly due to NIST providing a voluntary framework as opposed to a regulatory directive like NIS. RDG (2017) references both NIST (2017) (NIST is updated every year and so RDG referenced the version current at the time of its own publication) and (BSI, 2013) 27001. In turn NIST (2017) includes both (BSI, 2013) 27001 and a number of the 62443 standards (as IEC publications) in the standards it references. The question remains: which standard is most appropriate for Digital Trains and, importantly, will satisfy the requirements of NIS?

In a lecture at Stanford University, Weiss (2011) described the fundamental differences between IT security and the security requirements of IACS (he called it ICS). Much of what he said is still true today and illustrates why 62443 is different to 27001. The objectives of Information Security are often stated in terms of the triad CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability), listed in that order of criticality. Additionally, non-repudiation and other factors are considered as well but CIA is the baseline. In IACS the emphasis changes because the systems are concerned with making things happen rather than protecting intellectual property.

CIA

IT Objectives

IACS Objectives

C

Confidentiality is the priority for IT as it is protecting information that is private to an individual or organisation either of which has entrusted it to the system. The responsibility for protecting this information is enforced through GDPR.

Confidentiality is generally unimportant to IACS. There may be proprietary information involved but largely data is in the form of control signals that are created and then consumed. Safety is the prime directive.

I

Integrity is important to IT as it is either storing or processing information and needs the confidence of its users that it can replay the information without corruption.

Integrity is also important to IACS as the system must be sure that the command received is the same as the one that was sent as corruption could have physically disastrous consequences resulting in injury or loss of life.

A

Availability in IT is about enabling access to information for the right user at the right time. Time criticality is not usually a factor. Business processes generally include a fair amount of latitude.

Rebooting is the panacea for desktop support.

Availability in IACS is paramount as system failure could result in immediate and catastrophic consequences. A delay to allow for a reboot is unacceptable. If a valve is not opened or a brake applied at the right time then, as with integrity, it could be catastrophic. Time-criticality is also much more important especially where ‘real-time’ systems are involved.

N-R

Non-repudiation is probably equally important in IT as IACS. Where in IT it is important to know the source of information, so it is in IACS, and in both cases the source could easily be a user or a system component.

Safety does not feature in 27001, yet in IACS it is even more important than either confidentiality, availability or integrity. In a cyber-physical environment the consequences of a system failure could result in loss of life or limb, which is why safety standards are part of industrial culture whereas security is not.

However, as Humphreys (2016) states, the ISO 27000 range of standards provides well-tried and well-tested processes that are wellestablished in over 100 countries. The first issue of BS ISO/IEC 27001 was in 2005 with the subtitle BS 7799-2:2005 in recognition of its development from that British Standard. As the guidance in BSI (2015) describes, 27001 was completely restructured in 2013 with changes that included alignment with BS ISO 31000:2009 for risk management and to strengthen management involvement in leadership and review. As BSI (2013) 27001 itself states, the standard defines the requirements for an Information Security Management System (ISMS) with the objective of preserving the triad of Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability. The ISMS is intended to be tailored to the organisation; the standard is generic and intended to apply to all types of organisation irrespective of their size or nature.

As an alternative, the emerging set of standards under the 62433 heading illustrated in Fig. 3.8 below doesn’t appear to offer such a stable platform.

A large part of the standard set is still unpublished and, oddly, although BSI has issued 62443-2-1 as a BS EN standard at the time of writing it has not done the same with 62443-1-1, which includes the terminology, concepts and models that underpin the rest of the set. There seems also to be some recognition from the authors of 62443-2-1 that it should have been more closely aligned to 27001 as it includes the note “The revision of this international standard will be initiated shortly after this standard is published. The next revision will be aligned more closely with ISO/IEC 27001, which addresses many of the same issues but without consideration of the specialized requirements for continuous operation and safety that are common in the industrial automation and control systems environment” (BSI, 2010) 62443-2-1. It is unfortunate that the statement was made such a long time ago especially as 62443-2-1 cross references the 2005 version of 27001.

Fig. 3.8.The 62443 series of standards.

Those observations aside, 62443 is making some headway towards establishing itself, particularly in industries where safety is the ‘prime directive’ and where the IEC version of the standard is placed alongside IEC 61508 and IEC 61511 which address functional safety. Sieber and Hildenbrandt (2016) note that “the IEC 61511 (safety) and IEC 62443 (security) standards coincide on the demand for independent layers of protection”. EN 50129 is the railway specific standard that includes IEC 61508 general requirements and so when IEC 61508 is referenced it can be assumed that for railways EN 50129 applies.

The diagram shown in Fig. 3.9 below shows the relationship between the safety standards and the published 62443 standards:

Note that 62443-4-1 and 2 were both published in 2018 in February and August respectively and that although 62443-4-1 has been adopted by BSI, 62443-4-2 has yet to be.

62443-2-1 defines the requirements for a Cyber Security Management System (CSMS) and although it has used a different term, in its first paragraph, BSI (2010) 62443-2-1 refers to the output of 27001 as a CSMS. The 62443 CSMS however, reverses the information security triad and precedes it with safety, to become Safety, Availability, Integrity and Confidentiality, in recognition of the HSE implications of cyber security in an industrial environment. In the same way as 27001, it requires the implementation of risk management and review processes that support the CSMS lifecycle.

The fundamental differences in approach between 27001 and 62443 become more apparent in 62443-3-3 (although some of the content in this part of the standard is destined for inclusion in 62443-1-1 as the standard develops) which describes the use of security vectors, a term credited to Gilsinn and Schierholz (2010). A parallel is drawn between SLs (Security Levels) and SILs (Safety Integrity Levels), the latter being the measure applied in 61508, and supporting standards, which include 61511.

Fig 3.9.Associated safety and security standards.

SLs are determined during the 62443 risk assessment process; as part of the network segregation controls, the IACS network is divided into zones, each zone grouping system components that require the same level of protection. An SL-T (Target Security Level) is assigned to the zone according to the level of protection required, i.e.

•SL 0: No specific requirements or security protection necessary

•SL 1: Protection against casual or coincidental violation

•SL 2: Protection against intentional violation using simple means with low resources, generic skills and low motivation

•SL 3: Protection against intentional violation using sophisticated means with moderate resources, IACS-specific skills and moderate motivation

•SL 4: Protection against intentional violation using sophisticated means with extended resources, IACS-specific skills and high motivation

Each system component is then assessed against security requirements defined in the standard to assess its SL-C (Security Level Capability). If the SL-C is greater than or equal to the zone’s SL-T then no further controls are required, but if it is of a lower value then either the residual risk must be formally accepted or further controls are required. It is likely that there will be a mix of SL-Cs for the systems in any particular zone, in which case it is the lower value SL-Cs that must be addressed to achieve the SL-T.

For verification, the system can be inspected, audited or otherwise security tested and an SL-A (Actual Service Level) determined by the inspector. Risks are managed using these three values: ST-T, SL-C and SL-A.

62443-2-1 intends that SLs will ultimately provide a quantitative approach to addressing security for a system or a component part of it. This is presumably a long-term aspiration, not to be realised until more data becomes available through wider adoption of the standard. It is also intended to deliver a repeatable model and be applicable to both devices and countermeasures.

The safety risk analysis process defined by 50129 is concerned with safety hazards and how often they occur rather than security threats. It explores the consequence of any failure in terms of accidents, near-misses or ‘safe failures’ and whether the outcome is acceptable in safety terms. It uses SILs as “a means of matching the qualitative approaches (to avoid systematic failures) with the quantitative approach (to control random failures), as it is not feasible to quantify systematic failures” ((BSI, 2003) 50129). Systematic failures are those introduced by human error at some point during the system lifecycle, and are managed by process, e.g. quality management. Random failures result from the reliability of hardware components, which can be calculated from known failure rates and expressed as a THR (Tolerable Hazard Rate). The safety level requirement expressed by the SIL is a combination of process and an acceptable THR.

Adopting the use of SLs and assuming similarity to SILs and SLs could be misleading in that the two measures are somewhat dissimilar. As Braband (2016) advocates, the probabilistic approach applied to SILs does not really apply to SLs and IT security as it is not possible to rely on statistical data or experience as the threat landscape can change immediately and without warning.

The similarities and the differences between safety and security risk assessment are explored in some depth by Braband and Schäbe (2016) who assert that the risk assessment processes for safety and security are very similar and that it would be logical to apply the same process for each. The article goes on to identify that safety risk assessments defined by international safety standards are based on ‘probability’ whereas security risk assessments are based on ‘likelihood’. ISO (2009) defines these two different words respectively as “a measure of the chance of occurrence expressed as a number between 0 and one, where 0 is impossibility and one is absolute certainty” and “the chance of an event happening”. Safety standards are based on the concept that there is a probability that a dangerous failure will occur at some point in time and that the chance of it happening can be measured. The failures could be systematic or random; the occurrence of random failures can be calculated and for systematic failures there is a commonly agreed upon set of countermeasures that is generally accepted across the industry. Likelihood is far less precise and relies far more on subjective opinion. The reason that safety can deliver more objectivity is that the safety environment is slow to change and much can be learned from past experience. Security is far more volatile and can change from day to day. This can frequently be observed in information technology as new vulnerabilities emerge and the threat landscape changes. A good example of the latter can be observed on the NCSC’s Alerts and Advisory web pages (NCSC, 2018b):

State actors are likely to be the most capable and resourceful attackers, which could raise the SL-T requirement of any potential target to SL 4 to give it any possible chance of being able to withstand an attack.

Kriaa et al. (2015) take a similar stance to Braband and Schäbe, recognising that safety hazards are relatively stable over time and feedback from analysts on previous accidents is reliable, whilst security attributes are less predictable. This situation makes it more difficult for security analysts to assess and particularly, quantify, potential scenarios. It is observed that the use of quantitative approaches is more widely adopted in the field of safety but is not so readily accepted within security disciplines.

Nevertheless, the development of the 62443 series continues and 2018 has seen the publication of two more standards: 62443-4-1 in February and 62443-4-2 in August, both addressing supply chain factors. Figure 3.10 shows their relationship with the rest of the set.

62443-4-2 is a particularly helpful step forward as it defines how product suppliers in the IACS supply chain can achieve an SL-C for a system component. Where there is confidence that a claimed SL-C has been verified, e.g. by certification, this supports the system integrators and operators in their overall risk assessment and mitigation. Even though 62443-4-2 was only published towards the end of Q3 in 2018, there is already evidence that suppliers are recognising compliance with the standard as a valuable marketing tool. In a white paper published by a major supplier of IACS (including railway) network switches, Chen (2018) announced firmware upgrades to make their equipment compliant to the 62443-4-2 standard “to ensure the integrity of data and the network from known security leaks and unknown attacks”.

Fig 3.10.62443 for product suppliers (BSI, 2018) 62443-4-1.

3.3.Critical Infrastructure

As Digital Trains are within the scope of NIS, compliance is obviously a requirement. In its first year of operation it is clear that Competent Authorities (CAs) are setting the bar fairly low in order to allow industry to become compliant without undue pressure. NIS is only interested in systems that support or deliver critical services; it does not address scenarios where organisations can suffer other impacts such as financial loss, or loss of reputation. The current criteria for requiring a cyber security incident to be reported to NCSC are for a significant proportion of a TOC’s services being cancelled. This makes it clear that NIS is focused on the impact on the country rather than the TOC. TOCs that only address NIS compliance and do not apply good cyber security practice to all of their services are only addressing part of the cyber security problem.

In its guidance on how to comply with the directive, NCSC offers a number of guidance sources. The 27000 and 62443 series of standards are well represented in these sources but it is interesting to note that in some cases NCSC offers guidance from its own website instead even when the standards clearly cover that topic. Risk management, for instance, is covered in depth in 27001, 27005 and 62443-2-1 but NCSC prefers to offer more general guidance of its own. This is possibly because the systems that support critical services are both corporate and operational, and although 62443 recommends that its requirements apply to the whole business, in many cases it will be used to complement an existing 27001 ISMS and organisations are unlikely to re-work their existing processes when they are connecting control systems to their corporate ones. Until 62443 is updated to achieve its stated aspiration to be more closely aligned to 27001 there will be gaps between the standards that need to be dealt with in other ways, either by filling the gaps or securing the border between the two environments. This is illustrated in Fig. 3.11 above which is a consolidated view of the references NCSC provides.

*including 27019

Fig 3.11.Standards referenced in NIS guidance (NCSC, 2018a).

3.4.Conclusion

Fraga-Lamas et al. (2017) state, “Rail operators have to comply with a set of international industry and government standards on the topic of security (e.g., ISO 27001, NIST SP800-53, ISA/IEC 62443 or APTA)”. This is simply not true; although the article is otherwise generally a well-informed one and differentiates between Train Control Systems and Train Management Systems, there is certainly no such requirement on TOCs. In its overview, the article also lists cyber security as a requirement only for Train Control Systems, although why it takes that position is unclear. Cyber security must apply to the complete Digital Train both to protect all operational systems and to minimise attack vectors for safety-related systems.

In another seemingly well-informed article Valdivia et al. (2018) correctly state that neither 61508 or 50129 safety standards cover security issues. They go on to claim that the standards mention intentional malicious activity and propose the use of 62443 to deal with this, which is not strictly true; only 61508-1 makes any such recommendation, whereas the railway standard, 50129, which can be used in isolation from 61508, does not. One might expect both of the above claims to be correct but this does not make them so. It does however highlight the safety standards’ presumption that safety incidents are the result of accidents and security ones are malicious whereas the logical view is that “the only difference between a malicious attack and an accident is the motivation of those involved” (Weiss, 2011).

Although 50129 doesn’t consider security, it isn’t ignored by the safety community altogether. The NRSP (National Rail Safety Plan) in its Section 14 widens the scope to include risk to assets, reputation, operation as well as putting lives at risk. But the NRSP is only concerned with safety-critical systems, it is not concerned with operational or business systems that also exist on trains.

What is clear is that safety is paramount on the railway, where safety processes are embedded in the culture. Cyber security represents a safety hazard but this is largely unrecognised by the safety standards. It is probably true to say that a system cannot be safe unless it is secure but it can be secure without being safe, but that doesn’t help either discipline very much. However, 62443 takes safety into account whereas 27001 doesn’t.

62443 approaches security with a similar process to 61508 but the skill set is different and the results aren’t equivalent. There are similarities in the process though which could be used to create synergies and exploited to develop opportunities to improve security acceptance.

62443 would appear to be the better fit for the industrial parts of rail but business systems are in many cases already 27001 compliant. However, not many are certified. Given the current demands on security resources it would not be sensible to rework the existing ISMS into a CSMS. 62443 states the intention to align more closely with 27001 in future versions so the suggested approach is to take it at its word and implement the CSMS as an extension to the ISMS, supplementing the ISMS with any additional policies that are required, but following the 62443-2-1 approach for its delivery. This would enable the engineering functions to gain the benefit of supply chain compliance, with standards such as 62443-4-2.

The 27001 and 62443 approaches are not that dissimilar. For instance, both recommend network segregation as a fundamental control. The difference is that 27001 offers it as a recommendation but 62443 provides a step by step approach for delivery, with a process that engineers will recognise.

A key part of any solution will be to recognise that many components in an IACS have no inbuilt security whatsoever and so if there is a security requirement it will need to be applied as a supplementary control. Hardening of network zones and conduits is likely to be a key feature. Hardening the complete network will have an impact on cost and so the identification of 62443 SLs will inform the prioritisation of that process.

Chapter 4

An Approach to Identify Risk-Based Human Behaviour Profiling Within an Office Environment

Jon Cosson*, Haider M. al-Khateeb† and Stephen Sampana‡

*JM FINN, London, UK
jon.cosson@jmfinn.com

†University of Wolverhampton, UK
H.Al-Khateeb@wlv.ac.uk

‡Refinitiv (previously Thomson Reuters)
steve.sampana@refinitiv.com

ABSTRACT

Documented cases involving Edward Snowden (Greenwald et al., 2018) and Chelsea Manning (Lewis, 2018) highlight the need for an effective employee risk mitigation process.

Mitigation has generally focused on system and network access controls to determine the risk level and where possible neutralise the threat. However, these controls rely on access to a computer network before behaviour analysis can determine the threat potential.

Determining the threat posed by individuals is a challenging concept as human behaviour can be unpredictable as there may be an exponential number of factors that can influence movement patterns. There are also environmental considerations that may have a direct impact on the movement of an individual.

To address this threat, an algorithm has been developed that attempts to identify anomalous human behaviour patterns within a controlled physical environment. The algorithm incorporates multi-dimensional factors such as office entry points, trajectories, time analysis and the physical attributes of the environment. The algorithm also incorporates categorical (qualitative) and continuous (quantitative) attributes within the detection process.

The algorithm was embedded within a threat detection application that was designed to be independent of the monitoring solution providing the source data. It achieved this through a data restructure process to ensure it met the criteria of the anomaly detection process.

The algorithm was evaluated within a real-life scenario, leveraging data from a Bluetooth proximity human monitoring solution installed within a financial services institution located within the City of London. The data tracked the movement patterns of 50 contractors working for the target organisation. This then fed into the algorithm to determine the potential threat posed by trusted contract employees operating within a multi-storey, open plan office building.

Keywords: darktrace, human behaviour, risk, insider threat

4.1.Background

In recent years the computer security industry has seen a rapid growth in network-based behaviour systems. Technologies such as Dark Trace Enterprise (Darktrace.com, 2018) and NUIX Adaptive Security (Nuix.com, 2018) have made significant strides in incorporating behaviour patterns into their threat detection matrix. Vendors have identified weaknesses in traditional intrusion detection design, incorporating machine learning techniques and advanced algorithms to enhance the ability to determine subtle variations in usage patterns.

Advanced behaviour analysis is now used in a plethora of security products, some providing out-of-the-box solutions that claim to detect the slightest nuances in usage patterns that can determine a threat to an organisation. As an example, Dark Trace Enterprise uses world-leading machine learning and Artificial Intelligence (AI) to detect, classify and visualise cyber-threats that evade other defences from within the enterprise (Darktrace.com, 2018). These solutions all rely on a steady stream of data extracted from network traffic, system logs or end-point applications. Using the same behavioural principles, the researcher aims to analyse data based on human movement patterns within a controlled business environment and to determine if the target represents a risk to the business.

In its simplest form the process of analysing human movement has similar attributes to behaviour-based network threat detection. They both process data through an algorithm, attempting to identify anomalies and ultimately reduce risk. The algorithm could therefore be considered the key component when constructing a threat detection model. This paper will detail the methodology undertaken to construct an algorithm based on theoretical research and live data collected through a proximity location system deployed at the target organisation.

4.1.1.The target organisation

For the purposes of this research paper, the target organisation will be referred to as Dakota.

Dakota is a UK-based investment management company employing 500 staff operating from 5 UK offices. Dakota’s primary business focus is high net worth individuals, and it offers a bespoke service to meet its clients’ financial requirements.

Dakota’s head office is located within the City of London where 400 London staff occupy 5 floors of a low-rise modern office building.

Like many organisations operating within the highly regulated UK financial services sector, Dakota are risk-averse. This posture has been reinforced by the impending Senior Management Regime (SMR), which comes into force in 2019 (FCA, 2018).

Dakota have identified insider threat, specifically that posed by 3rd party contractors, as a significant risk to the business. All Dakota staff are screened before they are employed by the organisation. The screening process can take a month to complete and includes rigorous background checks, including a criminal records search. Dakota do not own their offices, they lease from a corporate landlord who employs a management agency to facilitate and maintain the building. Dakota must therefore rely on numerous 3rd party contractors working predominantly under the control of the managing agents to maintain the nine-storey office building they share with four other corporate tenants.

As their 3rd party contractors predominantly fall under the direct control of the building management company, Dakota have little control over the screening process and employment of the contractors employed to maintain the building. Dakota senior management have identified this as a risk to the business, which will require additional mitigation controls.

Due to the nature of the role, external contractors may require access to sensitive areas of the business. These occurrences may be unsupervised and outside of normal operational hours.

Regulation dictates that financial institutions within the UK must ensure its permanent and fixed-term contract staff undergo pre-screening prior to employment (fca.org.uk, 2017).

Contractors employed through 3rd parties may not be subject to the same rigorous screening regime that is enforced throughout Dakota. Organisations may have little choice but to rely on the integrity and due diligence of an external party.

Whilst 3rd party agreements can arguably address some of the risk, the quality of external contract staff may never be fully verified especially given the highly sensitive, unmonitored access that may be required by some roles.

4.2.Security Architecture

As Dakota’s London headquarters is located within a shared office complex, a communal entrance is in place. The reception is staffed continuously by security guards employed by the managing agents and forms the first layer of defence at the building perimeter.

All visitors are required to sign a register before being issued with a pass, which must be displayed at all times. Visitors may only access Dakota’s private reception area on the 1st floor, as a buildingwide access control solution prevents non-authorised individuals accessing other floors occupied by Dakota.

The building access control solution used by tenants is based on Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) technology. RFID is classified as a wireless identification and data capture technology (Barjis et al., 2010). Dakota’s access control system is deliberately separate from the building’s solution, as this provides an additional layer of control and assurance. To ensure seamless conformity between the landlord’s and Dakota’s access control solutions, a technology standard was agreed on to ensure a single access pass could be programmed to operate between areas controlled by the landlord and those controlled by Dakota.

An access control pass is only assigned to permanent staff, or contractors requiring access to floors other than the Dakota reception area. Whilst access control can arguably provide some security assurance through the prevention of unauthorised individuals entering private areas where there are physical controls such as a door, the technology could be deemed weak if deployed as the sole line of defence against unauthorised physical access.

Dakota addressed the perceived limitations of the RFID technology by implementing a proximity-based monitoring solution. The proximity solution is based on Bluetooth technology and works in parallel with the RFID access control system, adding advanced real-time monitoring features that can be analysed by security staff. The proximity system forms an integral part of Dakota’s access control solution, combining a door entry system that incorporates elevator access and Closed-Circuit Television (CCTV).

Dakota was chosen for the experiment because the researcher had full access to the security technology and the data. The organisation was also considered a typical example of an open plan modern office environment.

4.2.1.Proximity technology

There is currently a broad range of access control solutions on the market, providing a wealth of security features and functionality. Many of these solutions rely on the physical attributes of a building such as internal partitioned walls to separate operational units or specific areas of a business. Whilst it could be argued that these traditional access control systems are able to secure physically separated areas, they still rely on human observation to prevent tailgating and unauthorised access.

To mitigate the risk of tailgating, organisations can consider deploying a proximity monitoring solution that incorporates access control functionality whilst providing location-specific visibility. Dakota decided to implement a proximity monitoring solution based on Bluetooth technology (Bluetooth.com, 2018), which leveraged a series of beacons, strategically deployed throughout the building. Each Bluetooth beacon is powered and linked through a structured Power over Ethernet (PoE) network. The beacons communicate with, and are controlled by, a virtualised communications server hosted locally.

Figure 4.1 depicts how the proximity solution can be deployed within a typical working environment. Whilst access control can determine who has access to a specific room, it has inherent weaknesses within an open plan environment.

Open plan environments have become very popular in recent history as many organisations believe an open plan office encourages openness and enhanced productivity (Joseph, 2018).

This can be challenging for security personnel and traditional access control solutions that rely on physical separation to enforce security controls.

If proximity zoning technologies are incorporated, it is possible to visually determine the location of staff within an open plan environment and potentially alert security personnel to unauthorised access. The ability to identify and locate employees within a controlled environment can prove useful for health & safety purposes. However, it is reasonable to assume such data could be superfluous if the target has legitimate operational reasons to be at that location.

Fig. 4.1.Typical real-time location system.

Simply identifying an individual within an area at a specific time may not provide sufficient data to prove the target is acting suspiciously, or poses a threat to the business. The deployment strategy of the Bluetooth beacons can be considered important and is dependent upon the physical attributes of the office design. Beacon deployment should be carefully planned and installed at strategic areas of the office or where the radio frequency dictates (Zonith, 2018). The open plan characteristics of Dakota’s London headquarters are typical of the financial sector. To accommodate this design the beacons are configured to facilitate virtual zoning within an open office space.

Figure 4.2 depicts Dakota’s beacon deployment on one of the floors within their London office. The beacons are located at strategic locations based on the physical attributes of the floor space and the criticality of the desks. It is important to note the receiving variance of each beacon can be independently controlled. This is considered important when designing specific zones, particularly if the zone is deemed sensitive and requires precise detection.

Fig. 4.2.Dakota 3rd floor beacon locations.

The power and sensitivity of each beacon is controlled through the communications server. This allows authorised staff to manipulate the monitoring environment to meet the needs of the security personnel or if the layout of the office changes.

4.2.2.Data source

The research data has been sourced directly through Dakota’s proximity solution and stored within a proprietary database that is located on the same server as the application software that controls the proximity security system.

It is evident that this research project is critically dependant on the source and accuracy of the data. Care has been taken to ensure that the data source accurately reflects the movement of staff and that the security personnel had adopted sufficient procedures to ensure the correct pass was issued to the contractors.

Table 4.1.Raw data from proximity solution.

source: Dakota

Once the pass has been issued and activated, human movement data is transmitted from the security pass into the Bluetooth beacons. The data is then sent via the ethernet structured cabling into the security database, which forms an integral part of the control server.

The raw data stream supplied by the Bluetooth proximity solution provides limited information. Whilst this is sufficient to monitor the position of an individual, it was not considered to contain enough detail to construct an effective mechanism to detect movement patterns.

The database contains data streams that are sent by each Bluetooth pass as it is initially detected within each zone. Table 4.1 depicts each field within a typical data stream.

Each cell plays a pivotal role when determining the pattern of movement and the time spent within each specified zone. There is no personal data transmitted within the data streams; the ‘User ID’ field determines which Bluetooth pass is being used.

The fields within the stream are constructed as follows:

REC ID: Contains a specific record identification value. This is important as it identifies each data stream, which allows the time spent within each zone to be calculated

Date: Date the signal is received.

Time Stamp: Time the signal is received.

User ID: Identifies the unique identifier of the Bluetooth ID badge holder. This is cross-referenced in the security database to identify the individual.

Entry/Exit Flag: As the Bluetooth badge is identified by a specific beacon a ‘1’ is applied to the data field. Once the Bluetooth badge leaves the zone covered by the beacon a ‘0’ (zero) identifier is applied.

Enter ID: To determine the time spent within a zone the application must determine an entry point for reference. For example, using the data within Table 4.2, ‘Record ID 1’ refers to the entry point and ‘Record ID 2’ refers to the exit point. The ‘Enter ID’ field (within ‘Record ID 2’) must therefore reference the entry point which was identified in ‘Record ID 1’.

Zone: This field depicts the specific zone the Bluetooth ID card has connected with.

Timing: The Timing field displays the time spent within each zone. A calculation is made between the ‘Time Stamp’, the ‘Entry/Exit’ flag and the ‘Enter ID’ fields.

Table 4.2.Proximity data stream.

As the Bluetooth security card passes through each zone, a new data stream is created. This will provide the digital footprint of the individual as they move through the controlled environment.

Along with the recorded data stream, a live depiction of the current location of the individual is displayed through a security monitoring application that is used by security staff. This can provide valuable real-time data that can be used by trained security professionals to potentially determine a threat to the business or a potential health and safety issue.

This chapter has focused on the physical security architecture and the data stream as it is evident that these attributes are an important factor when designing a suitable and effective threat detection model. This data will be used when constructing the algorithm that will form the nucleus of the research project.

4.2.3.Design approach

Whilst there has been a significant amount of research pertaining to video and network surveillance, there appears to be limited work within the public domain in reference to threat detection through proximity sensors.

Determining human movement within an area can present specific challenges and the outcome depends on the methods used to monitor movement patterns. Fong et al. (2007) argue that the detection of suspicious patterns in physical environments, using multiple reference points to detect human movement patterns, can provide an increased threat detection method within a business environment.

It is evident that the physical environment can play a pivotal role when determining movement patterns. As an example, an area with natural barriers such as an office space with multiple meeting rooms, or a doctor’s practice with private consultancy surgeries, can provide reference points and natural transient areas.

Conventional access control and monitoring systems can leverage the design of a building, incorporating monitoring points at key access areas. Fong et al. (2007) define a logical security model based on an access-controlled door-entry system, which can log entry and exit metrics to determine movement patterns.

Whilst it can be argued that this type of design is able to provide movement detection metrics through control points, it does not address the inherent risk of tailgating. There can also be an apparent lack of controls attributed to a one-dimensional access control solution, which can be easily circumvented, intentionally or not.

A key aspect of any anomaly detection technique is the nature of the input data. Input is generally a collection of data instances (also referred to as object, record, point, vector, pattern, event, case, sample, observation, or entity) (see Tan et al., 2005).

Assuming movement is monitored through access control logs, determining anomalies based on entry and exit times may prove challenging. Fong et al. (2007) describe ‘known penetration scenarios’, which are essentially sequences of actions that are able to identify human movement as it shifts from a normal to a compromised state. By detailing an anomaly detection model, one can detect threats based on the data mined from a generic access control database.

One of the primary objectives of the research project is to identify anomalous behaviour patterns using data derived from a generic data source. However, as the target organisation (Dakota) operates an open plan environment, the technology adopted for the research project will be based on proximity sensors.

The researcher has taken a holistic approach to anomaly detection, creating an algorithm that is adaptive by design. This decision is based on the apparent lack of controls through a one-dimensional access control solution.

As an example, processing access control data requires a physical device, with sensors on each side of the door to detect entry into and exit from the controlled zone. This method has an intrinsic risk of tailgating as a door opened by one member of staff can allow access to others without the need for those others to be authenticated. As staff enter a door in groups only one card is registered on the access log, which can distort the data when those individuals leave the controlled zones using their access cards.

Leveraging data derived from the location tracking technology that is seamless with respect to the individual being monitored can be considered important, particularly in an open space environment that does not have access-controlled entry/exit points.

The data is therefore key to the algorithm and its attributes should be understood before the security model is constructed. Data attributes can be described as binary, categorical (qualitative), or continuous (quantitative). Each data instance might consist of only one attribute (univariate) or multiple attributes (multivariate). In the case of multivariate data instances, all attributes might be of the same type or might be a mixture of different data types (see Chandola et al., 2009).

The nature of the data attributes determines the anomalous detection method applied. Input data can also be categorized based on the relationship present among data instances (see Tan et al., 2005). The algorithm will require multiple data instances measuring time, duration and date, etc. These can be described as continuous and will be associated with the individual and the location (categorical).

The attributes used within the algorithm are depicted in Fig. 4.3.

Murenin et al. (2017) explore human movement and interaction patterns between employees within an office environment. This may provide a valuable insight when determining natural human movement patterns within an office environment. Murenin et al. (2017) extracted data from various entry points within a typical office building and analysed access control logs within controlled zones. Leveraging employee data, including job function and sector location, and cross-referencing this against the specific physical characteristics of the building, a threat model was created.

Whilst this research focuses on anomalous employee behaviour within an office building using proximity monitoring data, there are other threat detection solutions, based on a variety of different technologies, that may also be considered.

4.2.4.Insider threat

An insider can be described as a person who possesses some combination of knowledge and access that distinguishes his or her relationship within the organisation from that of the people that are outside (see Gelles, 2016). One of the core objectives of this research paper is to recognise and address the risk that an insider poses to an organisation. The Centre for the Protection of National Infrastructure (CPNI) describes an insider as a person who exploits, or has the intention to exploit, their legitimate access to an organisation’s assets for unauthorised purposes (cpni.gov.uk, 2018), see Appendix D.

Fig. 4.3.Algorithm attributes.

Employee disgruntlement has been identified as a recurring factor in insider compromises, particularly in cases of insider IT sabotage. An insider’s disgruntlement can be caused by a single event or multiple factors, these can include:

•inadequate salary increases or derisory bonuses

•company resource restrictions

•diminished responsibilities

•perception of unfair working practises

•co-worker bullying or intimidation

These factors can play a vital role when determining if a trusted worker becomes a threat to an organisation (resources.sei.cmu.edu, 2018).

4.3.Behaviour Traits

Behaviour traits can be considered an important factor when determining the potential threat of an insider and can provide valuable insight when designing a security model. It is important to establish what constitutes normal behaviour so a baseline can be constructed and used to identify suspicious activities.

Baseline construction would involve active monitoring of normal operational activity. This needs to be carefully carried out to ensure the accuracy of the data. It may not be sufficient to only deploy the proximity solution and analyse the movement data before one builds a robust baseline; it is possible that this approach may not be thorough enough. The researcher therefore decided to actively monitor staff, covertly, to ensure there was no contamination of the results.

This was achieved through a passive time and motion process for each job role. Over a period of two months (December 2017–Jan 2018), a clear picture of the working practises was constructed to reinforce the data being collected by the proximity monitoring solution.

Understanding and identifying adverse behaviour traits using human movement patterns can be considered difficult as one is dealing with a quantitative process. Building in qualitative elements may be subjective as the emotive state of the target may not be quantifiable.

The research here closely monitored each of the targets, identifying common behaviour patterns and routines.

This included such criteria as:

•How they entered the floor

Elevator or stairs

•If elevator, which entry point

Left or right

•Did they have a regular pattern

•Did they take a toilet break

What route did they take

How long did they spend in the toilet

•Did they take a tea or coffee break

What route did they take

How long did they stay in the break area

•Did they spend an unusual amount of time in any particular area or desk group

•Were there any unusual events that should be considered when building the baseline

The data was cross-referenced against the data collected by the proximity monitoring solution to ensure accuracy. The findings were conclusive. The proximity monitoring solution data matched the observation data exactly, with no exceptions.

The data did not produce any surprise results except for the amount of time the contractor spent in some areas. This data is considered important as it needs to be incorporated into the algorithm.

Human interaction with staff was also observed as this may impact the movement patterns and the time spent within each area.

Through the exploration of the potential employee interaction patterns, it is possible to produce heat maps that may identify potential human gathering points or hotspots. This can provide valuable data when determining deviations in movement patterns that may denote anomalous behaviour (see Murenin et al., 2017).

4.4.Threat Detection Methodology

Employees can have an in-depth operational knowledge of an organisation, how it functions and its inherent weaknesses. Whilst this can be considered an asset, if those employees have malicious intentions they can represent a significant risk to the business.

Since the collapse of Enron (royce.house.gov, 2018) and post the 2008 financial crisis, organisations have been under renewed scrutiny and are increasingly becoming risk-focussed. Businesses now face heavy penalties if they fail to address the threat of a data breach. A Gartner report (gartner.com, 2018) suggests organisations are making significant capital investments to mitigate the likelihood of a successful cyberattack, including new technologies designed to identify spurious or unusual network or system activity.

Whilst it could be argued that new security solutions have significantly reduced the risk of a technically-based attack, the threat of a data breach instigated by an insider with malicious intent represents an unacceptable level of risk to many businesses.

The threat of a data breach was Dakota’s primary business driver when implementing an enhanced proximity monitoring solution. Senior management believed the level of risk relating to the insider threat was unacceptable and agreed to implement an enhanced security solution to reduce the risk.

Due to data protection and privacy laws, specifically the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) that was enforced on the 25th May 2018, organisations wishing to monitor staff movement must carefully consider the legalities relating to staff monitoring (see regulation and privacy laws) (ico.org, 2018).

Dakota decided that the highest risk relating to the insider threat came from 3rd party contractors and therefore decided to address this specific area. This is contrary to the findings of the Centre for the Protection of National Infrastructure (CPNI) (2013) paper ‘Insider Data Collection Study’ that revealed the majority of malicious insider activity was undertaken by permanent staff (88%), with only 7% of cases involving contractors, and 5% involving temporary staff (cpni.gov.uk, 2018), see Appendix D.

4.4.1.Roles and relationships

The core objective of this research paper is the creation of a robust threat detection model that will incorporate an effective algorithm that could be applied directly to the movement of contract staff within a controlled business environment.

Prior to the construction of the security model, the researcher needed to identify and analyse the targets and their function.

To facilitate the maintenance of a modern building, numerous external specialist personnel are required. These individuals may require constant access to an organisation’s office space and dependent on the role, are potentially unsupervised.

Within the target organisation the roles have been identified as follows:

•8 × cleaning staff

•4 × electricians

•4 × air conditioning maintenance engineers

•6 × catering staff

•8 × building maintenance staff

•4 × structured cabling specialists

•6 × outsourced IT staff (peripherals)

•4 × waste engineers

•2 × datacentre maintenance staff

•4 × security

Each of the 50 contractors will have specific and potentially unique characteristics that need to be analysed and incorporated into the threat detection model.

These roles may be focused around a singular function or task; however, some roles may be multi-functional, which presents a complex challenge when designing an effective algorithm to detect a threat to the organisation.

The researcher observed that simply understanding each job function was insufficient when constructing a threat model. The building and specific office characteristics are unique to the organisation and this may have a significant impact on the working practices of the contract staff.

As an example, air conditioning engineers would require access to all levels of the building; however, the air conditioning fans and coils are only contained within specific zones in the office. Therefore, it would be acceptable if an air conditioning maintenance engineer was detected for a period of time within that specific zone. However, an additional layer of complexity is introduced as the monitoring of the ambient temperature of the office may require access to other zones within the office environment.

Other considerations must be incorporated into the model, such as the location of toilets and beverage areas that have the potential to become ‘hot-zones’ where staff congregate. The researcher observed that the natural human movement of staff will have an impact on roles within an organisation. These form part of the normal human interactions and therefore must be understood and incorporated into the model to limit false positives (see the section on human interaction patterns).

4.4.2.Zoning

To ensure the algorithm was able to effectively detect potential threats to the organisation, the proximity data needed to be crossreferenced to specific locations within the office. It was therefore considered important to understand the key business areas and the physical attributes of the building position. This data could be used to position the Bluetooth beacons at optimal locations.

The researcher needed to work with Dakota to understand the key operational areas of the business and specific infrastructure elements that, if compromised, posed a specific threat to the organisation.

4.4.3.Infrastructure features

Working with Dakota’s Facilities Management team, the researcher was able to identify the building’s critical infrastructure. This included structured cabling wiring closets, electrical cupboards with fuse arrays, air conditioning control units and CCTV locations.

4.4.4.Business areas

Along with the critical infrastructure, key business locations were identified. Dakota based its teams and departments on specific desks. This policy was adopted to assist staff who could consequently locate a team’s resources in one area when they needed to access them. When the team or department was too large to be positioned on one group of desks, additional desk groups were assigned. This policy made it easier when identifying key locations within the office space.

As an example, Dakota are a financial organisation and employ a team of traders to purchase and sell stocks, shares and bonds from various global trading locations. It is therefore evident that these locations are important to the organisation and should be identified as a key business area.

4.4.5.Locating beacons and aligning with risk areas

Once the key infrastructure and business areas were identified the Bluetooth beacons could be located in the most effective location, and tuned accordingly.

A key requirement of the threat detection model is the ability to detect a threat based on the proximity, the time and the movement pattern of a contractor. To effectively build the algorithm that can detect potential threats, the researcher had to see the zoning process and the identification of critical areas associated with specific zones as an important element of the research project. Figure 4.4 depicts the critical areas within Dakota’s 3rd floor; these are outlined in red. The Dealing area beacon also encompasses the structured cabling wiring closet (although this room is separately secured via RFID access control and CCTV).

The other areas include the electrical riser cupboard, which controls the power to the entire floor, and the Compliance department. The Compliance department contains sensitive client and staff data, which the business has identified as a key area of risk.

A similar process of critical area identification has been undertaken by the researcher to ensure the movement profiling within the security model can prioritise selective areas of importance and assist when detecting anomalies. Table 4.3 details the key business departments, their locations and any specific security controls.

Fig. 4.4.Dakota proximity beacon deployment and critical areas.

Table 4.3.Business critical operational areas.

Understanding these critical areas is considered important, as is understanding the associated adjacent zones. Doing so can assist in the movement pattern analysis that can be used to determine a potential threat. This can be considered pertinent in an open plan office area, which has limited physical barriers.

The example depicted in Fig. 4.4 features a typical floor layout adopted by Dakota and highlights critical areas that represent the highest risk to the business.

4.4.6.Mapping roles

Once the physical attributes of a controlled office space were identified and the critical areas analysed, the researcher focused on the roles of the targets.

There are 50 contractors that are either directly or indirectly employed to service Dakota’s head office. Each is employed through various 3rd party contracts; each performs a specific function within the business and requires differing degrees of access to the building. Table 4.4 provides a detailed breakdown of each contractor role. This includes the floors where access is required, the zones within each floor and the standard operating hours for each specific role. Additional information relates to secondary zone data and whether the contractor will be supervised by security or a permanent member of Dakota staff.

As Dakota operates an open plan environment, contractors may stray from their assigned allocated zone. This needs to be incorporated within the algorithm to limit the chance of a false positive.

Table 4.4 also highlights high risk zones, which may contain sensitive information or key utilities, and identifies whether the contractor operates within a hotspot zone.

Hotspots are areas of the office where staff congregate, such as the water cooler or coffee machine. Murenin et al. (2017) explore the impact of interaction between employees within organisations and the importance of staff movement patterns when designing a security model. This is explored in more depth in the section on human interaction patterns.

Table 4.4.Dakota contractor roles, floors, zones & working practices.

4.4.7.Human interaction patterns

The spatiotemporal patterns of employees and the interactions between them can be considered important when designing a threat detection security model. To fully understand the significance of these patterns and their ultimate impact on the design of the algorithm, the researcher decided to monitor staff movement within the organisation and particularly the interaction between departments. Specific personnel who traverse teams and floors within the building were also identified as this could impact the natural movement pattern of staff.

Whilst the primary resource of this research paper is the data derived through the proximity monitoring solution, to ensure the data can be interpreted effectively it is considered important that the data derived from the natural movement patterns of permanent members of staff that are not under the scope of the proximity monitoring solution must be taken into consideration. Contractors may interact with permanent staff. This is human nature and does not necessarily indicate a threat to the business.

As a wealth management organisation, the relationship between investment management and investment administration staff is considered an important business characteristic.

Investment management and administration staff also regularly converse with ‘middle office’ departments such as HR, Finance and IT. This was also considered important when constructing the security model.

Through the analysis of the access control sensor logs (derived through each employee’s RFID pass) a picture of human movement patterns between departments located on separate floors was identified.

Murenin et al. (2017) have observed that using such data to analyse a set of moving points or trajectories could sufficiently increase the understanding of the existing work patterns.

Constructing behaviour patterns from trajectories could also make it possible to detect anomalies through the observed data set.

Whilst it can be argued that the data derived through the access control sensors is limited, it can provide a useful insight on how permanent staff exit the building and what floors they visit throughout the course of the day.

Access control sensor logs were analysed for all contractors and permanent members of staff and characterised as follows:

•Floor entry points

Elevator access

Primary stairwell access

Secondary stairwell access

•Alternative floor access

Access control sensors are only used when entering the office space located on each of the floors within the building. Therefore, there is no sensor data available when exiting any of the 5 floors Dakota occupies. This policy has been enforced to satisfy health and safety concerns.

Whilst the data appears limited, it can indicate movement patterns between floors and departments. It may also provide valuable entrance-derived data that could identify hotspots, or access points for tailgating.

Figure 4.5 depicts a typical floor layout at Dakota, identifying all the controlled access points into the office.

Using the data taken from these access points and cross-referencing them with job roles, the researcher is able to construct a heat map of popular entry points and to determine how staff interact between floors.

There are obvious limitations as the data will only depict basic movement between floors. This may not be granular enough to determine the specific team or department visited but could be incorporated into the algorithm as it will indicate potential hotspots that may impact the threat detection model.

4.4.8.Hotspots

Exploiting the data derived from the access control system, the researcher was able to extract some interesting results.

Fig. 4.5.Dakota access points.

The key findings of the sensor log analysis do provide some interesting statistics that can enhance the security model. Using the data analysed from the 3rd floor it is evident that the majority of staff used the elevator and access point B (to the right of the elevator shaft). This is irrelevant of the position of their desk and in relation to the nearest entry point.

Further analysis identified that staff were more likely to visit the toilets or the communal kitchenette area that contained a water cooler and hot beverages. Those staff using the stairwell also chose the access point nearest the toilets and the kitchen area. However, as this is the primary stairwell, the data is not so conclusive.

Figure 4.6 depicts the hotspot entrance areas observed by the access control sensor logs. This data has been used to determine a hotspot zone (3-7) that will be incorporated into the algorithm.

Fig. 4.6.Dakota hotspots and critical areas.

4.5.Anomaly Detection

Anomaly detection can refer to the problem of finding patterns in data that do not conform to expected behaviour (Chandola et al., 2009). Nonconforming patterns can be described as anomalies, peculiarities or exceptions. Anomaly detection is used in a variety of applications such as credit card & banking fraud, insurance claims and security surveillance.

The detection of an anomaly within a dataset has been studied as early as the 19th century (Edgeworth, 1887). This has led to numerous research studies carried out to analyse a variety of anomaly techniques that have been developed for specific applications.

Anomaly detection can be described as the translation of data into categories based on specific criteria. For example, spurious data travelling through a computer network could be considered an anomaly that has been caused by a malicious intruder, malware or a software bug. This event may subsequently trigger an alert or initiate a workflow dependent on the activity and how it is categorised. Anomalies in credit card transaction data could indicate credit card or identity theft (Aleskerov et al., 1997), or anomalous readings from a space craft sensor could signify a fault in some component of the space craft (Fujimaki et al., 2005).

4.5.1.Data noise
