Rousseeuw et al. (1987) and Teng et al. (1990) both describe the relevance of data noise when determining anomalies. Noise can be defined as a phenomenon in data that is of no interest and which becomes an impediment when analysing data. Noise removal is driven by the need to remove the unwanted objects before any data analysis is performed. Noise accommodation refers to immunising a statistical model estimation against anomalous observations (Huber, 1974).

Within Dakota, data noise can be described as crossover zones that contractors enter on their way to their destination. The intersection of zones could also be identified as data noise that should be eliminated from the detection algorithm. The data derived from the crossover area between two zones has been identified within the dataset. This can be observed as flickering between two zones over a prolonged period.

To eliminate the crossover effect and data retrieved when contractors are in transit between zones, a minimal time period has been incorporated into the security model. As an example, the researcher identified the time taken by contractors when walking between zones by analysing the time they entered and exited fields within the data stream. To improve accuracy the researcher also physically monitored human movement patterns within the Dakota environment to cross-reference the Bluetooth data with observation data (see the section on physical monitoring).

It was evident from the data retrieved from the proximity monitoring solution, in addition to the observation data, that a 10-second limit should be set within any zone to eliminate data noise.

4.5.2.Detecting anomalies

At an abstract level, an anomaly is defined as a pattern that does not conform to expected normal behaviour (Chandola et al., 2009). Therefore, in its basic form, anomaly detection can be described as the identification of normal behaviour, and, within a specific environment, observing any changes that are different from the normal pattern.

The anomaly identification process can be very challenging as there are many factors that need to be taken into consideration:

•Understanding normal behaviour and identifying the nuances of how humans integrate with others within a working environment.

•Determining the boundaries between normal and abnormal behaviour may not be an exact science. There are potentially an infinite number of contributing factors that may alter the perceived normal behaviour pattern.

•Individuals with malicious intentions can adapt and attempt to disguise their actions to look normal.

•As what is defined as normal behaviour will potentially evolve over time, continuous realignment will be required to prevent false positives.

•The definition of an anomaly may be different depending on the role and even the specific individual within an organisation.

•Noise within the data can alter the perception of the threat and trigger an alert. The environment will need to be explored and superfluous data ignored.

4.5.3.Classification

The primary purpose of this research paper is to construct a security model that incorporates an algorithm that will detect a potential threat through an anomaly detection process. An important aspect of the detection process is the classification of an anomaly once the anomaly is detected.

The research has classified the anomalies into the following groups, classes or sets.

4.5.4.Point-based anomalies

Based on data collected over a period of time, an individual whose movement patterns are considered anomalous in relation to the baseline data would represent an anomaly. Chandola et al. (2009) describe anomaly detection as the problem of finding patterns in data that do not conform to expected behaviour. They define the term anomaly as identifiable patterns in data that do not conform to a well-defined notion of normal within a twodimensional dataset.

This can be visualised in Fig. 4.7 which depicts a typical pointbased anomaly approach.

N1 and N2 represent the baseline data areas that have been identified as normal behaviour. T1, T2, T3 and T4 are classed as anomalies (potential threats) as they fall outside of the boundaries of the baseline areas denoted by N1 and N2.

Fig. 4.7.Point-based anomaly approach (source: Chandola et al. (2009)).

A simple example of a point-based anomaly could be a bank account, where N1 and N2 represent normal spending patterns. T1, T2, T3 and T4 represent abnormally high spending patterns, or spending outside of normal geographical locations.

Whilst this could be considered a simple example, it does demonstrate how pattern analysis can be used to detect spurious patterns and how it has real-life applications. The detection of anomalies in credit card transaction data could indicate credit card or identity theft (Aleskerov et al., 1997). The anomalous patterns within an MRI image may indicate the presence of malignant tumours (Spence et al., 2001).

4.5.5.Contextual-based anomalies

Contextual or conditional (Song et al., 2007) data is anomalous but only in a specific context. In other ways the data may conform to normal behaviour. The contextual attribute of the data will determine if it represents abnormal or normal behaviour.

Contextual anomalies are defined through two attributes:

•Contextual

Determines the context or location of that instance. As an example, in geospatial data, latitude and longitude could be used as contextual attributes.

•Behavioural

The behavioural attributes of a data set could be defined as the non-contextual characteristics of each specific instance. As an example, in a spatial data set representing global average temperatures, the temperature of a city would be considered behavioural.

Figure 4.8 depicts a graph demonstrating contextual abnormality within a temperature time period.

The temperature (data) is the same in T1 and T2; the context of that data within the different time periods has an impact when determining if the data is abnormal for the season. T1 is normal but T2 can be seen as an anomaly for the time of year.

Fig. 4.8.Contextual anomaly approach.

4.5.6.Collective anomalies

If a collection of related data instances is anomalous with respect to the entire data set, it is termed a collective anomaly. The individual data instances in a collective anomaly may not be anomalies by themselves, but their occurrence together as a collection is anomalous (Chandola et al., 2009). This does not imply that individual data sets are anomalies, but that their occurrence collectively with other data sets can be classified as an anomaly.

As an example, during August 2017, Dakota’s access control logs displayed an unusual increase in staff located on the 3rd floor visiting other floors, and in particular the floor directly below. The data was analysed and the entry point used by the vast majority of staff was to the right of the elevator. Under closer inspection the log data also appeared to only affect male members of staff.

The issue was quickly identified. The male toilets on the 3rd floor were unavailable for 24 hours so staff had to use the facilities on other floors. The toilet was also located to the right of the elevator, so staff used this access point.

A single observation (member of staff) visiting another floor is not unusual, but a collective data set (multiple staff) could be considered anomalous and can be classed as a collective anomaly.

4.6.Threat Model and Algorithm

The primary objective of this research paper is to reduce the risk posed by an insider through the development of a robust threat detection model which incorporates an effective and tested algorithm.

Dakota’s recently implemented proximity monitoring solution provides a constant stream of human movement data that is interpreted and processed within a dedicated security server.

Whilst Dakota security personnel are able to selectively monitor movement of the Bluetooth security badges, Dakota senior management believe it is not cost-effective to deploy a team of dedicated security staff to permanently monitor the movement of 50 separate individual contractors. It is also believed impractical for security personnel to understand the regular movement patterns of contract staff, their working practises and the specific zones in which they operate.

Leveraging data obtained from the Bluetooth proximity monitoring solution, a purpose-built application has been constructed to process the data using an algorithm that determines the threat posture of each individual contractor.

4.6.1.Extracting the data

The proximity solution is provided by Zonith, a Danish-based security solution provider who specialises in security, alarm handling and notification solutions (Zonith, 2018). Zonith’s proximity solution is based around generic hardware components that are not vendorspecific.

The Zonith solution comprises adapted Bluetooth Beacons, Bluetooth enabled devices (including Bluetooth security badges) and the Zonith application. The Zonith application is known as the Real Time Location Solution (RTLS), and incorporates customised schematics of the client office space. Dakota have preloaded a plan for each of the floors it occupies within its London headquarters.

RTLS is hosted on a single dedicated security server, running Windows 2016. The front-end application is delivered through an Internet browser environment using an Apache Tomcat server. The data is stored on a dedicated proprietary database, which is located on the same server (Project, 2018).

Fig. 4.9.Zonith RTLS.

Data is fed from the Bluetooth-enabled ID badge to the beacon. This is then sent to the RTLS server and stored onto the embedded database. Figure 4.9 outlines this process.

After analysis of the data provided by the RTLS system, it was discovered that in its native format the data was not sufficient to construct time analysis. Additionally, the native data set did not provide the sequence number that would be required for time calculation or movement profiling.

Sufficient data from all the job roles was therefore required to provide a baseline for the algorithm. To achieve this an extraction of two months’ historic data was analysed to determine recognised movement patterns and anomalies within the data set.

The data was reassembled, and a sequence number was added at the beginning of each data set. To reduce the length of the data processed, a unique User ID field was also added. This associated the Media Access Control (MAC) address of the Bluetooth proximity ID pass with a simple, much smaller numerical value. An entry and exit flag was then included as this would indicate if the Bluetooth ID pass entered or exited a zone.

To identify the time spent in each zone, two data sets were required for the calculation, one made up of instances when the Bluetooth ID badge entered a zone (or beacon) and one made up of instances when it left a zone. By default, each beacon sends a signal when the Bluetooth ID badge enters a zone and a second signal when it leaves a zone. To connect these two data sets together an Enter ID flag was inserted. As the Bluetooth ID badge enters a zone, a null value is added to the data set, but when the badge leaves the zone, the Enter ID flag is set to the sequence number associated with entering that zone. Table 4.5 depicts how the two fields and data sets are connected, thus identifying the time spent within each zone.

By calculating the difference between the entry and exit time stamp fields (connected by the entry/exit flag and the enter ID field), the time spent in each location was calculated and displayed within the Timing field.

Using Fig. 4.9 as an example, the individual entered the zone and generated the REC ID ‘1’ at 13:46:20 (time stamp), the entry/exit flag was set to ‘1’ (denoting an entry) and the enter ID field was set to null (no connection with another data set). When the individual left the zone, a second data set was created, sequence no ‘2’ (within the rec ID field) at 13:46:25.

Table 4.5.Typical data set manipulated for the algorithm.

The entry/exit flag was set to ‘0’ (exit indicator) and the enter ID was set to ‘1’ as this refers to the sequence number depicted in the rec ID field.

4.6.2.Threat detection application

To build a threat detection system that could identify anomalies from movement data retrieved via the RTLS system, a threat detection application was created, named Shadow Guard.

Shadow Guard was written as a progressive web based application using Hypertext Mark-up Language (HTML), Cascading Style Sheets (CSS) and PHP: Hypertext Pre-processor (PHP). A MySQL database was embedded within the threat detection server to store and process the data.

Figure 4.10 depicts how movement data is detected and passed from the ID badge to the beacon (using Bluetooth) and then into the RTLS server through an Ethernet connection.

Once the data was written into the Zonith proprietary database, a trigger was created (within RTLS) that copies data from the RTLS database into the Shadow Guard server where the data is reconstructed and stored in the new format.

4.6.3.Baseline behaviour

Once the data collection method was constructed and the data sorted into a readable format within the Shadow Cloud application a series of baselines was constructed to determine the normal working patterns of Dakota’s contractors.

Extensive testing was undertaken by the researcher, who was assisted by Dakota’s facilities staff. Each security pass was checked to ensure each of the beacons was able to detect the badges and the zoning was correct with minimal bleedover.

Referencing the job roles outlined in Table 4.5, Dakota’s security personnel staff were engaged and each of the Bluetooth access cards was activated and handed to each of the contractors working within the office area of Dakota’s head office in London.

Fig. 4.10.Data stream between RTLS and Shadow Guard.

The 3rd party contracts were scrutinised by lawyers to ensure the advanced monitoring required for anomaly-based threat detection did not breach any privacy laws or contractual concerns.

Each of the Bluetooth badges was charged and permanently attached to the building RFID access control card (see Appendix B).

To ensure sufficent data was collected to provide an effective baseline, an initial two-month collection period was implemented. As the amount of data collected would be dependent on the specific job role, the researcher decided to concentrate the analysis on one specific role within the organisation.

Using the data contained in Table 4.5, which outlines the access required by each of the contractor roles and the standard operating times, it was evident that the cleaners would provide the level of data required to build a baseline. Whilst data from all contract staff was collected, the initial baseline analysis was concentrated on the 9 cleaning contractors employed by Dakota.

Data was collected from November 2017 until January 2018; this included the Christmas holiday period. The data was then reconstructed into the new format that included a unique sequence number, user ID (to replace the ID badge MAC code), entry/exit flag, zone (based on the beacon MAC code) and the timing field, see Fig. 4.10.

4.6.4.Analysing data

Once sufficient data was collected the analysis process could take place. The data was separated into individual floors. To detect abnormal behaviour patterns it was evident that there could be multiple determining factors that indicate potential malicious intentions. To understand and analyse the risk factor, the data was separated into different sections.

4.6.5.Entry points

As each floor had its own unique characteristics, including specific hotzones, critical areas and entry/exit points. It was considered important to analyse each floor’s entry point as this could indicate an anomaly.

As an example Dakota’s 3rd floor has four separate entry points, these are as follows:

•Elevator A

•Elevator B

•Stairwell A

•Stairwell B (fire escape)

As the three elevators that service each of the floors are communal, there was a risk of unauthorised access to Dakota’s private floorspace. To reduce this risk Dakota installed two glass doors on either side of the exit/entry path from the elevators.

Figure 4.11 depicts Dakota’s 3rd floor layout, incorporating two security doors. Note that each access point requires RFID access control to enter and triggers separate beacons (zones) at each entry point.

Fig. 4.11. Typical Dakota office access point.

Two stairwells also service the 3rd floor and are located at separate areas of the open plan office. These extry/exit points also require access control and trigger separate Bluetooth beacons.

As the contractors must enter the zone using their respective RFID access control cards (which are attached to the Bluetooth badges), they will be picked up by a beacon as they enter the office area.

Although the specific entry point may be considered less important when determining the threat level, it can still represent anomalous behaviour that may impact the threat detection algorithm.

A key aspect of any anomaly detection technique is the nature of the input data ( Chandola et al., 2018). It can therefore be considered important to determine the relevance of the data collected and its importance when defining the algorithm.

As an example, based on the data collected over the two-month baseline period, it was clearly evident that the cleaners accessed the floor through the same entry point 90% of the time. This can be explained using the chart in Fig. 4.12.

Fig. 4.12.Entry point statistics for the 3rd floor.

These results were cross-referenced and verified using RFID access control data. Whilst there may be legitimate reasons to use different access points, the evidence indicates a clear pattern forming.

The rationale for using the elevator access point A is also clear, as the cleaners regularly start their shift at the small kitchenette area, which is located nearest to the elevator access point A.

As an additional layer of assurance and based on the times each cleaner visited the 3rd floor, the researcher was able to verify the theory that the kitchenette and potentially the toilet (which is located adjacent to the kitchenette) were the targets of the cleaners each time they visited the 3rd floor.

4.6.6.Time of day

Using the data acquired through the access control logs and the Bluetooth beacon data, the next process to be measured was the specified time the cleaner accessed the floor.

Using the data within Table 4.2, it is straightforward to calculate the time of entry against the contractual agreements. The data can be verified and cross-referenced using the access control and beacon logs.

It is worth noting that whilst an individual can gain access to a floor using tailgating techniques, it would be considerably more difficult to prevent the beacon detecting the Bluetooth ID badge.

Dakota’s cleaners’ specific operating hours are regimented and are mostly based outside of normal business hours.

As Dakota are a financial services organisation, their operational hours are based on the London Stock Exchange’s (LSE) trading hours. The cleaners visit the office from 5am–7am, 12–2pm and 5pm–7pm from Monday to Friday.

There may be specific occasions where cleaning staff are authorised to work over the weekend and lunchtime, but this is for specific tasks that are not included in their regular duties. The extra hours worked are not considered normal working hours.

It is evident that the identification of anomolous activity requires careful consideration and analysis of 3rd party contracts and historical data collected by the proximity monitoring solution. This element of the overall anomaly detection process could be considered subjective and dependent on the role of the people being tracked.

As an example, cleaners usually work contracted hours that may be specific to the business, so it is easier to measure and detect discrepancies in their working patterns. The working patterns of electricians or specific maintenance staff who may have sporadic working patterns, on the other hand, could prove challenging to analyse.

4.6.7.Time spent in a zone

Once an individual has entered a secure area that has no further access control barriers, zone analysis must then be incorporated into the anomaly algorithm. Using historic movement data, it is possible to detect routes taken within an open plan office based on the sequence of zones the proximity sensor has entered. However, routes are subjective and may be difficult to quantify.

Using baseline data, specific patterns can be detected based on the time spent within each zone. Using the cleaners’ data as an example, Fig. 4.13 depicts the data collected over the baseline period for a single zone.

The cleaners are assigned specific areas and supported by other cleaners where necessary. Cleaners are also expected to cover an alternate floor when another cleaner falls sick or goes on holiday. As an example, Cleaner 8 is the primary cleaner for the 3rd floor. However, other cleaners will provide support where necessary. For example, they might help to collect the refuse once the individual desk bins have been emptied.

Using a point-based anomaly approach, Fig. 4.13 analyses the cleaners’ access data for Zone 1 on the 3rd floor (over the baseline period).

The data highlights an interesting pattern: The regular cleaner (Cleaner 8), spends more time in the zone and visits the zone more frequently.

Fig. 4.13.Average daily activity in a single zone.

The non-regular cleaners’ data is clearly grouped, they collectively spend a shorter period of time within the zone under analysis.

This pattern is reflected across the entire floor, showing the primary cleaner spending considerably more time within each zone, whilst the supporting cleaners enter the zones less frequently and for a shorter period. Based on the working practices of the job role this could be considered normal behaviour.

Using the same point-based anomaly approach, a single zone was analysed over a 7-day period. The purpose was to identify normal and abnormal activity.

Figure 4.14 uses a point-based anomaly approach, detailing the time each cleaner spent within a typical zone.

Using the data provided, there is a clear demarcation point between standard and unusual activity.

This data set is typical across all the zones, except when a cleaner was at a hotspot. In that case, the time spent within that area increased.

Fig. 4.14.Typical zone activity.

When determining threat metrics, it is important to understand the thresholds for normal, unusual and anomalous behaviour.

Figure 4.15 references the demarcation point as a percentage of normal operating activity that includes a margin of error based on the data collected. The chart includes a detailed breakdown of user activity within one zone over a 7-day period.

Activity has been correlated into three bands — normal, unusual and abnormal activity. It is evident that the normal time spent within this specific zone by one job role accounts for 95.5% of all activity. It can therefore be assumed that this data group represents normal activity.

The data defines a much smaller grouping that can be identified as unusual behaviour (3.5%). The last recorded data point for this zone was between 7–8 minutes (1.5%) and this has been designated as abnormal.

Data recorded beyond this demarcation point would be considered a potential threat and an alert would be generated.

The snapshot of data detected within Zone 3/1 is typical of other zones within the target organisation. Whilst each zone may have differing time values, which can be dependent on the specific zone or the job role, the percentages stay constant.

Fig. 4.15.Point-based anomaly chart detailing user activity (source: Dakota).

Novikova and Murenin observe that making note of the duration each employee stays in the controlled zone allows one to identify anomalies and potential malicious behaviour (Novikova and Murenin, 2017).

4.6.8.Zone metrics

Once the individual leaves a specific floor, their activity can be analysed and appropriate metrics applied through the algorithm. When the individual leaves a controlled zone, it can be detected as the data set will have no corresponding data set on that floor, see Table 4.6.

Figure 4.16 depicts zone data extracted from the proximity solution and confirms the working practices of selected job functions. Using Fig. 4.16 as a reference, it is possible to determine in which floors a cleaner predominately operates.

Fig. 4.16. Average zones visited.

This can provide a baseline metric to highlight significant changes to the work patterns that might indicate unusual behaviour. Determining thresholds can be challenging as it may be necessary to temporarily reassign staff to different floors.

Working on the same metrics used when determining anomalies within zone activity, a similar threshold can be applied when determining significant pattern changes.

Using a single individual as an example, Fig. 4.16 details the average number of zones visited by Cleaner 5. The metrics are taken from the proximity monitoring solution and confirm the floors in which the cleaner is a regular visitor.

Data was collected and processed over a two-month period and used to construct a baseline; however, once the Shadow Cloud application is fully deployed this metric will be updated in real-time.

Using the 2nd Floor as an example within Fig. 4.17, one can see that Cleaner 5 has a daily average of 75 zone hits. Using the same margin-of-error metric previously employed when measuring the zone activity, behaviour is considered unusual if the number of visits in a particular day ≥50% of the average day’s zone visits.

Fig. 4.17. Zones visited by Cleaner 5.

Again, using the same methodology, behaviour can be considered an anomaly when the threshold reaches ≥100%. If daily zone visits are ≥200% then an immediate alert is triggered.

4.6.9.Pattern triggers

The final analysis phase of the anomaly detection process could be considered the most complex. Movement analysis through an open plan office, with limited physical controls, can be challenging.

Fig. 4.18.Movement patterns of Cleaner 8 through multiple zones.

Data recorded by the proximity monitoring solution movement was analysed over a period of two months to identify specific patterns based on the job role and other mitigating factors such as hotspots or desk configurations.

The cleaners were used as an example as they provide a regular stream of data that can be analysed over the baseline period. Figure 4.18 details an extract of data recorded on the proximity monitoring solution over a period of an hour. Movement patterns appear to be controlled, following a predictable path. The cleaner entered the floor at the expected entry point and stayed within adjacent zones until the three spikes in the movement pattern were identified and highlighted. Cross referencing these zones with the floor map can provide some clarity and explains the slight deviations in movement. These do not represent and may not indicate anomalous behaviour.

Using historic pattern analysis, one can detect anomalies that can affect the baseline data. However, subtle changes need to be accommodated so that the risk of false positives is reduced. Historic pattern analysis may not be possible for some roles as the data may not be available due to the nature of the task.

As an example, a plumber may not visit the premises regularly, potentially only when an emergency occurs. They may also require access to all areas within the building to address a water leak.

As part of the experiment, where there was sufficient data available to construct a baseline pattern of movement analysis, data was analysed in an attempt to identify a standard pattern for each role on each floor. Figure 4.19 depicts the movements within three separate days at the same time. It is evident the movement pattern was too random for accurate pattern analysis and could cause too many false positives as there were potentially too many variables to consider when constructing an effective threat model. This was evident when analysing the cleaners, whose movement can be erratic and who may have a legitimate excuse to move freely around an open plan office area.

Fig. 4.19.Pattern analysis over three separate dates.

However, it is possible to construct triggers based on historic pattern analysis when analysing other job functions whose movement is dictated by the task. As an example, air conditioning engineers will operate in or around the airflow extractor fans on each floor. These are located at specific locations within an office, so a trigger could be incorporated if they moved to other areas without legitimate reason.

Figure 4.20 outlines data captured over two days of tracking the same individual. This allows one to visualise how movement patterns can be completely different on a daily basis and illustrates how an anomaly can be detected within a complex movement pattern.

A single event may not indicate anomalous behaviour and could cause false positives. The threat anomaly solution is not based solely on a single method to detect anomalous behaviour. It relies on multiple factors and processes. Each has the potential to raise an alert or increase the risk counter until a combination of events triggers an alert. Murenin et al. (2017) describes how anomalous behaviour can be detected through the analysis of human movement trajectories and anomalies in routes using uncommon controlled zones.

Fig. 4.20.Movement patterns that incorporate a trigger.

4.7.The Algorithm

One of the primary objectives of this research paper is the construction of a robust and effective algorithm that leverages data retrieved from the recently deployed proximity monitoring solution. The algorithm is an integral part of the Shadow Cloud application that was created for this research project. The algorithm is constructed from active elements, each with the ability to alert and increase a running threat counter. As the contractor enters Dakota’s controlled office space a counter is reset to ‘0’ (zero).

The main elements of the algorithm are as follows:

•Entry point

•Date

•Time of day

•Time spent in each zone

•Number of zones entered

•Zone pattern anomaly

Figure 4.21 depicts the algorithm as a process flow.

4.7.1.Verification process

Once the proximity solution had been fully integrated within the working practices of Dakota and its 3rd party contractors, a verification process was initiated. With the assistance of the facilities department and the security staff, the algorithm, which formed part of the Shadow Cloud application, was tested to determine any anomalies and false positives.

Triggers were configured at each stage of the algorithm and triggers were analysed to ensure the metrics fell within an acceptable margin of error.

Figure 4.22 depicts each stage of the algorithm and the average percentage of triggers within each stage over a two-month period. As an example, the time spent by each cleaner within each zone was within the permitted parameters 95% of the time. This is visualised in Fig. 4.15, which can be seen as indicative of normal behaviour.

The algorithm has been designed to incorporate some false positives. These would allow a margin of error to be incorporated. As an example, the threat threshold for Dakota has been set to ‘3’. This is based on the analysis of the targets and the data collected. The threshold for another organisation may be higher or lower depending on the risk appetite, the job functions or the physical attributes of the building.

4.7.2.False positives

The initial testing phase of the threat model produced some false positives that needed to be addressed. Detailed analysis was undertaken at each stage of the algorithm process to ensure the appropriate controls were incorporated into the design.

Fig. 4.21.The algorithm as a process.

Fig. 4.22.Algorithm triggers.

Focussing on the 8 cleaners, Fig. 4.22 depicts the number of triggers as a percentage over the two-month baseline period and through the various phases of the algorithm. Table 4.6 details the number of instances when each specific cleaner activated a trigger over the baseline period.

Each trigger was investigated to ensure the threshold values were sufficient to prevent unnecessary false positives within the overall algorithm. To ensure the experiment did not create false working patterns the data subjects were not directly approached. Facilities and security were questioned to ensure the cleaners’ activity was normal. There were two methods that could be used to set the threshold levels. One of these could be carried out at the algorithmic function stage and the other required changes to be made to the overall threat detection level. To provide the most flexibility, each stage of the algorithm was adjusted to allow a margin of error based on the false detection rate.

Table 4.6.False positive triggers over a two-month baseline period from December 2017 to January 2018.

4.7.3.Experiment validation

Whilst it can be argued that historic data analysis can determine trigger thresholds, an independent test of the parameters can provide additional assurance. Dakota regularly engages independent cyber and physical security specialists to conduct social engineering tests against the organisation. Once the proximity solution was implemented and Shadow Cloud configured to accept data, a physical penetration test was conducted against Dakota’s London headquarters. A team of two ethical social engineers gained access to Dakota’s London office using social engineering techniques. They posed as sensitive waste disposal contractors, using bogus identification to gain access. They obtained two security passes, with Bluetooth tracking embedded. They gained access to three of the five floors within Dakota’s private office space, as sensitive waste disposal contract staff are only permitted to access selected floors within the building. Due to the time they arrived, tailgating was not an option as no staff were present. The social engineers gained access to the three floors where sensitive waste bins were located, as their access passes permitted them to do.

Figure 4.23 details the expected floor entry point and the zones visited. It also depicts the actual entry points and the floors visited by the social engineers.

Fig. 4.23.Social engineer movement and triggers.

Table 4.7.Social engineer proximity data.

Source: Dakota.

The algorithm triggered numerous times during the period the social engineers visited the 3rd floor. Table 4.7 outlines the data collected and the specific triggers.

The threshold value for Dakota was set to ≥3. The social engineers triggered an alert due to the zones they visited and the time spent within those zones. This was prior to the ‘zones visited’ and ‘pattern offset’ elements being processed. Whilst this could be considered an extreme example as social engineers were used, it validates the algorithm based on the thresholds set using baseline data.

4.8.Regulations and Legal Considerations

4.8.1.GDPR

The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which comes into effect on 25th May 2018, will impact all EU organisations that collect, store and process personal or sensitive data (Ico.org.uk, 2017). To provide an effective threat mitigation solution, Shadow Cloud will record and process human movement data that is not anonymised. As part of its GDPR preparation process Dakota enhanced its privacy and data protection policies, seeking legal advice to ensure the data recorded was lawful and met the ICO’s regulatory requirements.

4.8.2.Privacy laws

Bruce Schneier (Schneier, 2016) describes surveillance as a technical and a legal problem. A key project deliverable is the identification of threats based on data collected on human behavior patterns.

As Shadow Cloud requires the tracking of individuals it will inevitably pose privacy questions. Whilst it could be argued that analysing data to prevent threats is ethically acceptable, using the data to target individuals for other purposes, which may include discriminating against the target, could breach privacy and human rights law.

To ensure Dakota comply to privacy regulation a clear and concise agreement with all 3rd party organisations was reviewed by the Data Protection Officer and the organisation’s legal representative to ensure the enhanced proximity monitoring process did not infringe on the individual rights of its contract staff. Law professor Eben Moglen once wrote ‘if people are doing nothing wrong then they have the right to maintain a balance between the individual and the power that is monitoring’.

4.9.Conclusions and Recommendations

This research project has explored the relationship between human movement patterns and the potential threat posed by an insider with malicious intentions. The real challenge perhaps is to understand how employees navigate a specific environment, how they process physical obstacles and how they interact with co-workers.

Whilst it can be argued that humans have distinctive movement traits, such as using the same entry point, it is evident that trajectories within an open plan office environment can be influenced by a complex set of variables.

Understanding the characteristics of the building and including areas where staff congregate, such as the water cooler, were considered integral when designing a threat model.

The primary focus of the project was the creation of an algorithm that would form part of an overall threat detection solution. The algorithm would initially leverage the data supplied from the target organisation but could be adaptive and used by other human monitoring solutions.

As the target data was analysed it was evident that the algorithm could not rely on a single trigger as this would produce too many false positives. It was clear that a multi-dimensional approach measuring a set of contrasting variables was required.

The algorithm was dissected into seven components, each able to process the specific characteristics of the targets, analysing the time, the date and their movement patterns. The research had intended to identify specific movement patterns that were evident within other research papers that focused on door entry data.

The data provided from the proximity monitoring solution highlighted the complexity of the human decision-making process. When a binary decision had to be made between different access points, the targets would invariably choose the same option; this was evident when entering a floor, as 90% chose the same entry point. However, when presented with multiple options the patterns were far less predictable.

This is why the algorithm could not rely on one measurement metric and incorporated a variety of data sets to determine an anomaly, ultimately reducing the risk of false positives.

Chapter 5

Ransomware

Usman Javed Butt* and Arvind Kumar†

*Brunel University, London, UK
usman.butt@brunel.ac.uk

†Northumbria University, London, UK
arvind.kumar@northumbria.ac.uk

ABSTRACT

In this modern era, malware has emerged as a malicious cyber threat to critical information and communication infrastructure. Ransomware is a type of malware which holds the victim’s computer hostage by encrypting the data available on it, which makes the data unusable and inaccessible to its legitimate user. The attacker demands that the user pay before the decryption key is released to reverse the attack. This chapter explains about ransomware and its classification, how it impacts different platforms, the severity of ransomware, the methodology used by ransomware to penetrate target machines, the attack vectors used, the latest ransomware attacks, the most common targets of ransomware attacks, how to prevent ransomware attacks, and ways to recover.

Keywords : malware, ransomware, botnets, cryptography, bitcoins, crypto-lockers, attack vectors, exploit kits, RSA public key, MD5 algorithm, AES, symmetric key, WannaCry, Petya, SimpleLocker, TeslaCrypt, NotPetya, IoT

5.1.Introduction

According to Kapersky, as computers evolved from floppy-disk bootable machines into more sophisticated workstation devices such as laptops and smartphones, malicious software technology or malware as it is most commonly known evolved along with them (Kaspersky, 2018a). Kaspersky also suggests that malware was existent from information technology’s infancy but that the use of malware only bloomed when personal computers began to be accessible to everyone. The first malware was called the “Elk Cloner Virus” (Tasril et al., 2017). Examining the features of the Elk Cloner Virus, we see that this malicious technology, which once used simple motifs and techniques, has become more sophisticated and now does more serious damage to computer devices. The Elk Cloner Virus was formed as a “prank” and did not do much harm. Its self-spreading feature relied on social engineering techniques such as floppy-disk insertions (Touchette, 2016). Cyber criminals built upon these foundations until they formed the cyber crime industry as it exists today.

Cyber crime, which has cost industries approximately 100 billion USD, is classified according to the types of malware that the industry produces. Research done by Kapersky has identified the types of malware in a diagram in Fig. 5.1 called the “Malware Classification Tree” (Kaspersky, 2018b).

According to the same report, the classified malwares are considered “specific function” malwares, which means that these malwares are only capable of designated damage and do not produce a complex effect on devices. In contrast, cyber criminals have devised multi-dimensional and multi-functioning malwares. 65.32% of these are botnets which affect devices worldwide, and 34.68% of these are a combination of trojans and worms as shown in Fig. 5.2 (Soni, 2018).

Fig. 5.1.Malware classification tree.

Fig. 5.2.Pie chart of multi-functional malware vs. single-function malware (Trojans).

Cisco has classified these versatile malwares as “Advanced Malwares” and has identified the most prominent advanced malwares as the following: riskware, spyware, adware and ransomware with ransomware being the deadliest due to its capabilities (Cisco, 2018). Esset defines riskware as a type of malware which increases security risk by using encryption methods to identify user procedures and diverting the procedures into digital transactions (e.g. using a credit card) without the user’s permission (Esset, 2018). Spywares are types of malware which, as can be deduced from their name, collect data about a device, encrypt the information and send the data back to the origin of the malware. These data are used illegally to blackmail the people from whom the data is collected (Stavrou et al., 2010). Avast, an anti-virus company, adds that spywares are usually accompanied by adwares, which bombard the user with inappropriate and unwanted pop-ups or advertisements which are harmful to the device (Avast, 2018). Finally, when these features are combined and tailored for a bigger purpose, ransomware is produced.

An observation can be made that most of the advanced malwares were enhanced by the development of encryption and of new ways to cipher text. The field of cryptovirology was developed when researchers realised how these cryptographic techniques could be used to develop malware (Young, 2017).

5.2.Ransomware and How It Impacts Different Platforms

Ransomware has affected several companies worldwide by making it necessary for them to pay a large amount of money to their attackers without actually gaining anything beneficial. For instance, Arran Brewery, a brewing company in Scotland, recently paid 2 Bitcoins worth 9,600 GBP to a group of anonymous hackers just to restore the company’s system after all the computers of the company had been locked down (BBC, 2018). A similar incident also happened to the United States government when the Pennsylvania Senate Democratic Caucus had to pay Microsoft to reconstruct the senate’s IT Framework after it was breached on March 3, 2017 (Cimpanu, 2019). The same report states that hackers were demanding 28 Bitcoins as payment, which comes up to 30,000 USD, but instead the government decided to reconstruct for the hefty price of 700,000 USD in order to discourage future attacks to government offices. As these incidents start to increase, attacks are reportedly getting worse.

Ransomware is a type of advanced malware where the victim is held at ransom for infected files or documents. The files will not be made available to the victim unless payment is given to the attacker, at which point the attacker will remove the malware from the system (Young, 2017). Ransomware is believed to be one of the most effective malwares for the year 2017, with a total amount of more than 12 million malware counts. The number of malware counts increased by 36% in the last quarter of 2017 (McAfee, 2017). The fact that ransomware accounted for 5 billion US dollars lost globally in the year 2017 led Europol to conclude that ransomware was the most dangerous malware threat, and to say so at their conference entitled “Internet Organised Crime Threat Assessment (IOCTA) 2018” (Walker, 2018).

As ransomware has turned into a booming business, ransomware authors have devised two types of ransomwares: locker ransomware and crypto ransomware (Deloitte, 2016).

Locker ransomwares are the types of ransomwares which do less damage since these ransomwares do not encrypt the files of the victim. Locker ransomware is used to terrorise the victim by prompting the victim to pay for a fine charged for misusing the internet (i.e. watching pornography or downloading illegal programs from torrents). These ransomwares usually come with an interface credible enough for the victim to believe that the warrant is legitimate. Attackers may include the targeted user’s sensitive data, such as their IP address and their last viewed malicious website, to make the warrant more convincing (Deloitte, 2016).

Crypto ransomwares (crypto-locker ransomwares) are the types of ransomwares which do more damage to the device and to the financial stability of the victim. Crypto-lockers are a type of ransomware which infects a device and encrypts the victim’s files until the ransom has been paid. Some of these crypto-lockers even delete the back-up from the system, making it harder to recover the victim’s files (Richet, 2016).

5.3.Methodology of Ransomware

The word ransomware comes from the words “ransom” and “malware”. One could define the word ransom as a payment or acquiescence to certain demands in exchange for the release of a hostage or of something held hostage (Merriam-Webster, 2018). So, understanding the criticality of a malware capable of holding virtual platforms to ransom and how the procedure is undertaken is deemed essential.

Much research related to ransomware has pointed out that different ransomwares can have different approaches of propagation, but all ransomwares follow a pattern of propagation that has five phases beginning from the point when the victim’s system is compromised. The five phases are as follows (Brewer, 2016):

1.First Phase: Acquisition, Utilisation and Infection

The process of acquiring ransomware is similar to the process of acquiring any other type of malware (Ali, 2017). Norton by Symantec suggests that ransomware and other forms of malware can be categorised into five types depending on how they are acquired, and these are as follows (Norton, 2018):

•Software-integrated malwares: This is when a user downloads a software which is tagged as “free” but which actually comes with the hefty price of having one’s system infected by malware.

•Peer-to-peer virtual sharing: This is when a user shares files electronically by using BitTorrent, uTorrent etc. This does not only refer to file sharing between familiar peers but also refers to the illegal download of applications via anonymous uploads.

•Removable media: This is the most common method of malware acquisition. Malware is transferred to the victim via electronic devices such as USBs, CDs, External HDDs, etc.

•Network acquisition: This happens when a device connected to the internet comes across a website which has malicious cookies or pop-ups and the victim falls into the trap by exploring the links integrated into these digital platforms.

•General lack of protection: This happens when a device is not kept secure by software which offers protection from malwares.

Attack Vectors of Ransomware

Although there are plenty of ways to be infected by malwares, researchers have identified that fortunately, there are only a few ways of acquiring ransomware. These vectors could be divided into those which are acquired through virtual means and those which are acquired through physical means.

Virtual Means of Ransomware Acquisition:

a)Emails are the main source of ransomware attacks. Statistics show that there are approximately 354.5 billion emails delivered daily worldwide and 85.35 percent of these emails are spam, which means only 14.64 percent of emails are legitimate (Cisco Talos, 2018). IBM estimates that there was a 350 percent increase in spam mails from January 2015 to December 2016 and, alarmingly, despite the fact that not all spam mails contain malwares, the total malware content in spam mails by percentage is increasing. Malware-containing spam mails made up approximately 10 percent of 100 percent of spam mails sent in January 2015. By 2016, spam mails had increased by 450 percent, and malware-containing spam mails made up 210 percent of the 450 percent (IBM, 2016) as shown in Fig. 5.3.

Symantec suggests that these malwares are spreading largely due to a botnet named Necrus which was established just to send out spam mails worldwide (O'Brien, 2017). Symantec also states that ransomware, if acquired through email, can be activated through one of the following steps (O'Brien, 2017):

•Malicious attachments being opened

•Malicious attachments initiating third party JavaScript or PowerShell commands

•Malicious attachments initiating the download of exploit kits

Fig. 5.3.Volumes of malicious and non-malicious spam.

b)Exploit Kits literally exploit the vulnerabilities of a computer. Exploit kits are used to take advantage of a particular device’s weaknesses via web browsers, programs or operating systems. Most exploit kits are integrated into websites, and once a user visits that particular site, the kit is activated in the user’s device. The kit will then scan for vulnerabilities in the device used to navigate the website and, subsequently, it will implement the malware into the device in question. The infected website is not necessarily a malicious website since legitimate websites like BBC or Yahoo could be infested through advertisements as well (Monrose et al., 2015). According to a study done by Malwarebytes, as shown in Fig. 5.4, 61 percent of all exploit kits contain exploit payloads for ransomware (Malwarebytes Labs, 2016).

Physical Means of Ransomware Acquisition

Social Engineering is used as a sure but risky way to spread malware. Social Engineering is the manipulation of human psychology in order to persuade a person to perform a behaviour which may have a devastating effect on that person, another person or a group of individuals. Researchers may refer to it as “hacking” a human for an intended purpose (Mann, 2008).

Fig. 5.4.Exploit payload summary.

Kevin Mitnick’s Proposed Social Engineering Methodology (Gallegos-Segovia, 2017):

•Information Gathering: This is the step where details of the victim are gathered by certain individuals.

•Trust: This is the step where the attacker establishes a deeper connection with the victim. By doing so, an appropriate attack vector could be identified by the attacker.

•Exploitation: This is where the attacker executes the plan of exploitation and the ransomware infects the device.

•Reach: This is where the system is finally compromised. Usually the attacker is not in contact with the victim at this point.

The December 2015 Ukraine Power Grid Cyber Attack is an example of how these methods have been used. Numerous reports suggest that the incident was a well-planned attack on Ukraine’s power company named Ukrenergo (BBC, 2017). Most investigators were amazed by how well the information and trust gathering was executed and further blamed the Russians for devising a way into the Ukraine’s SCADA system then manipulating the system through an infection caused by a USB (Zetter, 2016).

These proposed methods of social engineering can be further used to identify the different types of attacks that can be established. These are as follows (Gallegos-Segovia, 2017):

•Ego Attacks: The attacker tries to create a personal connection with the victim by offering help and proving the reliability of the attacker’s intelligence to the victim. Once the victim falls for a transparent manipulation, the attacker executes the ransomware on the system.

•Sympathy Attacks: The attacker uses emotional means to create a connection with the victim. When the victim starts trusting the attacker, the attacker executes the ransomware on the system.

•Bullying Attacks: The attacker uses force, dominance or black-mailing to gather information. This is the most common and most effective type of social engineering attack.

2.Second Phase: Consignment and Implementation

The next step is the process of installing the malware on the system, encrypting the ransomware program inside the device and further establishing a secure platform for the upcoming command and control network.

The ransomware uses a simple RSA asymmetric public key (Emsisoft, 2018) that will call a GET or POST request at some point (Securonix, 2018). The GET or POST request would consist of the following parameters to be collected (Emsisoft, 2018; Securonix, 2018):

•computer name

•processor information

•volume serial

•operating system

•active drives

•Public IP in a pattern of: { ipv4bot[.]whatismyipaddress[.] com}

•disk space

Researchers (Emsisoft, 2018) have identified the reasons why ransomware developers use RSA public keys in coding ransomwares and these are the following:

•They take up lesser space in memory and can be easily transported.

•Third parties or malware analysts surveying the network would only see plain texts and scrambled encrypted network traffic.

•This gives the malware authors a chance to use their own server during the communication with the deployed ransomware.

After identifying the victim through their unique hashed identity (using the MD5 Algorithm), the ransomware would identify whether the process was running via root or admin access (Rajpal and Kotov, 2014). If the ransomware was running through either root or admin access, then further installation of the ransomware would take place through the following steps (Rajpal and Kotov, 2014):

As shown in the flowchart, the ransomware would unpack itself to the memory of the device or the hard disk and then would execute itself. The software would then create multiple copies of a stage dropper and inject the payload into explorer.exe and svchost.exe. In the next phases, the ransomware would also delete all shadow copies and back-up files and finally disable the device’s ability to restore the system.

Fig. 5.5.Ransomware installation procedures.

These processes normally take only a few seconds to execute and usually are executed without the user’s knowledge (Brewer, 2016), as shown in Fig. 5.5.

3.Third Phase: File Encryption and Command and Control (C2)

Command and Control Establishment

This phase is the most important phase of a ransomware since, in this phase, a ransomware will do whatever it has been coded to do. After making sure that all packages of the ransomware have been successfully injected into the system, the ransomware platform in the device would now communicate to the command centre (host) via an RSA key pair (Brewer, 2016). A .bit namecoin would then be used to query.bit domain-friendly DNS servers through the code: {ns1.crop[.]corpservers[.]ru; a[.]dsnpod[.] com}. Once the connection is established, this is where the information gathered via a GET or POST request would be sent to the host in the Base64 encoding format [31].

Researchers have (Rajpal and Kotov, 2014) identified that over the past few years, ransomware developers have shifted from using HTTP to using TOR and SSL during the communication phase of command and control establishment. The simplest reason is that it is more complex to decrypt TOR and SSL data in contrast to HTTP data. Data encrypted with RC4 encryption, which is the most commonly used method to encrypt HTTP data, can be decrypted and fingerprinted using the simple mathematical expression [a – z]\ = [z – z 0 – 9]+, also called Regrex (Kaspersky, 2016). TOR and SSL’s full encryption makes it difficult for developers to code a network signature for initial stage detection; however, TOR is less used due to multiple network restrictions (Rajpal and Kotov, 2014).

File Encryption Process

The following files and folders are excluded from encryption:

•desktop.ini

•autorun.ini

•nuser.ini

•GDCB-DECRYPT.txt

These are excluded to allow the command server to connect to the device controlled (NJCCIC, 2018).

The encryption of files is done through a combination of RSA 2048bit (public key) and AES 256bit (victim data) encryption. After data encryption, the ransomware is expected to encrypt the files by assigning a public-private key for the randomly generated symmetric key. This process is shown in Fig. 5.6.

This type of encryption does not need any shared secret key, which makes it easier for the attacker to keep the ciphered text and only allow the victim access once ransom is paid (Emsisoft, 2018).

Fig. 5.6.Process of encryption used by ransomware.

In most ransomwares, Virlock is commonly used for encryption. Virlock consists of two layers of encryption in which the first layer is a combination of XOR and ROL encryption which is backed up by a second layer of XOR encryption (Lindskog and Zavarskya, 2016). All the encrypted files are converted into .GDCB or .KRAB files which then prompt a report back to the command centre using the same GET or POST request (Rajpal and Kotov, 2014).

4.Fourth Phase: Back-Up Corruption

Unlike most malwares which are usually designed just to implement the infection that the program is designed to spread, most ransomwares are designed to delete the back-up of the victim’s files or at least the back-up of the ransomware (Brewer, 2016).

Ransomwares usually end by deleting the shadow copies of the victim’s files by either of two available methods: the VSSAdmin service or the WMI service. The two methods are identified in (Securonix, 2018), which also shows the exact code used by the ransomware to delete all the shadow copies. This code can be seen below.

5.Fifth Phase: User Detection, Payment and Clean-Up

The FBI has claimed that the Barack Obama Blue Blackmail Virus has been one of the biggest issues faced by the USA. The virus resulted in numerous people logging in to their devices and suddenly seeing President Obama’s face along with an FBI notice asking them to pay a certain fine (Osborne, 2018). This news is a perfect example of the aftermath of a ransomware attack. Attackers demand a certain amount of pecuniary reimbursement for the locked files, which should be paid within a certain period of time.

Due to the advancement of technology, most attackers require victims to pay using bitcoins but there are other viable means of payment like credit or debit card payments, etc. (Rajpal and Kotov, 2014).

Table 5.1 suggests that most ransomware attackers require victims to pay from a range of 100 USD to 500 USD or from 0.5 BTC (3,280 USD) to 0.8 BTC (5,250 USD).

Usually these instructions are saved in the hard drive with file names such as “HELP_DECRYPT” for CryptoWall V3 or “HELP_YOUR_FILES” for CryptoWall V4. Once payment is given to the attacker, the attacker will decrypt the files and the ransomware will clean up by itself (Brewer, 2016).
