5.4.Latest and Most Prominent Ransomwares

As explained before, ransomware is an evolving business with malware developers as its vendors and cyber criminals as its customers. Due to this “booming” trend, many variations of ransomwares have become available in the market. The following are the top five strongest ransomwares in the last five years, as identified by an organisation of security decision makers called CSO.

Top Five Strongest Ransomwares (Fruhlinger, 2017):

1.CryptoLocker: considered the most generic variation of ransomware due to its ability to encrypt all the files inside the victim’s device. These ransomwares use law enforcement-themed GUIs to threaten the victim into paying the ransom, which they must do since decryption is near to impossible. All back-up files are deleted as soon as the infection starts (Cannell, 2018). CryptoLocker is usually called the “primitive ransomware” since the developers have not updated the features of the said ransomware (Fruhlinger, 2017).

2.TeslaCrypt: considered a subvariant of CryptoLocker; this ransomware started claiming victims in 2015. This ransomware used gaming websites to spread itself and to infect devices, which is why those affected by this ransomware were mostly gamers. This ransomware only encrypted files with a file size lower than 268 MB (Osborne, 2018). The developers of the ransomware have decided to shut down operations and upon doing so, the developers also posted the universal decryption key which helped infected devices to recover successfully (Koller, 2016).

The final message of TeslaCrypt, which included the master decryption key, read as follows:

“Project closed! Master key for decrypt: 440A241DD80FCC5664E861989DB 716E08CE627D8D40C7EA360AE855C727A49EE. Wait for other people make universal decrypt software. We are sorry!”

3.SimpleLocker: a ransomware effective on the Android platform which gathers the IMEI, the model number and the manufacturer details for the command and control centre. Encryption is done via the AES encryption method and the ransomware also accesses the camera to take a picture of the victim. This picture is used to further threaten the victim into paying the ransom (NJCCIC, 2016).

4.WannaCry: considered one of the deadliest ransomwares to be developed. This ransomware shut down multiple hospitals across the United Kingdom and Ukraine. The developers of WannaCry were able to detect vulnerabilities in Windows which were first discovered by the United States National Security Agency. Symantec later on began to suspect that the developers originated from a North Korean-linked group called Lazarus (Fruhlinger, 2017). This ransomware is also one of the latest. 6,912 appointments were cancelled and 19,000 affected when WannaCry affected NHS operations in the year 2017. This attack, despite being “unsophisticated” as Kingsley Manning suggests, became so successful due to the fact that the different NHS offices were “intertwined” with each other, thus quickening the spread of the ransomware (BBC, 2017).

5.Petya and NotPetya: launched a week after the WannaCry outbreak, this ransomware is confirmation that a new age of ransomwares has begun (Fruhlinger, 2017). Petya or NotPetya was spread by attackers who sent a job application document via email in the PDF file format. When the PDF file was accessed by the company, the ransomware was unleashed. NotPetya is the very first ransomware which does not need any spam emails to be sent or social engineering to be carried out in order for infection to occur and administrative access to be gained. As long as there is a network connection in between two devices, Petya or NotPetya can move from one to the other (Fruhlinger, 2017).

Aside from these famous ransomware attacks, there are a few other ransomwares making their name in the market. One of the most prominent in recent years is GandCrab which just released their latest version, Version 4, in July 2018. GandCrab acts exactly like CryptoLocker and is also considered deadly since the ransomware converts files to .KRAB extension files once encrypted (Abram, 2018).

5.5.Platforms Affected by Ransomware Attacks

Malwares in general can affect multiple technological platforms, but recent studies have shown that ransomware has only affected three technological platforms so far. During the height of the WannaCry ransomware attacks, banks and bank users in India were falsely warned through circulating Whatsapp messages that the ransomware had actually breached ATM machines throughout the country. These allegations were proven to be hoaxes upon deeper investigation by one of the leading banks of India, called the Rural Bank of India (NDTV, 2017). Had this been true, ransomware could have been considered a deadly terrorism weapon by governments around the world.

Researchers have identified that ransomware has affected mobile platforms, computing platforms, and IoT and cloud computing platforms. Out of these three types of platform, it is most vital to keep IoT and cloud computing platforms secure.

a)Computing Platform: Computing platforms have always been those most affected by ransomwares. As previously discussed, ransomwares act on computers by infecting the system and encrypting the files in the system until a certain amount of ransom is paid. A large number of ransomware attacks on computing platforms — 86.87 percent of total ransomware attacks in 2016 — are directed at home users (Walton, 2017).

b)Mobile Platform: Due to people spending more time on their mobile phones, doctors have concluded that most people are suffering from mobile addiction (SC Magazine, 2017). Having this in mind, cyber criminals have taken advantage of people who are “addicted” to mobile phones.

Android — This has been the biggest target of ransomware attacks on mobile platforms. This is mainly due to the “openness” of the Android platform. With mobile ransomware increasing by 137.8% from the first to the second quarter of 2017, SC Magazine predicted that there would be a spike in mobile ransomware in 2018 (Snow, 2016). However, in Android ransomware and in mobile ransomware overall, cryptolockers are less common since file encryption would be useless on mobile platforms due to the cloud backup feature that most mobile devices have. This is the reason why most Android ransomwares lock applications with a coded GUI which shows the details of the ransomware once the application is opened (Norton, 2018). The newest mobile ransomware, specifically dedicated for Android, is better implemented. This ransomware, which is tagged as Android.Lockroid.E, locks the whole mobile device instead of just locking the specific applications inside the mobile device. This way, the user’s mobile device would be locked and unusable until the ransom had been paid (Savage et al., 2015).

iOS — According to a report released by Symantec, iOS devices are mostly secure due to Apple’s Technological and Security Ecosystem Structure. The only way that an iPhone can be vulnerable to ransomware is when the mobile device in question has undergone the process called “jailbreaking” (Ismail, 2018). Despite all the protection that Apple offers for iOS phones, researchers suggest that Proton Remote Access Trojan (RAT) has affected plenty of iPhones worldwide (Snow, 2016).

c)IoT and Cloud Computing Platforms

As previously discussed, the invention of NotPetya paved the way for a type of ransomware which does not need third party connections like spam mails or social engineering to infect and gain administrative access to any device. This led developers and researchers to think of the next step that ransomware would become capable of. Although there has been no reported ransomware attack on any IoT or cloud computing platform, the implementation of this idea is not too far away, especially now that IoT is being plagued by DDoS attacks such as Mirai (Cobb, 2017). Since ransomware developers can now understand and create ransomwares which can multiply by themselves on a shared network, IoT technologies are not safe any more since all IoTs share a common network, that is, the cloud (Budd, 2016). Although speculation about Microsoft 365’s cloud-based technology being attacked by a ransomware named CERBER or RANSOM_CERBER. CAD has not been fully proven, TrendMicro researchers have stated that the ransomware in question can encrypt 442 file types using AES 265 and RSA encryption techniques. However, it seems like the coding of cloud ransomware is just in its initial stages since the only command that the ransomware can successfully deliver is to play an audio message in a computer-generated (creepy) voice (Sneed, 2016). These incidents may actually hint at a growth of ransomware in the IoT and cloud industries.

d)Industries

Ransomwares are not only built for the sole purpose of affecting regular citizens but are also built for a larger cause. Since malware development can be used for money making and has already become a booming business, malware developers have concentrated attacks on industries where more benefit could be derived. A report by Scientific American Magazine states that cyber criminals have been targeting and crippling important “institutions that everybody relies on” through different types of ransomware (Martin, 2017). According to a report by CSO, the three industries which have been most affected by ransomware attacks are the following: healthcare, government and education. Out of these, healthcare has been the most affected of all (Osborne, 2018). These industries are targeted more since they run 24/7 and thus need their updated files all the time. Serious threats can arise when institutional or organisational data from these industries is leaked or sold on the dark web. This is why these industries tend to pay for the ransom quicker than the other ransomware victims (Cylance, 2018).

Alarmingly, it has been made clear in a report by Cylance (called the 2017 Threat Report) that healthcare has obviously been targeted the most, and that law enforcement and/or ICT developers within the healthcare industry do not seem to have any methods to overcome these threats.

The pie charts below show the ransomware attacks performed on each type of industry over the span of a year (Kidron, 2017). Whilst there was a significant drop in the percentage of total ransomware attacks affecting almost every industry from 2016 to 2017, as shown in Fig. 5.7, the percentage of total ransomware attacks affecting the healthcare and food industries increased (by 24 percent for the healthcare industry). Scientific American Magazine (Martin, 2017) has reported that, aside from the Pennsylvania Senate incident, police stations such as the Swansea Police Department (2013) and Fire Departments in Maryland (2015) have been struck by ransomwares due to the simple fact that these organisations hold sensitive and important data about citizens which is vital for the proper functioning of the government. The police department of Swansea had to pay 750 USD just to recover their files but the Fire Department of Maryland opted not to pay in order to discourage further attacks.

Fig. 5.7.Industries impacted by ransomware (Kidron, 2017).

Scientific American Magazine’s report (Martin, 2017), delivered a clear warning to those in charge of law enforcement and cyber security. These cyber attacks are happening to the health industry and the government now, but a day will come when these malicious attacks could become worse. Critical infrastructures such as dams, power grids or worse could be attacked. Supervisory Control And Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems, which must be frequent users of the internet in order to function, could also be attacked. A report suggests cyber criminals have coded a ransomware which is dedicated to infecting SCADA systems and this ransomware is named LogicLocker (Kidron, 2017). This ransomware uses socket APIs and manipulates weak credential-authentication mechanisms into infecting the workstation. After infection, the ransomware does not encrypt the files but instead deletes all current authentication passwords and lets the command and control centre change the password to one of the attacker’s choice. This way, the company affected needs to pay the ransom for the new authentication details (Turpin and Harmsworth, 2001).

5.6.Preventing Ransomware Attacks

Different companies, different researchers and different anti-virus brands have different suggestions for preventing ransomware infection and spreading. Although different research studies have yielded different and sometimes opposing opinions on how to prevent ransomware, the general approach to preventing ransomware is always the same. Prevention can be done in two ways, which we call human prevention and advanced prevention.

a)Human Prevention

Information Dissemination: With the advancement of technology, people are now expected to gather information, be vigilant and educate themselves about the latest news in the digital society (Ali, 2017). Information about harmful software, not just ransomware, should be disseminated on different platforms so that they reach a wider audience. These platforms are as follows (Carbon Black, 2018):

•Mail (Physical Mail or Email)

•Newsletters

•Company or educational briefings

•Websites

•Reports

•Conferences

•Workshops

•Other media (Social Media etc.)

Although people can learn plenty from these sources, they should be wise enough to choose credible sources like the government or IEEE. Websites accessed for information regarding malwares should ideally be from anti-virus company blogs such as Kaspersky, Avast, Esset, etc.

b) Technical Prevention: A few technical but simple steps are suggested by multiple research studies in the field of malware. These steps are subcategorised by different digital vectors and most of these steps can be found online.

Back-up, Back-up, Back-up! (Rajpal and Kotov, 2014):

•Regularly Back-up Data: Back-up could be done in two different ways. Since there is a minimal chance of being hit by ransomware on both your device as well as a selected cloud application, users are advised to use a cloud back-up for important and sensitive files. This is the same reason why mobile ransomware does not encrypt files inside the mobile device but just locks the whole system instead.

•External Hard Disk Back-up: An external hard disk can also be suggested as a back-up measure, but researchers suggest that after back-up, external hard disks should be unplugged from the computers (Ali, 2017).

•Deploy User Account Control: This will help limit the access of ransomwares since most ransomware procedures require administrative permissions.

Email Security (O'Brien, 2017):

•Prevent downloads of unknown attachment files.

•Do not open spam mails if the mail is sent by an unknown user.

•Install special email defender applications that have real-time link following.

•Disable macro scripts on the files received via emails (O'Brien, 2017).

Anti-Virus:

•Anti-virus software should always be updated (Ali, 2017).

Other Important Preventive Measures:

•Disable remote services if not in use.

•Disable Bluetooth services if not in use.

•Limit access to unreliable websites (i.e. porn sites).

•Limit clicking on links provided by colleagues; instead, type the full address into the link bar.

Prevention for Mobile Users (Ismail, 2018):

•Apps should only be installed from trusted application stores.

•Check the permissions of the application being downloaded to see if the permissions are appropriate for the use of the application.

•Try as much as possible not to jailbreak iOS platforms

c)Advanced Prevention

Multiple research studies online have given suggestions for different approaches that bigger companies can use in preventing ransomware attacks. A few of the most effective advanced prevention techniques are (Zetter, 2016):

•Key back-up

•Process monitoring on Android platforms

•Using a connection monitor and connection breaker

•Honeypot techniques

Ways to Recover from Ransomware Attacks

An incomplete ransom attack is when the user gets to know that there is a possible ransomware attack due to appearances of .KRAB and/or GDCB-DECRYPT.txt files but the files are not yet encrypted. In order to recover from an incomplete ransom attack, the user is advised to automatically run the anti-virus application, which will do a virus scan of the system. It is also suggested that all devices infected with the ransomware should be disconnected from the network to protect cloud based or external back-up files (Brewer, 2016).

It is much harder to recover from a successful ransom attack. Organisations and researchers always ask a common question: To Pay or NOT To Pay? There is a good reason why researchers and organisations ask the question and it all has to do with the rate of success of file recovery and the eradication of the ransomware. Even when the ransom has been paid and the files decrypted, the user can never be sure that there are no more residual files from the ransomware left in the system (Brewer, 2016). The ransomware residual files can actually hide in mailboxes or directories without the user knowing and these files can be triggered at any time that the user is logged in to the computer. If the user opts to pay for the ransom, as previously stated, the ransomware should delete itself and hostage files should be returned without any alterations. The article (Brewer, 2016) finally suggests that buying a newer device is wiser especially if files are backed up online since this would help reduce the likelihood that the ransomware developer will produce more ransomware applications.

5.7.Conclusion

Although ransomwares are ranked as only the sixth most prominent malware in most cyber crime reports, ransomware is still a deadly malware. This is due to the fact that ransomware has the capability to do damage by means of infecting a user’s device and encrypting either all the files or the whole device. The damage will only stop when the victim has paid the ransom, and in most cases, the length of time given for the victim to pay the ransom is limited. If the deadline passes, multiple research studies have suggested that the victim would then be obliged to pay double the original ransom price. Multiple research studies also suggest that despite the victim being able to pay the ransom price, there is no guarantee of his files being returned and/or the ransomware being eradicated completely from the system.

Most of the prominent ransomwares such as WannaCry, CryptoLocker, TeslaCrypt, SimpleLocker, GandCrab, Petya and NotPetya use RSA 2048-bit encryption for the public key and AES 256-bit encryption to encrypt the victim’s data. Ransomware’s most prominent feature aside from encryption is the command and control feature which actually gave birth to a new type of malware. This step made Kaspersky predict that the new trend for 2018 is for a shift from ransomwares to cryptomining to occur. Cryptomining is a term that describes an attacker’s use of better ransomware.

Human Involvement

Human involvement in an attack is key since ransomware as a simple hard-coded software is useless. Ransomware cannot spread and infect devices on its own. Human involvement actually gives life to ransomware and the way ransomware infects devices. Humans create the ransomware software and humans spread the virus. As previously stated, most acquisitions of ransomwares occur due to a human falling for the spam email trick set by hackers. Social engineering, which was previously discussed, also plays a vital part since social engineers use psychology to achieve illegal ends. Humans are also responsible for activating the malware since most ransomware activation happens when .exe files disguised as PDF or Word files are executed. Cyber criminals are also responsible for the encryption of files inside the victim’s device. Finally, once the trap is set, humans are also responsible for choosing whether to pay or not to pay.

Human empowerment, along with the proper dissemination of information, is key, as it is important for the public to know what ransomwares are and how to fight the attacks. With proper education about this topic, humans can actually reduce the likelihood of these types of cyber attacks by means of early-stage prevention. Finally, ransomware attacks can only be prevented if the humans in the computing environment are willing to critically educate themselves about the digital advancements in different computing industries.

Chapter 6

Protecting and Securing Data Through Blockchain Across Industries

Stefan Kendzierskyj* and Hamid Jahankhani†

Northumbria University London, UK

*stefan.kendzierskyj@northumbria.ac.uk

†Hamid.jahankhani@northumbria.ac.uk

ABSTRACT

Blockchain is being viewed as a mechanism that can further protect and enhance the security of data due to its properties of immutability, auditability and encryption, whilst providing transparency between parties who may not know each other and who therefore are operating in a trustless environment. It’s true that blockchain has its roots in cryptocurrency applications and is still evolving for that purpose in the financial sector, but many other organisations across different industries are beginning to see the non-crypto use cases in which this mechanism can be used to record data that cannot be changed or reversed or as smart contracts (as a way to time-stamp transactions between parties). Consequently, blockchain is becoming extremely relevant and purposeful. Organisations have various options. They can run blockchain as permissionless (anyone can join), permissioned (invitations are required) or hybrid (like a consortium). They can also choose whether data should be held on-chain or off-chain in data lakes. With industry entering its fourth industrial revolution (Industry 4.0), the addition of blockchain as a complementary technology has its place; there are some industries very suited to the significant impact it may bring. Also, the advances made in areas such as Internet of Things and Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence may have considerable impact on the amount of data we collect for analysis and the ways in which we store, manage and analyse it. They may also increase the likelihood of cyber attacks and the ripple effects they cause. This has also become complicated, as cyber attacks have become much more sophisticated in recent years. Cyber attacks come in different configurations, and various industry sectors have suffered from a range of these different attack vectors, resulting in some devastating outcomes. These cyber attacks have manifested in the shape of ransomware, malware, manipulation methods, phishing and spear-phishing. Whilst data breaches are a serious incident, there is a growing concern in most organisations regarding attacks that are designed to have a more destructive effect, such as the Ukraine cyber attack in 2015 that resulted in a shutdown of the power grid, or the WannaCry ransomware attack in 2017 that caused widespread chaos with healthcare institutions unable to carry out any tasks since access to data/systems was unavailable.

Keywords: blockchain, Industry 4.0, smart contracts, cyber attacks, IoT, AI, ML, WannaCry, immutability, auditability

6.1. Introduction

With the fast-growing development of cloud-based architecture, smart technology such as Internet of Things (IoT) and many other new developments of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) have caused a large increase in data volumes and more complexities to arise during the process of finding a more secure and efficient way to handle and manage the data. This is heightened by the increasing cyber attacks and the wide range of attack vectors. Cyber attacks have become a lucrative and more organised criminal behaviour with the availability of ransomwareas-a-service, as an example. It’s becoming apparent that even with attention to the various business structures and methods to mitigate cyber security risks, such as continual review of policies/compliance, training, patching, deploying Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS), etc., the cyber security breach effect has not been lessened. In fact, more diverse types of cyber attacks are increasing and growing year on year at a faster and faster rate, particularly in the healthcare industry. Attacks on the healthcare industry account for more than 50% of all cyber attacks. From an organisational perspective, there are of course many advantages to having access to modern software and system developments, and to living in a ‘data on demand’ culture. Organisations will benefit in many ways, particularly with the more recent developments in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning. However, there is a feeling that data usage and access to data are not very strictly controlled. There are also concerns over the possible impact this may have. For instance, it may lead to criminal activity such as identity theft and victimisation.

With these points in mind, there is a growing motivation for industry to look at the benefits blockchain can offer in the shape of providing another layer of security and privacy to the organisation’s data and allowing the option to control data permission and use. This can provide an added layer of security which can work in harmony with the traditional cloud security systems and allow for a more secure and transparent way to handle data. The synergy between cloud and blockchain might be useful, especially as putting all data on the blockchain may place too heavy a burden on the blockchain in terms of processing, performance and scalability. Also, one must take into account the requirement of GDPR that those whose data have been collected by the organization must have the right of erasure. This prohibits the storage of personal data on a blockchain level. It might be useful in some cases to handle data off-chain and use blockchain as an immutable mechanism to capture details in chronological order and to authenticate access to data held off-chain in data lakes.

6.2.What Is Blockchain?

Blockchain is said to be one of the most disruptive computing paradigms after the Internet (Swan, 2015). The technology has advanced such that it is now more than just a means of financial and economic trading. Recently, different arms of industry have started to harness the technology to take advantage of its benefits and the many ways it can be applied.

The concept of blockchain was first circulated as a white paper (Satoshi, 2008), and created under the pseudonym Satoshin Nakamoto. As it was originally developed for use with a cryptocurrency (Bitcoin), blockchain is often referred to as Blockchain 1.0 when it is used with cryptocurrencies (Swan, 2015, p. ix). Blockchain 2.0 refers to the blockchain technology underlying smart contracts which go beyond just cash transactions, and Blockchain 3.0 describes blockchain technology which can be used in healthcare, government, intellectual property, etc. The healthcare industry is a good example of an industry in which issues surrounding privacy, security and access collide. It is also under pressure in several different directions, as there is a growing global demand for medical services as the elderly population grows and the number of elderly patients increases, an increase in the amount of data to be stored, an increase in data breaches, and so on. Blockchain adoption in the healthcare community is becoming widely accepted, as some surveys by leading industry providers indicate.

A recent survey (carried out by the IBM Institute for Business Value in 2017) of 200 healthcare executives (a mix of payers and providers across 16 countries) found that 16% were expecting a block-chain solution for healthcare to be deployed soon. This survey suggests that the percentage of healthcare executives who expected a blockchain solution to be deployed in their industry in 2017 is much higher than the percentage of executives from other sectors such as banking/finance and commerce who expected a blockchain solution to be deployed in their industry in 2017. This is despite the fact that blockchain methodology has been established in these sectors longer than it has been established in healthcare. It also serves as a timeline of how the healthcare industry will react to adoption.

6.2.1. Blockchain overview: How does it work?

Blockchain technology has allowed records to be ‘shared by all network nodes, updated by miners, monitored by everyone, and owned and controlled by no one’ (Swan, 2015, p.1).

Blockchain is based on a decentralised system — a distributed ledger database where identical copies of a sequential inventory of transactions are shared and maintained by numerous individuals over network nodes. Its qualities include being tamperproof, being immutable and being maintained by multiple parties through the use of a timestamped audit trail. The timestamp links to the previous record and is never removed, so becoming immutable. Cryptography is the key to the security used to link the chain of records. Multiple parties hold the consensus on the data and its validity rather than one individual (hence blockchain technology is decentralised; see Fig. 6.5 for an illustration). The exact procedure depends on the type of blockchain, but miners, or persons who validate the new transactions, mostly follow the same general steps to reach a consensus. Miners will try to solve a cryptographic puzzle for each block of transactions by matching a hash (randomly generated numbers and letters) to its target. The miner who solves the puzzle broadcasts to the network. This is validated by other miners, who approve and add copy to the first miner’s node. This method is usually referred to as ‘proof of work’. If this were, for example, the Ethereum blockchain, then the miner would be awarded ether (a form of coin to support or power the Ethereum network). The hash value can be controlled by the network, so, if it takes too long to solve the puzzle (more than the usual 14 seconds on Ethereum), adjustments are made to the computational puzzle. However, a large amount of computing power is required so a potential miner should evaluate the likely profitability of bitcoin mining before investing in the necessary equipment. The hash value is used to encrypt the contents of the block of transactions.

Fig. 6.5.Shift from central databases to distributed ledgers for information sharing (Ølnes et al., 2017).

In addition, when each transaction is made, a pair of keys is generated: a public key which can be accessed by all and a private key for the originator of the transaction. Only those with the private key can gain access to their cryptocurrency and authorise transactions. Also, one must rely on one’s private key to decrypt a message authorising a transaction.

Cryptography also offers a protection against attack, since more than 51% of the blockchain network would need to be compromised for a successful attack to occur. Engelhardt (2017) summarizes this immutability, which is a key component of blockchain. As he says, each block in the chain contains exact information on the creation of the block, the cryptographic signature in the preceding block in the chain and the transaction data being recorded in the block. The signature — a hash which is a unique record identifier — has a cryptographic sequence of a particular length and is alphanumeric. This signature uniquely determines the digital entity. This is how one can identify if the blockchain has been compromised by someone changing a previous record — there would be a break in the chain. Records cannot be removed, only added. This must be done with the approval of all the miners, who must reach consensus. This is one way in which blockchain technologies have difficulty complying with GDPR’s mandate that all users should have the ‘right to be forgotten’. If the information associated with a transaction is immutable, it cannot be forgotten.

Auditability is another important aspect of the blockchain as transparency allows all stakeholders to see the data. Auditability might also help improve the transparency of clinical research data, as discussed in this research study. When new transactions take place between parties, they are broadcast to the network for all to see and the network miners will verify them. It’s this collective verification that will only allow new blocks to be added. This is how the ‘trustless’ method works. It does not rely on a single entity to be the only authority to verify transactions, as with the centralised models. For various sectors of industry (Blockchain version 3.0), having additional data requirements such as smart contracts and flexibility in regulation makes sense, as this increases the trust people have in data.

6.2.2.Public and private blockchains

As there are different types of blockchain, the stakeholders need to decide who can enter a particular blockchain community. Each industry needs to be matched with the blockchain methods that are best suited to them. These methods can be either permissioned or permissionless. Understanding these two types of blockchain will help organisations decide what type of blockchain technology should be deployed for a particular data set and how they should allow permissions/authentication.

Permissionless Blockchains: Also referred to as public blockchains, these blockchains allow anyone to participate with no restrictions on the reading/submitting of transactions. Examples of these are Bitcoin and Ethereum. On the other hand, entry to public permissioned blockchains is restricted, but anyone can read/submit transactions.

Permissioned Blockchains: These private blockchains will restrict access to the network and control who may enter it. Transactions can only be validated by those recognised as authenticated on the ledger. Access to private permissioned blockchains is usually totally restricted. Examples of such blockchains include Bluemix by IBM or Rubix by Deloitte.

Consortium Blockchains: Approved entities validate transactions. A business ecosystem would find this type of blockchain more suitable since all parties have a say in deciding which data workflow process should be included, etc.

6.2.3.Blockchain data storage

A white paper that was selected as one of the winning papers from more than 70 submissions sent in for an ONC ideation challenge entitled The Use of Blockchain in Health IT and Health-Related Research (Deloitte, 2016) advises organisations on how they should evaluate the technical and confidentiality constraints of blockchain technology and how best to execute a particular model of block-chain technology depending on the type of data collected, the people who need access to that data, and how sensitive that data is. A compromise between speed/scalabilty and security may need to be made as storing large amounts of data off-chain presents potential difficulties with slow processing speeds and scaling. Security, however, is higher (Deloitte, 2016). The other option is providing encrypted links which direct a user to a separate centralised database when activated by the private key. It is also possible to store some standard data sets directly on the blockchain (this is beneficial for immediate permissioned access) and to otherwise rely on off-chain data links where appropriate.

For transaction purposes, blockchain can store data as two methods. These are summarized as follows:

On-chain: Data is stored on the blockchain structure. The advantage here is that the data would be immediately visible. However, storage size can be an issue and this method could prove to be much costlier than the other should file sizes become large. This method would generally be used for more standardised data in summary format.

Off-chain: This would suit larger data sets. In addition, data of any format can be stored, even data such as medical details, X-Ray images, MRI scans, etc. The access links are saved on blockchain and act as authenticated indicators to data stored in other centralised networks/databases. However, more integration and blended technology may be required if data is to be stored off-chain in data lakes. For instance, good management is required to ensure there is no data decay on the blockchain. Presumably though this is more likely to be a permissioned type blockchain and so management and governance would form part of the methodology.

6.2.4.Benefits of blockchain

Surveys mentioned earlier in this chapter indicate heavy support for blockchain in most industries. This is due to severe problems associated with interoperability, security, data integrity, and privacy issues in centralised networks, as well as other challenges faced by the users of these networks. As more people begin believing that blockchain will be part of their business in one shape or form, a few industry-leading white papers have emerged that voice a similar message.

The IBM Global Business Unit (2016) white paper, which was consulted by the government during their market research, states that ‘blockchain promises to put privacy and control of data back in the hands of citizens’. Blockchain might also be a good way to save costs. Costs in healthcare, for example, have risen dramatically over the years, and for some countries the rising costs herald a crisis. Over the last 10 years there has been a 60% increase in health expenditure (The World Bank, 2015). This is compounded with the issue of an aging population in developed countries. In the healthcare sector, blockchain is looked upon as the technology that can provide a solution by making possible the re-use of huge masses of anonymised healthcare data for clinical research. It not only protects the privacy of patients, but removes expensive middle layers and escrow services, thus connecting all stakeholders without great expense (Engelhardt, 2017).

Another interesting benefit of blockchain is that, due to the nature of its decentralisation, it may offer better protection against certain types of cyber attacks, such as the WannaCry ransomware attacks in 2017. In order for such an attack to succeed, a blockchain would need to be simultaneously attacked by numerous sites (Mattei, 2017). It is important that users are better protected as there has been a recent rise in identity theft attacks by malicious outsiders. The data showing this is provided and analysed later in this chapter.

The section below gives similar use cases across many industry sectors. Healthcare is referenced in places as a specific industry example due to the many possible applications of blockchain within the health industry.

Interoperability, transparency and longitudinal healthcare records — The data collected by an organisation is often trapped in data silos, and therefore not integrated. This can make it difficult to analyse and places restrictions on how it can be used. Ideally, there should be interoperability between the different systems in which different data sets are stored. In addition, those in charge of each system should be held accountable for how the data within that system is collected, stored and used. Other issues in this category include the limited control an individual has over their data, and the occurrence of data breaches which might result in data loss, or perhaps even identity theft. Blockchain technology can help by eliminating data silos and providing a more coherent and seamlessly integrated data model. Access to the data would be controlled through cryptographic methods, but all the relevant parties would be allowed access. These changes could lead to innovations such as longitudinal healthcare records for patients, which could be analysed to improve health outcomes.

Privacy and Security — Confidentiality, integrity, availability and authenticity (CIAA) are four information security concepts that should ideally be adhered to when data is being dealt with. In reality, internal issues such as accidental data loss, and issues caused by external vectors such as targeted malicious behaviour for the purpose of identity and data theft, are widespread. As previously mentioned, industry is trying to tackle this by carrying out the day-to-day actions that will help mitigate risk and continually learning new methods to keep data secure. Blockchain can help by providing an additional layer of security with the use of encryption. The use of a decentralised and distributed ledger system would increase the integrity of the data. Data encryption, as well as more complex permission settings, will provide good controls for a securely authenticated data exchange.

Time stamping and chronological ordering — If records and data are held in silos, there is more chance of corruption, fraud, the abuse of traceability and so on. One of the benefits blockchain can offer is its undeniable immutability. Even if blockchain is used only for authentication, perhaps to allow data to be stored in a ‘data lake’ (a centralised data storage solution which can be created in the cloud), the fingerprints associated with this type of activity would be time-stamped and kept in chronological order (as with smart contracts). No one would be able to tamper with the records. Depending on the type of blockchain, parties can then make use of smart contracts to help provide greater efficiency and integration.

Procurement and Contract Process — Using the properties of blockchain that make it suitable for use in smart contracts will help relieve a lot of the complex processes, negotiations and supply chain issues currently faced. This will be done by streamlining the process to promote efficiency and reduce cost. It will then be possible to provide automated supplier contracts and analytics to maximise productivity and control.

6.2.5.Potential security issues and limitations on blockchain

Whilst support behind blockchain technology is growing, and whilst the benefits of blockchain technology to both clients and industry are becoming better known, one must not overlook the risk factors associated with blockchain technology. By knowing these risks and carrying out further research alongside blockchain use, one can contribute to the formation and development of alternative procedures that may make blockchain deployment safer or mitigate its risks.

Quantum Computing — It has been much debated whether quantum computing poses a future threat to cryptography. In order to do so, quantum computing would need to be large and reliable so that it can perform millions of quantum bits (qubits) to break current cryptographic algorithms (Aumasson, 2017). As Aumasson mentions, it’s not yet known if quantum computing is scalable or fault-tolerant and general consensus believes it is not able to break current cryptographic algorithms yet. But it is good to know that cryptographers are looking at post-quantum cryptography (as the back-up plan for future-proofing).

Irretrievable Data — Blockchain data access will be facilitated with a key. This use of private key security will allow a user to control their own data, but if the key is lost, data will become irretrievable. However, solutions can be put in place. It is possible to introduce a ‘back door’ concept, but that potentially may replace one issue with another (Engelhardt, 2017).

Scalability and Performance — Further investigations must be carried out on the different types of blockchain and script execution. For example, the average transaction time on the Ethereum blockchain is approximately 14 seconds, while the average transaction time of Bitcoin is 10 minutes. It’s well known in cryptography that speed and security have an inverse effect on each other. Time is required to achieve consensus over the blockchain network, and to do the computation needed to verify a transaction. This will probably not be a show stopper, however. Over time, technology will improve and so too will speed and computation time.

Malicious Attacks — Xu (2016) researched attacks (both malicious attacks and fraud) that one can be exposed to while using blockchain technology. He comments upon these attacks and recommends defensive and preventative measures.

Google DeepMind Scenarios — The Google DeepMind project is an example of the mismanagement of data. In that particular case, patient data was recorded through an app. In order for the app to be created, the NHS allowed Google to access large amounts of sensitive medical information, not only from users of the app, but from the records of nearly 1.6 million NHS patients. Controversially, it was claimed that ‘implied consent’ had been given for the information to be released. This seems to suggest a lack of transparency and has muddied privacy and security concerns.

6.3.Threats to Mission Critical Data: Vulnerabilities and Cyber Attacks

The previous section in this chapter gave a formalised appraisal of how blockchain works, including its methods and key attributes. This section highlights the increasing number of vulnerabilities and the increasing scale of various types of cyber attacks, in order that the complexity of these attacks and the extent of the devastation caused can be understood. A high percentage of cyber attacks occur because a malicious outsider attempts to commit identity theft. There can be many types of malicious outsiders, ranging from users of low level malware-for-hire to hacktivists to state-sponsored attackers.

For example, the 2015 cyber attack on Ukraine’s power grid was initiated through phishing attacks, but it took six months for the cyber attackers to gather the security credentials they needed to compromise the SCADA network before the main thrust of the attack took place. Whilst 27 power distribution centres were knocked out of operation, the attack was made stronger by creating interference and inundating the call centres supporting the 225,000 customers that were affected with call traffic. During these chaotic types of attacks and potentially even during the build-up to the attacks, cyber attackers may be accessing core mission-critical data. This type of theft is masked by the chaotic nature of events. In essence, this also helps strengthen the case for blockchain, since it’s clear there are good use cases for blockchain technology that can be applied to various industries. However, there should also be another layer of security that offers protection to mission-critical data, since it is likely that cyber attackers will attempt to breach it. At least then if a cyber attack is successful, the core data remains uncontaminated.

It has now become extremely important that every business should have a set of key information governance policies so that they can retain control of and ensure the safety of assets and information. It is also hoped that this will improve user confidence in how the assets are stored, protected and processed. Information governance is also an important part of an organisation’s structure as it tells the Executive Board what the risk treatment plan should be. The risk treatment plan should match the business risk appetite. There are valuable benefits to managing risk in this way.

There are also various frameworks that contain good practices that an organisation can use to deliver IT service management such as ITIL. These frameworks complement policies like ISO 27001 or CMMi. They help in training staff, improving the quality of IT services and provide a backbone to help monitor risk and improvements. This is all designed to assist in identifying vulnerabilities and taking note of lessons learned so that everything about how the current landscape is changing can be documented. Based on this information, new strategies can be developed and followed. There are different types of cyber attacks and a wide range of cyber attacks within each type, and this variety can lead to a multitude of issues both with regard to the organisations affected by ransomware and the users of services provided by those organisations. The possible consequences are unknown, but it is likely that the users’ data will be compromised in some way, as a cyber breach generally leads to a data breach. This is where the problems begin for the client.

Organisations can bring forth technical countermeasures to tighten security against attacks and highlight user awareness through education but all this still does not provide protection to the client once the cyber attack succeeds and data is taken. The awareness through education is needed to lessen the chance for an attack to succeed, but there is more thought being given to using blockchain as another added layer of security to protect the data. The data need not necessarily be held on-chain (as it can be stored off-chain) but the access and authentication would be initiated through blockchain and all fingerprint information would be stored on blockchain with all the attributes mentioned in earlier sections.

6.3.1.Ransomware

What is Ransomware?

There has been a significant increase in the volume and diversity of ransomware attacks over the last two years (see Fig. 6.6 for growth details). Attack formations have become more complicated, and the perpetrators of ransomware have progressed from script kiddies to crime-for-hire (ransomware-as-a-service) and sophisticated hackers. As Parent and Cushack (2016) mention, ‘a new layer cake in cybercrime’ has arisen. However, attack success relies on the victim acting as the catalyst to initiate the chain of events.

Ransomware is sophisticated and malicious software that blocks the victim’s access to their files or that threatens to publish or make available the victim’s data (based on cryptovirology). What usually happens next is the request for a ransom to be paid so that the victim can access their files again. Over the last five years the extent and complexity of ransomware has increased, and some organisations have taken to paying the ransoms through digital currencies such as Bitcoin. The victim dilemma is there is no sure way to know after paying a ransom whether the attacker will release the decryption key. There are some victims that have paid the ransom and were successful in accessing the data once again. Others have paid but the cyber attackers did not release the decryption keys. Yet others paid and received the decryption keys but they did not work. There is always the possibility as well that after the organisation pays the initial ransom, the cyber criminals may continue to ask for additional ransom.

Fig. 6.6.Ransomware increases (McAfee Labs, 2018).

Without doubt, attacks are on the increase. Just three years ago, GCHQ and the Ministry of Defence warned the government of a serious cyber attack and suggested that the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) was a step in the right direction (Hutchins, 2017). In this newspaper article (Hutchins, 2017), General Sir Richard Barrons also mentions that the NCSC is not as powerful or as integrated as the US Cybercom model.

How does Ransomware work?

The intrusions made by ransomware are usually carried out using a Trojan (to the user this seems a legitimate file but is the disguised malware). This can occur due to a vulnerability in the network or because the user opened the file (often as an email attachment). The attackers rely on the curiosity in human nature which often leads us to click on a link without thinking of the consequences, even when we are unsure of whom the sender is. This causes the payload to run a program that then either locks the system or appears to lock it (Scareware program). The consequences for the user depend upon the type of payload downloaded by the ransomware. The level of sophistication of the attack depends on the attacker’s capabilities but there are many ‘malware programs’ for hire on the dark web (Tor/similar network) so even a moderately skilled attacker can cause a massive impact on single or multiple organisations. These malware businesses selling cryptovirology tools are collectively known as ‘ransomware-as-a-service’, as noted by Young and Yung (2017). The payloads can vary from simple applications that appear with fake warnings to top-end programs using strong encryption such that the only way to deactivate the malware is with the attacker’s decryption key (cryptoviral). Young and Yung (2017) describe the explosion of cryptovirology and how formidable a threat it is, with victims that include individuals, hospitals, police precincts, universities, transportation systems and government offices making daily news.

How is it spread?

Social engineering is the key skill used by attackers to spread ransomware, as they know it is easy to trick a user into opening a malicious email attachment. The attackers use many ingenious ways to disguise the malware as fake PDF/Word files. The issue is that the victim may not know the sender of the email or the fake company but as the email is made to appear official, often will click the email attachment. Other methods include tricking the victim to confirm, for example, an online order. There may be ways the attacker can convince the victim to run an embedded program. As an example of the speed with which malware can spread, the WannaCry ransomware attack began on 12 May 2017 and in just a day had infected 230,000 computers in over 150 countries. This is covered in the article Strategic Comments (2017).

How can we prevent Ransomware?

With the increase in ransomware, various individuals and organisations have offered focused guidance on how to respond to incidents/attacks. McGoogan (2017) lists a number of core rules to follow in the Telegraph newspaper shortly after the WannaCry attack. There are quite a few basic rules that will stop most attacks occurring and some that will make paying the ransomware unnecessary. It has become evident that ransomware appears to be the most profitable malware and that the amount of ransomware will not decrease soon (Cisco, 2016). Organisations are starting to understand the risks and to take proactive measures such as those recommended by Kaspersky Lab and Intel Security. They have given advice on how to avoid attacks and on what to do if attacked. They have also shared actual known decryption keys with the public (No More Ransom, 2017).

The following are generally recommended for most organisations:

File backups — This should be part of any Business Continuity Plan (BCP) and set of Disaster Recovery (DR) procedures so that in case of an attack, if the system is taken down, at least the system can be recovered to the point before the attack.

Emails, attachments and websites — As part of their IT Policy, organisations will have guidelines which advise staff not to open any emails or attachments from unknown or suspicious senders. This can also be part of training/awareness programs. Alert reminders can also be created to warn staff. These alert reminders could be triggered when staff members log on to the system.

Patching and installing updates — This is a critical aspect of attack prevention that is the responsibility of the Information and Communications Technology (ICT) department. Patch vulnerability was one of the reasons that some of the NHS locations were exposed to WannaCry.

Incident Response Team and Preparation — For example, there should be Service Improvement Plans and tasks concerning fast identification and mitigation allocated to specific team members. The core incident team should practice their response to the situation like they do with BCP and DRP scenarios, but the scenarios should be specific to ransomware attacks.

Non-payment of ransom — Admittedly, this is easier said than done, as there will be great pressure on the victim to pay the ransom in order to retrieve the data. It is advisable not to pay the ransom as it is not guaranteed that the decipher process will be released. It may also lead to more requests for ransom or more concerted attacks.

Regular Training — This is vital. As Arndt (2017) mentions, “organizations that phish-exercise their staff at least four to eight times a year have dramatically better awareness than organizations that don’t do it or that do it just once or twice a year.”

The most complex part to contain or control in handling cyber security risks is the human element. No matter what amount of training or what training programme is used in organisations to heighten awareness of attacks made by malicious outsiders, it seems evident that social engineering attacks such as phishing will still increase due to human curiosity. Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPSs) will help, but instead one could add an extra layer of security through blockchain. This would allow high value data (sensitive or personal data) to be protected so that even if attacks have succeeded there are other hurdles that require defeating encryption to overcome before a data breach occurs.

6.3.2.Social engineering: Phishing and spear-phishing

Phishing and spear-phishing techniques often contribute to the success of ransomware. As ransomware became sophisticated, so too has social engineering. Phishing has been around for some time and until users stop clicking on email from unknown senders or enabling programs in attachments, the attackers will still continue to succeed. In 2016, phishing attacks rose by 65% compared to in 2015, as mentioned by Sharma (2017), and are set to increase further again, with organisations more in the sights of the attackers than individuals. Social media may bring many benefits, but it also offers attackers a wealth of additional information that gives rise to more sophisticated phishing methods and increases the likelihood of a victim opening an infected email/program. Steer (2017) notes the existence of a more dangerous threat known as spear-phishing, where the email is targeted at specific individual employees. Attackers now search social media to make an email look convincingly genuine to mask the tracks of the ransomware. This ‘familiarity’ of appearance to a user makes this method a very dangerous entry point. The even newer dangers of malvertising include malwares that no longer require users to ‘click’ links to activate them.

Manipulation Methods: It is interesting to see the evolution/development of new attack methods, but successful entry to the victim’s system relies on methods like phishing or spear-phishing that are activated because victims do not easily change their behavioural patterns. There are some more manipulative means of entry; attackers can use sub-domains, hidden URLs (links hidden under plain text), misspelt URLs (bought domains that look similar to the real site e.g. google.com) and IDN homograph attacks.

Script-Based Malware: A McAfee (2017) lab report indicates a rise in malware scripting techniques. JavaScript, VBScript, PHP, Powershell, etc, are used to distribute ransomware, and in some cases, are even used in the ransomware (e.g. Nemucod ransomware uses PHP and JavaScript). Attackers take this route because doing so allows them to evade detection. This is the reason why this newer technique has seen a sharp rise over the last two years (McAfee, 2017).

Internet of Things (IoT): Yaqoob et al. (2017) discuss how there are expected to be 26 billion sensors and IoT devices by 2020. These will be deployed across wearable devices, connected smart homes, cars, health, utility, etc. On the one hand, it is a great technological advancement, but as Yaqoob et al. (2017) have discovered, over 70% of IoT devices are vulnerable to attacks. With the growth of ransom-ware it is inevitable that IoT offers a vast surface attack area: see Fig. 6.7 as per Yaqoob et al. (2017). It is important that confidentiality, integrity and availability (CIA) should be preserved in tandem with technological advancement. Safe ways to protect IoT from malware should take priority.

Botnets and other IoT issues: Yaqoob et al. (2017) state that ransomware can also be penetrated using botnets inside IoT networks. These botnets are usually activated through phishing and may compromise the whole IoT network. The research goes on to say that attackers can inject ransomware-as-a-service into the cloud and the ransomware may appear as a ‘legitimate service’ to the user. More research shows the extent of the potential issues with IoT. Some possible attacks include thermostat hacking (turning the temperature up), Flocker ransomware (which locks the smart TV with malware embedded in a fake movie) and Android Simplocker (which affects Android wearable devices). There have also been some tests on the practicality of ransomware used to attack smart bulbs.

Fig. 6.7.Security concerns in IoT (Yaqoob et al., 2017).

Malvertising and Ransomware: There has been a sharp increase in the use of malvertising to propagate malware, specifically ransomware (RiskIQ Research, 2017). This new type of technique threatens the benefits from digital marketing many organisations have legitimately enjoyed. Now, users may block ads for fear that they have become attack vectors for deploying malware. Users need not even click on the malicious ads and can be infected just by visiting the website. This is in itself a new technique that provides infection without user interaction (e.g. the Astrum exploit using a vulnerability in Flash). Palmer (2017) reported that a few UK Universities were hit with this ransomware, but it is very hard to consolidate the extent of the attacks as many education and government-type organisations resist openly discussing attacks made on them for fear of negative publicity.

Future Type of Ransomware Attacks: Future ransomware attacks may come in new forms. For instance, Mansfield-Devine (2016) suggests that ransomware distributed through mobile devices and the cloud will become increasingly common. This can be quite a concern since a user can upload an infected file to the cloud and unknowingly disperse it to the rest of the community (as users might assume it’s a legitimate ‘safe’ service to download). Also, more and more enterprises are seeking cloud- and SaaS-based models, believing them to be safer than on-premise models, even if this may not be the case. This is why a more thorough analysis of cloud security needs to be carried out. Educating humans not to click on unauthorised links or to be vigilant in checking the source of a link before clicking on it will be an ongoing process, and it still will not solve the problem of how to control data access and storage, or, in the event of a cyber breach, how to give the malicious attackers more hurdles to overcome by adding layers of security such as blockchain and encryption. Also, with blockchain there has been further research on using artificial intelligence (AI) to detect malicious outsider attacks and the patterns associated with them. This adds further levels of security so that the blockchain stays protected.

6.4.Cyber Breaches and Client Data Theft Concerns

It has already been highlighted that industry is under pressure from cyber threats which may result in data theft. Table 6.1 (breachlevelindex.com, 2018) shows the number of data breaches in each industry sector. Healthcare leads with the greatest number of breaches due to the value of the data. The data report and other extended reports on the site are provided by Gemalto, an organisation that collates and aggregates information about worldwide data breaches in various industries and that proactively monitors reports of data breaches worldwide through breachlevelindex . com. It can be assumed that the data collected is high-quality quantitative data. In their other reports, Gemalto measure a breach in terms of the data records lost/stolen, the type of breach, the source of the breach, how far the breach has affected the industry sectors in question and the risk factor of the breach. They have developed a scoring system to measure the risk factor of the breach, which is as follows:

Table 6.1.Cyber security breaches 2017 industry comparison (breachlevelindex.com, 2018).

source: BREACHLEVELINDEX.COM

1 – 2.9 (minimal)

3 – 4.9 (moderate)

5 – 6.9 (critical)

7 – 8.9 (severe)

9 – 10 (catastrophic)

Fig. 6.8.Data taken from the breachlevelindex.com site.

Fig. 6.9.Comparison showing the extent of the types of breaches (breachlevelindex.com, 2018).

6.4.1.Cyber breach analysis

Cyber-attack vectors can be categorised in the following way, which helps us define the type of breach and the source of the breach (breachlevelindex.com, 2018):

Type of Breach:

•Identity Theft

•Nuisance

•Account Access

•Existential Data

•Financial Access

•Financial Loss

Source of Breach:

•Accidental Loss

•Malicious Insider

•Malicious Outsider

•Hacktivist/State Espionage

From the Breachlevelindex analysis shown in Figs. 6.8 and 6.9, two factors stand out, that is, that the greatest number of records are lost due to accidental loss and that malicious outsiders committing identity theft have the next biggest impact. From these trends it seems that better training should be given to help mitigate the accidental loss and reduce the number of records lost. Staff members should also be vigilant to prevent malicious outsiders from committing identity theft. The Breachlevelindex analysis also discovered that there were fewer data breaches in which encryption was used.

6.4.2.Deep web impacts to the client

It is extremely unpleasant for a victim to discover that criminals have access to their identities and can use them to commit crimes because the organisation they have shared their data with has been breached by a malicious attacker. At least with GDPR in place, the authorities must be notified of data breaches within 72 hours or a penalty will be imposed. The consequences are worse when identity theft has occurred. A stolen credit card can be cancelled if the theft is discovered in time by the victim, but one’s identity cannot be changed. It is possible to steal someone’s identity with the aid of medical records accessed through an attack on a healthcare organisation. Medical records hold valuable data points that map a person’s identity. If the data breach goes unannounced or is announced too late, the attacker might have enough time to plan how best to use the stolen data.

The large-scale WannaCry ransomware attack (BBC news, 2017) highlights the dangers of a large-scale data breach. In one of these, no one really knows how far the identity theft will go. On the deep web, the value of medical data is said to be ten times that of stolen credit card numbers (Sulleyman, 2017) and if big data sets are available they can go for large sums of money. As a result, it can be very lucrative to attack the healthcare industry. There likely is a much larger adverse effect on those that suffered from identity theft and criminal victimisation because of the data breach, as identity theft is a deep violation of the patient’s privacy. The loss of data surrounding one’s identity is of course a problem, but so too can be having one’s sensitive medical history (e.g. HIV information) made public. Therefore the impact is far deeper and greater on the victim than a loss of credit card details would have been.

6.5.Is Blockchain the Answer Industry is Looking for Regarding Securing Data?

Many worldwide have considered how blockchain may fit into industry environments and into a number of different use cases. It is certain that a new technology such as blockchain has both risks and benefits, but more individuals and organisations are adopting and accepting the use of blockchain. This is probably because this technology provides a much better service than is otherwise available to its users and the organisations using it, whilst also offering higher levels of security. When we look at various industry sectors, it is possible to quickly understand these drivers, and also how blockchain facilitates securing data privacy.

-Healthcare: The healthcare industry suffers the most cyber attacks, and this is reason enough to find a way to better protect the core data. It is a well-known fact that healthcare data is worth 10 times the value of financial credit card data when offered by criminals on the dark net. In 2018, millions of records were breached, and consequently, more people have become aware of the impact of identity theft. Also, although medical records are now kept in electronic rather than in paper form, the main issue is that currently records are still mostly stored in silo environments. This causes major inefficiencies for providers and patients, and makes it difficult for a seamless healthcare data interchange to occur. If blockchain is applied, longitudinal medical histories can be generated from the data that used to be in various silos. Blockchain also puts the patient in control of their data, and also allows them to control who has access to it. Blockchain can also be used to store other types of sensitive data that are increasing in volume e.g. WBAN (wireless body area network) data that collects medical data through sensors and automatically syncs with storage systems. Since these storage systems contain sensitive data they are again of attraction to cyber attackers and so a great deal of attention needs to be paid to security.

Another use case is drug traceability. As it stands, counterfeit drugs are estimated to account for 50% of all drugs in low-income countries, with a global market range of $200 billion (DrugPatentWatch, 2017). Counterfeit drugs may not cure the patient, or may kill them. Blockchain allows the creation of a supply chain in which one can record all transactions without anyone being able to tamper with the records. The result is a transparent method to secure the chain of custody and data.

-Supply Chain: In the world of manufacturing and logistics, there are no longer small networks or groups of organisations. Instead, there are large and wide ecosystems comprised of multiple parties, from those processing raw materials to manufacturers to wholesalers and distributors. Each entity has to manage its processes, data and systems. Again, interoperability is important here if one is to avoid having islands of data, or duplicating the data. Blockchain can help all the parties record data so that they have a permanent record of every transaction that is immutable. Products would be traceable and tracking through the chain of custody would be ensured. In the case of the food industry, keeping records of products and tracing them to their source is essential (Marr, 2018). An example is Walmart, which uses blockchain to keep track of its pork sourced from China. Among the types of data stored are the sources of the meat, where it’s processed and stored, and its expiry date. In another example, De Beers utilises Blockchain for auditability and in order to track diamonds from the point where they are mined to the point where they are sold to consumers. They use their record as proof of their ethics and of the non-contamination of the diamonds they sell with conflict diamonds. Consequently, consumers are certain they are ethical and genuine (Marr, 2018). Smart contracts can also be deployed as part of the blockchain structure so that time-stamping can be used and payments or penalties can be triggered after transactions are recorded.

-Identity Management: With the world we live in as it is, online transactions that leave a digital footprint are unavoidable. Online transactions generally require that personal or financial details must be disclosed. The more online transactions one conducts, the more databases the information is stored on. Typically, the information will be cloned and might end up on numerous other databases (Pinto, 2018). The information in these datasets is accessed by other third party providers who in turn clone these datasets, usually without the owner of the data knowing. This takes ownership and control away from the individual concerned. Blockchain can give individuals the ability to deploy encrypted digital identities, making multiple passwords and identification names unnecessary. Estonia is one of the few countries that has adopted blockchain as an infrastructure to power the Estonia ID card that has replaced a number of other cards covering services such as (Thomson Reuters, 2018):

•legal travel ID for Estonian citizens travelling within the EU

•national health insurance

•proof of identification when logging into bank accounts

•digital signatures

•i-Voting

•checking medical records, submit tax claims, etc.

•using e-Prescriptions

—Critical National Infrastructure (CNI): Critical National Infrastructure (CNI) can be the physical or virtual systems, assets, facilities, processes and networks that are needed for a country to operate. Cyber attacks on critical infrastructure are increasing in velocity and are caused by advanced threat actors (CERT-UK, 2016). The threat to CNI is very real as there have been a number of successful attacks over recent years. The computer systems underpinning CNI that, for example, hold sensitive data in healthcare facilities or Industrial Control Systems (ICS), or that operate, control and monitor physical structures such as nuclear power plants, electricity grids, and railway networks, may have a number of vulnerabilities that cyber attackers are drawn to (Logsdon, 2016). The Ukraine power grid attacks and WannaCry were explained earlier in the chapter, and it’s possible these large-scale devastating attacks that leave systems in chaos have more sinister reasons for their occurrence than data theft. Currently there is research looking at how blockchain can support the cyber physical systems so that blockchain-distributed data storage, IoT sensing technology and cloud-based delivery systems work together harmoniously (Dong et al., 2018).

—Financial Aid Tracking and Transparency: Blockchain is being used in the tracking of foreign aid as one of the biggest challenges here is transparency. The issue is that as the chain of custody passes through various middlemen (this is what generally happens before international aid is received by a particular country) the tracking of the distribution of funds becomes difficult (Hjønnevåg, 2018). The immutability, tracking and auditability of blockchain can minimize fraudulent activity. For example, there is no need for cash to exchange hands in the Zaatari refugee camp as the World Food Program uses biometric technology as well as blockchain technology. A retinal scanner controls the provision of food, and every refugee’s identity is digitally stored in a biometric database. The point of sale verifies the buyer’s identity through the retinal scanner. The sale is recorded on the World Food Program blockchain so that it can be tracked, and to acknowledge that the account has been settled. Greater accountability will allow us to raise funds more easily as one of the concerns of fund raising is that fraudulent activity will take place and funds will be misused. Blockchain technology will therefore improve the welfare of those who need it most.

—Insurance and Claims Adjudication: Insurance and claims organisations face fragmented IT systems and data held in silos. These often create inefficiencies, delays, higher than necessary costs and fraudulent activity. Data volumes are increasing, especially with the large amounts of data being generated by IoT that make it necessary to sift through large datasets. Through blockchain, the verification of claims/payments data from third parties can be automated, and insurance companies can easily verify transactions. As a result, the records will show only one version of the truth (Cummings, 2018). The security of blockchain can provide assurance that there is no duplication of data and smart contracts ensure a better customer engagement cycle.

—Intellectual Property and Media: Intellectual Property (IP) has faced many challenges, especially with the availability of digitalised content which can be shared with minimal hassle through avenues like the Internet. The cost of software piracy in the US in 2015 was reported at over $9 billion (manufacuring.net, 2016). If IP rights are registered with blockchain technology (in the case of patents, for example), it will be much easier to verify who owns them. Any infringement can be challenged, and doubts can be counteracted by the use of smart contracts in which terms of engagement are set out.

6.6.Conclusions

The benefits of blockchain look to be clear and straightforward; blockchain technology can help to secure and protect data in many industry sectors. The defined properties of blockchain include the enhanced security due to encryption, the immutability that prevents any tampering, the auditability which depends on the use of chronological time-stamping/smart contracts and the transparency that allows precise tracking. In this chapter, the importance of securing data, especially in the sectors under heavy cyber attack such as the healthcare or energy sector, was discussed.

If we consider blockchain a mechanism which works in harmony with other technologies then it has the potential to offer an additional layer of security to protect mission-critical data. This could be deployed in harmony with the practices of rolling out policies/compliance, training, keeping patching up to date, IDPS and so on. These are to further protect the privacy of an individual’s data and enhance the security through methods of encryption which provide that added layer of security should traditional methods break down due to sophisticated cyber attacks and targeted methods used to obtain data and commit identity theft. Also, with the recent emergence of IoT and the value-add it brings to many organisations, it is important to consider how the huge increase in data should be handled and kept secure. The billions of additional smart wearable devices in use today may contain sensitive data on individuals which should be protected by a combination of traditional security methods and blockchain.

Blockchain security is itself interesting. More research in machine learning and algorithms may also help in protecting blockchain as machine learning and algorithms can detect intrusions from and recognise patterns in data collected through behavioural monitoring and profiling (Xu, 2016). This will help strengthen the defences against malicious attackers and prevent them from succeeding if the method is recognised by AI. The wider adoption of blockchain will also help protect users against malicious activity as more effort will be expanded on developing prevention systems. Certainly, blockchain has many applications, and can be made to work in synergy with traditional cyber security mechanisms. For the time being, blockchain is a formidable and strong security option. It is a useful mechanism which can provide support in many industries which collect sensitive and personal data, particularly in industry sectors which are most vulnerable to cyber attack.
