Chapter 8

GDPR Compliance: Incident Response and Breach Notification Challenges

Orret R. Grey* and Raymond Brown†

QA Higher Education & Northumbria University London, UK

*orret.grey@northumbria.ac.uk,

†ray.brown@northumbria.ac.uk

ABSTRACT

Over the last decade, the prevalence of new computing devices with greater processing power and ubiquitous internet-ready devices helped to facilitate the creation and sharing of vast amounts of data. This has brought increased risks to personal data and rendered previous regulations on data privacy less effective in the new digital age. The GDPR regulation was introduced across EU states on the 25th of May 2018 and brought radical changes that govern activities around the processing and sharing of data and how the protection of personal data is administered by various organisations. GDPR necessitates the re-assessment of existing frameworks in order to meet new requirements outlined in the articles and recitals of the regulation. This research addresses the existing challenges of integrating GDPR into incident response and breach notification plans, and proposes a conceptual Decision Support System (DSS) to address the challenges identified. Existing industry standard frameworks such as ISO27001, NIST, and SANS were analysed alongside Focus Group interviews with subject matter experts to gather feedback on the relevance and applicability of a DSS to meet GDPR compliance requirements. The findings of the study reveal a number of compliance gaps in existing incident handling frameworks which could be mitigated by employing decision support techniques as proposed in the study.

Keywords: GDPR, incident response, data breach notification, decision support systems

8.1.Introduction

An incident response plan is a formal document that outlines a series of measures to promptly identify and neutralise security threats and mitigate the associated risks to personal and sensitive information. It is typically established through technical controls, policies, procedures, and designated response teams with specific responsibilities. The proliferation of cyber attacks and important changes in regulation warrants a radical re-assessment of existing governance frameworks and security policies, in order to gain full visibility of data that traverse the internal and external sphere of an organisation.

Articles 33 and 34 of GDPR explicitly outline requirements for reporting data breaches within a specific timeframe and for organisations to demonstrate reasonable steps have been taken to secure personal data (GDPR, 2016). GDPR promulgates the foundation for a risk-based approach to assess the risk to personal data, and for privacy protection measures to be introduced by default when collecting and processing personal data. This requires organisations who are either controllers or processors of personal data to assess the risks relating to the rights and freedom of data subjects and formulate appropriate policies and security measures to protect personal data (Garber, 2018). This indicates that complying with GDPR necessitates a clear and consistent approach towards interpreting and integrating the relevant articles and existing incident response and breach notification plans.

The aim of this research is to investigate compliance challenges by formulating the following questions:

1.What are the main challenges and enablers of implementing GDPR into an incident response and breach notification plan?

2.What decision support process or system could be developed to address the challenges identified?

3.What method could be adopted to assess the relevance and usability of the design for meeting the new requirements of incident response and breach notification challenges?

8.1.1.Background

In recent years, the upsurge in cyber attacks and data breach incidents has become a phenomenon that represents an existential threat for organisations who fail to formulate robust security policies and stringent measures to safeguard valuable data. Appropriate preparation plans are imperative for effectively responding to the evolving threats that could cause irreparable damage to business operations and reputation. This helped to precipitate a paradigm shift in recognising the value of personal and business information, as well as the importance of adapting to the changing legal and regulatory landscape.

Despite this recognition and various measures taken by organisations to implement security policies via existing incident handling frameworks, new requirements for breach notification and communication in GDPR have created potential gaps in compliance that need to be re-examined. Moreover, there are no specific recommendations in GDPR that organisations can check against to verify they are fully compliant. According to Hedley and Jacobs (2017), verifying compliance will be done through either external audits or a process of self-assessment by individual organisations who interpret and implement relevant areas of the regulation into their existing incident handling frameworks with policies and procedures.

This indicates that organisations will need to justify and demonstrate to their relevant supervisory authority that stringent security safeguards are in place for securing personal data. The research director of Gartner, Mark Horvath (2018), elaborated that, even if appropriate security policies are established, organisations could still be held accountable under GDPR if employees intentionally or accidentally precipitate serious data breach incidents.

In 2015, a reported cyber attack on telecommunications group Talk Talk precipitated several deleterious consequences that included a rapid decline in stock market value, a loss of revenue amounting to £80 million, and the alienation of many of the customers affected. The Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) conducted subsequent investigations and a £400,000 penalty was levied on the company for failing to adequately secure their customers’ personal data (Ico.org.uk, 2018). Fowler (2016) noted that, under the stringent edicts outlined in the GDPR, the fines imposed could have amounted to approximately £70 million. The new mandatory 72-hour deadline outlined in Article 33 for reporting instances of data breach has left some organisations behind the curve in their efforts to establish appropriate frameworks and security measures for meeting compliance under GDPR (Mansfield-Devine, 2016).

The sophistication of new threats and the absence of appropriate response approaches and security policies can greatly increase the chances of a threat exploiting vulnerabilities in an information system with the result that personal data is compromised. Figure 8.1 illustrates a number of emerging threats that are contributing to the increased risks to personal and sensitive data.

8.1.2.Aims

The aims of this research are to examine the challenges that exist when interpreting and implementing GDPR through incident response plans, and to develop a structured process or decision support system to address the challenges identified. The research also aims to create an incident decision process flow to provide guidance for breach notification requirements. The objectives created for the research represent important building blocks for constructing and delivering the main goals of the research.

Fig. 8.1.Factors contributing to the increased risks to information (Hedley and Jacobs, 2017).

8.2.Literature Review

The contents of this section provide insights into scholarly articles and publications to help ascertain what has been done and what remains unaddressed in the subject domain. This will help clarify the context and relevance of the research and lead to a more indepth understanding of the challenges that exist in integrating GDPR into incident response plans. In the initial step, we examine the GDPR publication to identify the new compliance requirements, and then we critically analyse techniques and methods employed in previous works completed within the body of literature.

8.2.1.Changes in the legal and regulatory landscape

The introduction of the GDPR denotes a significant inflection point in which a minimum tick box approach to compliance and a self-regulation paradigm will no longer be sufficient for complying with the new requirements. Various emerging threats and new attack vectors being employed by disparate threat actors have contributed to the profusion of reported cyber attacks and increased data breach incidents. The implementation of GDPR across the EU in 2018 introduced a radical far-reaching approach that brings data protection laws in line with the dynamic and evolving way in which personal and sensitive data is collected and processed. The pervasiveness of internet-ready devices within a highly data-driven interconnected world has led to the generation of a vast amount of personal data that needs to be protected. Figure 8.2 illustrates important changes in data protection regulation over several decades.

Fig. 8.2.An illustration of regulatory changes in data privacy.

8.2.2.Exploration of a data breach and its wider impact

The rise in reported data breach incidents has become a notable concern for businesses and consumers because of the deleterious impact it can have on a company’s reputation as well as on the individuals who are affected by the data breach. To strengthen the privacy and security of personal data, GDPR regulations outlined important mandatory stipulations for data controllers and processors. Articles (24) and (31) outline the responsibility of the controller requiring the implementation of technical and organisational measures to demonstrate stringent measures to protect data and develop accountability (EU, GDPR, 2016). In recent years, numerous publications about data breaches have shown a litany of security failures that had contributed to vast amounts of data being compromised, and the trend shows no sign of abating.

Table 8.1.Data breach incidents and associated fines.

The introduction of the GDPR could also have wider implications for the legal sector if the personal information of clients becomes compromised. Due to the business model and the sensitivity of a client’s information, a serious breach of personal data could have ramifications that go beyond incurring substantial fines. The Solicitors Regulation Authority (SRA) recently highlighted information security as the foremost risk facing most law firms in the UK. The ICO data breach report in 2015/2016 indicates that 27% of security issues in the legal sector were attributed to theft of paper work and data being faxed or sent to the wrong recipient (Schwarz, 2016). Table 8.1 shows recent data breach incidents pre- and post-GDPR regulation. In 2016, a ransomware attack compromised personal data and rendered multinational law firm DLA Piper unable to access their client’s data (Steiner, 2018). It is therefore imperative to assess the risk to personal data and to implement appropriate security measures to mitigate the impact of a subsequent data breach incident.

One of the biggest data breaches recorded in 2017 was a cyber attack on US-based credit card rating firm Equifax. It affected approximately 145 million users in several countries including the UK [24]. The company later revealed that the vulnerability, “CVE-2017-5638” in the open source software Apache Struts was exploited (Cobb, 2018). This security breach highlights the importance of establishing effective security controls and vulnerability management to counter various threats. Research by Luszcz (2018) provided further analysis of the technical and security gaps in the design and implementation of new systems that can create various security vulnerabilities.

While new technological innovations provide many opportunities, the increasing number of data breaches also highlights a discernable chasm between effective internal security practices and substandard system development strategies for new and existing systems being implemented within the information and communication infrastructures. Reding (2010), argued in favour of a balance between the benefit of new technology and the assessment of potential risks, that if materialised could cause a serious data breach incident. Figure 8.3 illustrates a collaborative process between decision makers for managing risks. Now that the GDPR is in effect, assessing various risks and strengthening privacy policies for personal data are crucial for meeting compliance.

8.2.3.Privacy risks in IoT and third-party apps

The increasing trend of privacy issues involving Internet of Things (IoT) and third-party applications highlights new risks to personal data and a number of ethical concerns. A case involving misuse of personal data and breach of privacy occurred in 2015, when Facebook allowed a third-party application created by Cambridge Analytica onto their platform. The app was configured to surreptitiously harvest the data of 87 million profiles from which information was used during a UK referendum and US election campaign. A subsequent investigation by the ICO identified major failures in data protection standards and a £500,000 penalty was levied on Facebook for violating data protection laws. The fine issued at the time was the maximum amount under the Data Protection Act 1998 (DPA), however, the penalties under the GDPR could have totalled 4% of global revenue amounting to circa £1.4 billion.

Fig. 8.3.Collaborative process between decision makers for managing risks (Fischhoff, 2015).

Wood (2015), examined the privacy risks and unintended consequences arising from various internet-ready devices with built-in cameras. He elaborated on potential legal issues, highlighting an instance where hackers exploited a vulnerability in a network that hosts connected baby monitoring systems and shouted obscenities in a nursery that was using one of the devices. While some manufacturers extol the enticing virtues of new systems, serious ramifications can arise when they are implemented with substandard security measures. Bowles (2018), focused on potential new patterns of abuse and ethical issues. This included instances where partners of victims of domestic abuse used mobile apps to deliberately change functions on devices such as thermostats, door locks, and security cameras to cause distress and exert control.

8.2.4.Establishing privacy by design and default

As previously highlighted, the absence of appropriate measures to assess security risks during the development and implementation of third-party systems can significantly increase the chances of data becoming compromised. Innovative systems design may enhance business functionalities; however, it also represents a substantial security risk. Unlike previous legislations under directive (95/46/EC), the GDPR contains specific provisions that address substandard system development practices, where security is only incorporated as an after-thought during the design phase of new systems.

The capricious nature and complexity of threats such as advanced persistence threats (APT) means organisations must engage in continuous assessment and refinement of their security strategies in order to counter emerging threats. Solterbeck (2006), postulates that decisions to invest in advanced technical tools such as Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) and Security Information and Event Management Systems (SIEMS) will lead to the ability to analyse network anomalies and increase response capabilities. Conversely, Von Solms and Van Niekerk (2013), point out that these systems on their own will not prevent malicious attacks in all instances and argue that a more comprehensive approach incorporating people and processes will be required.

8.2.5.Encryption and pseudonymisation

Encryption and pseudonymisation techniques are among the measures that can be taken to secure personal data. They can be used to remove certain attributes from information that could be used to identify an individual. As discussed in Section 8.2.4, securing personal data and demonstrating robust security measures such as data protection by design and default are imperative in meeting compliance. The effectiveness of cryptographic technique was demonstrated in research by Bitar and Jakobsson (2017) who addressed data privacy requirements by utilising a hardware security model (HSM) as a cryptography method for anonymisation through encryption and access control.

A Delphi method was used to gather empirical data from subject experts to ascertain the most important aspects for meeting compliance within the GDPR. Bitar and Jakobsson (2017) demonstrated that access control, followed by data classification, was the most important aspect in securing personal data. These results were supported by Solterbeck (2006), who advocated that encryption methods can be adopted as an effective solution for protecting sensitive data. On balance, the strength of the findings provided insights for addressing relevant areas of GDPR such as Article 34 by employing the HSM encryption method. Nevertheless, the highly technical approach adopted for the research left other areas unaddressed, for example, the notification and communication of a data breach.

8.2.6.Comparison of incident response frameworks

A number of established industry frameworks are used by organisations as a blueprint for incident management; however, new regulations necessitate a reassessment of incident response phases in order to protect personal data and meet compliance. These include frameworks such as the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), the International Organization for Standardization (ISO 27000/27001), and the Enisa Good Practice Guide for Incident Management. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Special Publication 800-61 framework outlines guidance in three main areas: organisation capability, incident handling procedures and information sharing and communication as per Cichonski et al. (2012).

Fig. 8.4.Incident response life cycle outline by NIST.

NIST was primarily created for the federal government in the US and is responsible for developing guidelines and standards to address information security risks and incident management. Figure 8.4 illustrates four primary incident phases recommended by NIST for incident handling. The free publications are regularly updated and can be adopted for implementation within public or private organisations. Other frameworks such as the ISO/IEC 27001 are part of the ISO 27000 suite and are frequently revised. The information security framework is widely used in many organisations to establish, manage, and continually improve the information security management systems (Solterbeck, 2006).

The Enisa incident handling framework provides practical information management guidelines with the focus on incident handling techniques for incident response teams (Enisa.europa.eu, 2011). Although there are some overlaps within the response phases and the techniques adopted, there are notable gaps for the notification and communication of a data breach.

8.2.7.Security culture and leadership within incident response programs

As discussed in the previous section, the assessment of the human element plays an important role in the development of an effective incident response plan to enable prompt response to security incidents. Buchler et al. (2018) explored the human element of cyber security by assessing leadership and coordination challenges within cyber defense teams using an Observational Scaled Assessment of Teamwork (OAT) to assess the qualitative aspect of teamwork. The OAT model by Buchler et al. (2018) in Fig. 8.5 measures two distinct factors: (1) communication and collaboration, and (2) strong leadership.

Fig. 8.5.Interactions between organisation and data subject under GDPR [13].

The main findings identified strong leadership and face to face interaction as key attributes for building resilient CSIRTs. However, Wood (2015) adopts a contrary view and argues that leadership and collaboration should be explored at both the individual level and within the collective organisational security culture in order to improve the effectiveness of incident response.

New requirements in GDPR legislation mean that the previous tick-box approach by organisations that only addressed minimum compliance will no longer be adequate. Organisations need to make strategic decisions to assess existing systems and encourage proactive responses to security incidents to effectively counter various security threats. A recent report by PWC (2018), examined the merits of security culture within organisations and discovered that defining the security culture was an efficacious way to change individual staff behaviours and could also help strengthen overall security within an organisation. This indicates that, rather than focusing disproportionately on enforcing security policies, organisations should run appropriate cyber awareness initiatives that include staff as part of the security solution as these contribute to better security.

8.2.8.Summary of literature

The methods and techniques explored in the literature provided insights into important works that had been previously completed and provided context for challenges that need to be addressed. The General Data Protection Regulation has been in effect since May 2018 and has introduced a new legal mandate for governing how data is collected and processed in the EU. Given the wider remit in the new legal mandate and the option for imposing substantial penalties, it is crucial that organisations reassess existing frameworks for gaps in compliance and establish robust policies and procedures for interpreting and integrating the GDPR.

The literature provided a myriad of useful techniques and approaches for addressing various regulatory challenges. The research by Mansfield-Devine (2016) provides insights into common challenges organisations encounter when interpreting and integrating the GDPR. Bitar and Jakobsson (2017) adopted a technical approach by developing an HSM encryption model for securing data, while Alawadhi and Udeaja (2018) explored the need for assessing the human element in incident response programs. Nevertheless, the new requirements in the GDPR that make it compulsory to report instances of data breach and their impact on data subjects are beyond the scope of existing incidenthandling frameworks. This research aims to build on existing frameworks and to formulate a decision support system that can be used to meet compliance for incident response.

8.3.Development of Decision Support System

Prior to the introduction of the GDPR, some organisations were ambivalent about the level of impact they would incur if they reported serious data breaches. Consequently, they were reluctant to report some instances of data breach. While previous privacy legislation made implicit reference to this practice in order to deter it, the GDPR made explicit reference to the practice, asking for controllers and processors to demonstrate accountability and transparency. Article 5 (2) of the GDPR regulation explicitly outlines that controllers should be responsible for the development of appropriate frameworks and be able to demonstrate compliance with principles relating to the processing of personal data (PwC, 2018). This indicates that a demonstration of accountability goes beyond simply achieving the minimum compliance requirements outlined in the GDPR.

This research aims to address these challenges by formulating a conceptual decision support system for incident response and breach notification requirements. Research by Hevner et al. (2014), outlines principles within design science that can be employed in the development of artefacts, instead of verifying theories in research. Design science can be employed to guide the development of IT artefacts in a structured way and can include formal logic diagrams, software systems or rigorous mathematical-based design (Hevner et al., 2014). Design science paradigms can be used to solve complex IT problems and provide defined processes that can be used in conceptual system designs.

8.3.1.Pre-GDPR incident response frameworks

An incident response framework can act as a blueprint for responding to security incidents. This is an important part of business continuity and provides specific instructions that can be implemented to quickly identify and neutralise security threats and minimise their impact on normal business functions. A number of widely used incident handling frameworks such as NIST, SANS and CERT can be employed by organisations of varying size to guide incident response activities.

The NIST incident handling guide comprises a standard four-phase incident response which shares several similarities with other models employed within incident response programs. Nevertheless, new requirements in the GDPR such as the reporting of a data breach within 72 hours and the notifying of data subjects must be considered in order to comply with the GDPR.

8.3.2.Compliant GDPR framework design

The design of the DSS was informed by challenges identified in the literature and the mandatory requirements for incident response and breach notification. Existing incident response frameworks were extended and relevant areas of the GDPR were integrated into policies and process to meet compliance. The European Data Protection Board (EDPB) provides guidance for consistent interpretation and implementation of GDPR articles, while the ENISA incident handling guide offers demonstrable and practical steps for establishing incident management procedures (Cichonski et al., 2012).

The creation of the decision support framework aims to be flexible and adaptable and integrates a three-step approach. Firstly, the GDPR incident response dashboard provides an overview of additional response phases that are aligned with new requirements in the GDPR.

The subsequent steps include change restriction measures. These measures contain functionalities that can be leveraged to track and audit system changes and mitigate security incidents. In addition, these measures help to address the requirements in Article 32 that require organisations to demonstrate technical and organisational measures for protecting personal data. The final phase of the DSS presents a conceptual incident process flow that is structured using UML notations. The design of the DSS aims to extend the theoretical findings in the literature review by using a UML activity diagram to model breach notification processes and incorporate a technical element within the scope of the research.

The design included a distinct colour scheme and decision process flow to identify different levels of incidents such as minor, medium and major data breaches. The incident response dashboard expands existing frameworks by employing an eight-phase incident response cycle that incorporates the new requirements outlined in the GDPR such as the requirement to document the nature and extent of the data breach and the requirement to notify the ICO and data subjects within a specific timeframe.

The creation of incident scenarios forms part of a system design that provides practical steps for assessing security incidents and mitigates the adverse impacts and consequences of security incidents. The breach scenarios aim also to demonstrate the applicability of the DSS to aiding incident response activities and addressing various security incidents. This is complemented by the formulation of change restriction measures which include established tools and processes that can be leveraged to track and audit system changes, mitigate security incidents, and address the requirements in Article 32 of the GDPR that require organisations to demonstrate technical and organisational measures for protecting personal data. The change restriction measures can also be employed to govern access requests and ensure stringent measures are in place to protect personal data.

8.3.3.Justification for component selection

Design Science has been widely used in research to guide artifact development and solve problems identified in organisations as stated by Hevner et al. (2014). The organisational challenges identified in the literature provide a basis for the design of the artifact and accordingly Design Science provides proven principles to guide the development of the DSS. In order to formulate a comprehensive response approach, both the security and privacy characteristics of data need to be addressed.

The stipulation in Article 32, Paragraph (1) (b) outlines the need for robust security policies and procedures that continuously satisfy confidentiality, integrity and availability of personal data (EU, GDPR, 2016). Although there is no specific requirement to map the articles in the regulation, mapping the articles can be the first step towards meeting compliance with the GDPR. In order to simplify the design of the DSS, different elements of the decision support system provide the requisite functionalities to facilitate the consistent interpretation of GDPR articles to allow a prompt response to incidents.

This can be achieved by using diagrammatic modelling and categorisation of incident response processes to aid decision making. UML is an industry standard language with notations and methods for visualising conceptual system designs and it can represent the first step towards developing complex software systems (Fowler, 2016). The notation in UML was deemed suitable to enrich the design of the DSS and show interactions between different levels of data breach via a step-by-step decision process flow.

8.4.Focus Group

When assessing appropriate methods to employ in this research, the intent was to garner professional feedback on and in-depth insight into the design and usability of the decision support system. Focus group interviews are exploratory in nature and qualitative data can be gathered through feedback, opinions and attitudes (Kuada, 2012). To that end, a focus group interview was deemed suitable to achieve the objectives of the research. The design incorporated a two-step process: firstly, inferences drawn from the literature were used to inform the design of the DSS, then, focus groups with semi-structured interviews were conducted to gather feedback and analysis, and finally, the results were interpreted and analysed.

8.4.1.Recruitment of participants

The way in which participants are recruited can determine the success of the focus group. According to Kuada (2012), care should be taken to ensure participants possess the right attributes and experience to contribute to the discussions. The recruitment of participants was conducted using deliberate sampling, which was described by Hevner et al. (2014) as purposive sampling. Participants from different organisations and industry sectors with a minimum of 10 years’ experience in their fields were selected to ensure they met the criteria and could fully participate in the discussions.

The data-gathering instruments included a notepad, an audio recorder and a video recorder; however, as one of the participants was ambivalent about the video recording, it was subsequently omitted from the sessions. The focus group sessions commenced with general questions being asked before narrowing down to specific probes to obtain appropriate feedback. The first set of questions was a general introduction to initiate the discourse on the overall design of the system. The second set of questions introduced several case studies and asked about the usability of the system design.

The final set of questions allowed participants to discuss and assess the overall strengths and weaknesses of the system and to recommend future improvements (Kuada, 2012). The importance of the researcher in facilitating the discussions and enabling an open atmosphere where everyone could contribute was highlighted. The researcher was the only moderator conducting the session; however, the interactions and responses were carefully monitored and recorded, and probing questions and prompts were used to keep the conversation going. This facilitated more in-depth discussions, which were instrumental in gathering the required feedback to meet the objectives of the study.

8.4.2.Ethical consideration

Whilst conducting this research, it was necessary to correspond and interact with human participants (listed in Table 8.2) to capture their opinions and feedback on the design of the system; however, this can present various ethical and professional concerns. Hevner et al. (2014) outlined the importance of addressing ethical neutrality in the collection and analysis of the data. Therefore, while conducting the focus group interview, it was necessary to consider the needs, values and the views of the participants. After processing and reporting on data gathered from the focus group session (shown in Table 8.3), participants were given the opportunity to verify that their views were accurately represented.

8.5.Results and Analysis

The written and audio recordings were transcribed verbatim, after researchers continuously listened to the recording and made relevant notes.

Kuada (2012) emphasizes that focus group analysis differs from individual interviews, in that the data gathered will also come from observing participants’ reaction patterns and the overall interpersonal dynamics. The data gathered from the focus was analysed using a structured approach to present a range of evidence on the design, usability and efficacy of the DSS.

8.5.1.Results

The applicability of the system design was assessed by subject experts with working knowledge of GDPR who provided feedback on the topic. Over the last few years, organisations have seen an increased trend in data breach incidents and sophisticated attack vectors (P.1, P.2, P.3, P.4, P.5, Q.1, Q.2). Some of the attacks became more targeted. Such attacks are probably motivated by financial gain.

8.5.2.Usability of DSS for addressing privacy by design and default

The design of the system employing the UML process flow provides an overview of processes that can aid decisions to address security incidents as well as breach notification and communication requirements (P.39, P.40, P.41, P.42, P.43, P.44, Q.12, Q.13). When assessing the usability of the system with reference to the incorporation of privacy by design and default, the participants noted the relevance of the change request diagram and the distinct colour scheme of the UML process flow to developing and integrating security safeguards for new hardware and software systems (P.45, P.46, P.47, P.48, P.49, Q.14, Q.15). Further discussions on the mapping of articles against security controls noted the usability and relevance of the DSS mapping document for the interpretation and integration of the GDPR into the incident response plans (P.50, P.51, P.52, Q.16, Q.17).

8.5.3.Feedback and recommendations for improving design

The discussions and feedback provided by the focus group interviewees presented valuable professional insight into the GDPR implementation challenges and the use of a decision support system for addressing mandatory requirements. The feedback on the overall design described the system as having the relevant features for formulating GDPR incident response plans, however further improvements were recommended so that the system would have response procedures for incidents occurring outside of normal working hours. It was also recommended that the contacts of key personnel in the response teams be listed (P.53, P.54, P.55, Q.17, Q.18). Other recommendations for improvement in design included suggestions for the next phase iteration of the coding of the UML design into a software plugin.

8.5.4.Feasibility of DSS for implementation

After providing feedback and recommendations for future improvements of the DSS, the participants discussed the scope of the system design and its suitability for implementation within an organisation. Several implementation solutions were discussed and the DSS was assessed as appropriate for deployment along with existing systems as a guide for creating GDPR incident response plans. In addition, participants noted that business areas such as legal departments and change management departments would need to sanction the deployment of such systems in their organisation.

On balance, the recommendation for system implementation highlighted key functionalities of the system design that are appropriate for incident response and breach notification, however it was suggested that the DSS was suitable for implementation only as an annex to existing frameworks. In addition, further suggestions for improvements to and the refinement of the next phase of design included the development and testing of the DSS to automate some of the incident response phases (P.58, P.59, P.60, Q.20).

8.5.5.Summary of results and analysis

The feedback on the usability of the DSS design provided information on the relevance of the functionality of each component to addressing the challenges in implementing the GDPR. Discussions on the merits of the overall design of the DSS can facilitate the decision to establish a GDPR incident response and breach notification program within an organisation. Nevertheless, there were also recommendations for further improvements to the next phase of the DSS design, including recommendations to incorporate interactive response phases and to automate some of the functionalities of dashboards.

The development of the Decision Support System and the feedback provided by industry practitioners provided valuable insights into the viability of the design and its ability to meet incident response requirements. The participants suggested that the current design of the system could be implemented as an annex to existing systems integrating the GDPR. The feedback also confirmed some of the challenges found in the literature such as the need to have comprehensive incident response strategies and the issues associated with the ad-hoc and generic response approach for security incidents. The findings are further strengthened by the triangulation of the literature review, the analysis and the interpretation of qualitative data gathered from the feedback. Further insights into the context of the outcome can be obtained by evaluating the overall research approach and this is covered in the next chapter.

8.6.Evaluation of Research Process and Methods

Part of the objective in developing the system included contrasting different methods to garner feedback on the artefact design. Several distinct methods such as online surveys, one-to-one interviews and focus group interviews were critically assessed before semi-structured focus group interviews were adopted for the research. Focus group interviews are widely used in many disciplines, including the social sciences, to gather knowledge and opinions of a particular phenomenon. Hevner et al. (2014) demonstrated the use of a focus group for gathering feedback and the refinement of the artifact.

Although some computer-assisted qualitative data analysis software (CAQDAS) is available to help manage the data collected, due to the learning curve and the researchers’ lack of familiarity with any of the software mentioned, MS Word and Excel were used to process transcripts from the focus group. Although transcribing and coding the data using this method required more time and effort, with the requisite skills and persistence it was accomplished satisfactorily.

8.6.1.Research limitations

The research is limited to computer security incident response and data breach notification, but there are other important considerations when securing a system, including environmental and physical security. However, this is beyond the remit of this research. During the interview sessions, participants provided personal knowledge acquired from many years of experience. However, they could perceive themselves as representing their respective organisations and may be reluctant to provide information that might portray weakness or failures in their respective organisations.

The recording and transcription of the focus group interviews was limited to a single researcher. Whilst the participants were culturally diverse and heterogeneous in experience and the industry sector, the sample feedback could be considered relatively little in comparison to the views of experts in various and wider industries. Moreover, another limitation of the feedback on DSS is that it did not include the implementation or period of maturation within an organisation. For the purpose of this research only a single session of focus group interviews was carried out. However, the research provides a firm basis for the design to be extended in further research.

8.7.Conclusion and Recommendation

The numbers of reported data breach incidents have been increasing over the last few years and this highlights the need for privacy legislation to be strengthened in accordance with changes in technology and the new ways in which data is created, shared and processed. The research started out by posing the following questions.

1.What are the main challenges in interpreting and integrating the GDPR into incident response and breach notification plans?

2.How can the development of a decision support process or system address the challenges identified?

3.What method can be employed to provide feedback on the design and usability of the formulated solution?

To address these questions, the literature review was used to identify existing challenges and to help to inform the design of the Decision Support System using Design Science and UML notation. Focus group interviews were adopted to provide feedback on the usability of the system for meeting GDPR compliance requirements. The feedback from these interviews and the literature showed that a comprehensive response strategy is crucial for managing complex threats as well as the risks associated with third party entities. The research findings also highlight the importance of establishing data privacy by design and default and the potential consequences of failing to notify the relevant supervisory authority and data subjects in the aftermath of a data breach.

The findings further showed that the data breach scenarios and change restriction measures within the DSS were useful for situational analysis and mitigating security risks to personal data. Overall feedback on the usability of DSS indicated it that it was relevant for addressing incident response and breach notification challenges associated with the GDPR. For example, the findings show that the mappings of relevant articles could help facilitate the interpretation and integration of the GDPR into incident response programs. The design of the DSS builds on previous research by assessing the impact of data breaches on data subjects and by incorporating new requirements in Articles 33 and 34 of the GDPR.

The design of the system also provides guidance that can be used by organisations to facilitate incident response decisions and protect personal data. Moreover, further rigor is provided by adopting a hybrid assessment for the development of the DSS by using principles in Design Science and feedback from focus group interview sessions.

8.7.1.Recommendations for future work

While conducting the research, several noteworthy discoveries were made for viable future work on and improvement of the DSS design. Part of the findings revealed that no formal auditing of security policies or agreement for immediate notice of data breach was established between some organisations and their associated thirdparty partners. Therefore further research is needed to develop an incident notification framework between data controllers or processors based inside of the EU jurisdiction. The recommendations drawn from the findings also suggested that the possible next stage improvements of the DSS design could generate codes from each of the UML process flows to develop a GDPR software system as a plugin for integration with other systems.

Chapter 9

Evaluation of the Standardised Digital Forensic Investigation Process Model (SDFIPM)

ABSTRACT

The existing digital forensic investigation process models (DFIPMs) have often been developed by digital forensic practitioners (DFPs) based on their own personal experience and on an ad-hoc basis, without attention to the establishment of standardisation within the field. This has prevented the institution of both scientific and generic processes that are urgently required within the different fields of law enforcement, commerce and incident response. Therefore, a novel model — the Standardised Digital Forensic Investigation Process Model (the SDFIPM) — was developed to address these shortcomings. Following the selected research methodology, Peffers et al.’s Design Science Research Process (DSRP), the SDFIPM was also subjected to both Demonstration and Evaluation activities to determine how well it would support the solution to the stated research problem. Therefore, this paper presents the results of the Demonstration and Evaluation activities applied to the proposed model. Our study makes three significant and novel contributions to the field of Digital Forensics (DF): First, it implements a process model, the design of which is inclusive of all the advantages of the previous models through their synthesis, harmonisation and extension. No such model previously existed in the literature. Second, the SDFIPM is generic in that it can be applied within the three fields of law enforcement, commerce and incident response. Third, unlike the majority of the previous models, the effectiveness of which is unknown due to the lack of an evaluation process, the SDFIPM’s efficacy is demonstrated in relation to both components of ‘utility’ and ‘usability’.

Keywords: SDFIPM, digital forensics, cloud forensics, chain of custody

9.1.Introduction

In order for digital evidence to be admissible, investigators need to demonstrate that they have specialized knowledge and that the evidence was acquired using reliable principles and methods (Montasari, 2018; Montasari, 2016a; Kessler, 2010). Careful notice is taken in court of the manner in which the digital investigative process (DIP) has been carried out (Montasari, 2016a; Kessler, 2010; Cohen, 2011; Mason, 2007). A DFP might discover significant and incriminating evidence, but if they cannot present the evidence in a coherent and understandable way to the lay audience (such as the judge and jury), the case may be lost (Sherman, 2006). The complexity of tools and methodologies used to perform a DIP requires investigators to be able to explain the process in a manner that a judge and jury can understand (Kessler, 2010). Nevertheless, the field of DF still lacks formal process models that courts can employ to determine the reliability of the digital evidence presented to them (Montasari, 2017; Montasari, 2016b; Montasari et al., 2015; Valjarevic and Venter, 2015; Kohn et al., 2013; US-CERT, 2012; Agarwal, 2011). The absence of agreements associated with DFIPMs has been widely acknowledged by many researchers in the field (Montasari, 2016c; Montasari, 2016d; Montasari, 2016e; Valjarevic and Venter, 2015; Kohn et al., 2013; Agarwal et al., 2011; Rogers et al., 2006). Zainudin et al. (2011) state that one of the most significant problems encountered by DFPs is the absence of standardisation in the field of DF. Casey (2011) argues that the development of a formal process model enables a complete, rigorous investigation, ensures proper evidence handling and reduces the chances of mistakes created by preconceived theories, time pressures, and other potential pitfalls (Casey, 2011). Similarly, Valjarevic and Venter (2015) state that conducting a digital forensic investigation (DFI) requires a formalized process model, arguing, “There is currently neither an international standard nor a global, harmonized DFI process.”

One reason for the absence of formal process models is the relatively recent addition of DF as a scientific discipline compared to traditional forensic science (Cohen, 2012). The latter has developed, together with its fundamental biological sciences, over several decades (Beebe and Clark, 2005; Palmer, 2001), whereas DF science is still being formed and therefore lags considerably behind the better-developed, underlying Computer Science (CS) (Montasari, 2016a; Beebe and Clark, 2005; Carrier and Spafford, 2003). The DF discipline has developed without any of the initial research required to provide an essential, thorough, scientific foundation (Valjarevic and Venter, 2015; US-CERT, 2012; Peisert et al., 2008; Meyers and Rogers, 2004; Carrier, 2002). The United States Computer Emergency Readiness Team (US-CERT, 2012) notes, “Because computer forensics is a new discipline, there is little standardization and consistency across the courts and industry.” Meyers and Rogers (2004) take an even stronger view, warning that DF is branded as a “junk science” because of the absence of certifications, standards or peer-reviewed methods (Meyers and Rogers, 2004). Similarly, Carrier (2002) highlights that issues are raised in considering DF as a science due to the absence of generally agreed-upon standards and procedures. A further cause of the lack of formal models for DIP is the ‘ad-hoc’ approach taken by the authors of these models, who have failed to employ scientific approaches when developing them (Montasari, 2017a; Montasari, 2016a; Montasari, 2016b; Montasari, 2016c; Montasari et al., 2015; Agarwal et al., 2011).

Previous models have often been developed by practitioners who are not necessarily scientists. These models are based on their personal experience and are developed on an ad-hoc basis (Montasari, 2016a; Montasari et al., 2015; Valjarevic and Venter, 2015; Agarwal et al., 2011; Montasari, 2016c). However, as also stated by Karyda and Mitrou (2007), using ad-hoc methods and tools for the extraction of digital evidence can undermine its reliability and credibility. Referring to the same issue, Reith et al. (2002) state, “This is a problem because evidence must be obtained using methods that are proven to reliably extract and analyse data without bias or modification.” This is further supported by Beebe and Clark (2005), who argue that rigor in a DFIPM is achieved only through the use of “formal” and “scientific” approaches, and by Solomon et al. (2011), who argue that current procedures and tools should not be mistaken for a consistent investigative process. The latter authors contend, “Tools and procedures are developed from the experience of law enforcement and system administrators simply in an ad-hoc manner rather than coming from the scientific community where other traditional forensic sciences get their methodologies.” (Solomon et al., 2011).

Therefore, the adoption of ad-hoc approaches in developing previous models has led to a variety of process models with conflicting stages, activities and terminology, which in turn has prevented the establishment of the formal processes needed by courts and investigators alike (Montasari et al., 2015; Agarwal et al., 2011). As a result, many researchers have increasingly called for scientific approaches and formal methods for the DIP (Cohen, 2012; Carlton and Worthley, 2009; Garfinkel et al., 2009; Pollitt, 2009; Leigland and Krings, 2004). A further issue with the existing models is their tendency to focus on one specific area of DF, neglecting other environments (Montasari, 2016a; Montasari, 2016b; Montasari et al., 2015). Unlike in other domains of forensic practice, DFPs operate in various fields (Freiling and Schwittay, 2007; Beebe and Clark, 2005; Ciardhuáin, 2004; Carrier and Spafford, 2003). Therefore, as Carrier and Spafford (2003) argue, “A model must be abstract and apply to law enforcement investigations, corporate investigations, and incident response.” However, instead of being generic, previous models have often focussed on only one specific area, such as law enforcement, commerce or incident response (Montasari, 2016a; Montasari, 2016b; Adams, 2012; Pollitt, 2009), therefore failing to consider the requirements of those operating in different domains. The result has been the hindering of the development of a generic model that can be applied in the various fields of DF (Montasari, 2016a; Montasari, 2016b; Montasari et al., 2015).

A third significant concern associated with the previous models is that they are not comprehensive, failing to cover the entire DIP. Beebe and Clark (2005) argue that a more comprehensive and generally accepted framework is needed to enhance scientific rigor and facilitate education, application and research. Similarly, Ciardhuáin (2004) states, “A comprehensive model of cyber crime investigations is important for standardising terminology, defining requirements, and supporting the development of new techniques and tools for investigators.”

9.1.1.Research problem

The foregoing considerations were formulated in Montasari’s [3] study into the following research problem:

There does not exist a comprehensive model encompassing the entire digital investigative process that is formal, such that it can assist a court of law in determining the reliability of the investigative process followed, and that is generic, in that it can be applied in the different fields of law enforcement, commerce and incident response.

To address the above research problem, Montasari (2016a) developed a comprehensive model, the Comprehensive Digital Forensic Investigation Process Model (the CDFIPM), which the Standardised Digital Forensic Investigation Process Model (the SDFIPM) forms the middle part of. The CDFIPM, which encompasses the entire DIP, is formal in that it synthesizes, harmonises and extends the existing models, and also generic in that it can be applied in the different fields of law enforcement, commerce and incident response. The focus of this study is only on the middle part of the CDFIPM, namely the proposed SDFIPM. To this end, we first introduce and discuss the SDFIPM prior to presenting the results of the Demonstration and Evaluation activities applied to the model.

9.1.2.Structure of the paper

The remainder of the paper is structured as follows: Section 9.2 presents a background summary to the previous DFIPMs. Section 9.3 discusses the research methodology, while Section 9.4 provides an overview of the proposed model. Section 9.5 discusses the Demonstration activity, whereby the SDFIPM is applied to a case study, and a walkthrough of the model is performed. Section 9.6 describes the Evaluation Process, through which the SDFIPM is subjected to an external, independent evaluation by leading experts within the three domains of law enforcement, commerce and incident response. Finally, in Section 9.7, the paper is concluded, the research contributions are outlined, and future work is discussed.

9.2.Background to the Previous DFIPMs

Prior to the design and development of the SDFIPM, we performed a critical review of the previous models followed by an assessment of each of the models against three different sets of assessment criteria (Montasari, 2016a), including: the Daubert Test (Farrell, 1993) Five-Point Requirement, the Carrier and Spafford (2003) Five-Point Requirement and the Beebe and Clark (2005) Four-Point Requirement. The aim of this critical analysis was to gain an in-depth insight into the previous models and also to determine which could contribute to the proposed model. Since law enforcement, commerce and incident response were the three environments on which our research focussed, previous models within those three domains which most closely met the assessment criteria were considered for their possible contributions to the new model. Adams (2012) has adopted a similar approach in which he assesses the previous DFIPMs against the Daubert Test and Carrier and Spafford Five-Point Requirements.

Our approach for assessing the previous DFIPMs was considered important (Kohn et al., 2013; Cohen, 2012; Cohen, 2010) as any model institutionalized through subsequent intellectual discourse and practical use must take into account other researchers’ perspectives, approaches and “vernacular”. Having critically reviewed and assessed the previous models (Montasari, 2016a; Montasari, 2016c; Montasari, 2016e), our findings revealed that these models had often been developed by DFPs based on their own personal experience and on an ad hoc basis without any consideration of how standardization should be established within the field (Valjarevic and Venter, 2015). It was further revealed that this had prevented the establishment of formal processes that were urgently needed by courts of law (Montasari, 2016a; Montasari et al., 2015). As Table 9.1 (Montasari et al., 2015) clearly demonstrates, the previous DFIPMs display significant disparities in terms of the number of phases, the scope and the specific domains that they have been developed for. As a result, these models have often been criticised for being too specific (Carrier and Spafford, 2003; Reith et al., 2002), too high level (Beebe and Clark, 2005), too broad (Rogers et al., 2006), too technical (Venter, 2006) and too complex (Selamat et al., 2008). Therefore, the proposed model was developed to address the shortcomings of the previous models. It was demonstrated that an implementation of our model would be of immediate value to both DFPs and courts of law.

9.3.Research Methodology

The Design Science Research (DSR) methodology, widely adopted in the domain of Information Systems (IS) (Hevner and Chatterjee, 2010; Peffers et al., 2006; Hevner et al., 2004; March and Smith, 1995; Walls et al., 1992; Nunamaker et al., 1990), was selected as the methodology to conduct this research. The main aim of DSR is to achieve or develop knowledge and understanding of a problem domain by building and applying a designed artefact (Van Aken, 2005; Hevner et al., 2004). DSR involves the design of novel or innovative artefacts and the analysis of the performance or use of such artefacts (Watts et al., 2009; Kuechler and Vaishnavi, 2008). The development and evaluation of artefacts form an important part in DSR (Hevner et al., 2004; March and Storey, 2008). Artefacts include, amongst others: models, methods, constructs, instantiations and design theories (March and Storey, 2008; March and Smith, 1995), social innovations, and new or previously unknown properties of technical, social or informational resources (March and Storey, 2008). The artefact related to this research is a new model, the SDFIPM, which encompasses the middle part of the larger model, the CDFIPM. The organisational context associated with the research is that of law enforcement, commerce and incident response. Our research also addresses the hitherto unsolved problem that there does not exist a DFIPM that is formal in that it synthesizes, harmonises and extends the existing models, and that is generic in that it can be employed in the different fields of law enforcement, incident response and commerce. Our adoption of the DSR methodology as a research methodology in a DF study is informed by Adams (2012), who originally applied the DSR methodology to a study in DF.

The selection of the DSR methodology over other alternative methodologies such as the Grounded Theory (GT) methodology or Requirements Engineering (RE) methodology was due to its relevance to the task of design and the subsequent evaluation of a new process model. Hence, because this study also has at its focus the design, development and subsequent evaluation of the SDFIPM, the DSR methodology was considered to be the most appropriate choice. It is also preferable as it is more pragmatic than alternatives such as the Explanatory Science Research (ESR) methodology [46] and as it can be used to solve a problem for which no solution has already been found (Peffers et al., 2006; Hevner et al., 2004). Therefore, since this research is a problembased study, again the DSR methodology was deemed the most appropriate methodology. Moreover, the DSR methodology uses both inductive and deductive processes. Since our original study, from which this paper is derived, is aimed at producing a new knowledge and literature (through the inductive process), as well as testing its two research hypotheses (through the deductive process), once again the DSR methodology was considered the most appropriate choice.

Various researchers both within and outside the IS domain have provided guidance to define the DSR and have described what goals should be followed in its production (Hevner and Chatterjee, 2010; Peffers et al., 2006; Hevner et al., 2004; Vaishnavi and Kuechler, 2004; Adams and Courtney, 2004; Rossi and Sein, 2003; March and Smith, 1995; Walls et al., 1992; Eekels and Roozenburg, 1991; Nunamaker et al., 1990; Takeda et al., 1990; Archer, 1984). These researchers have often proposed various methods, processes or theoretical frameworks to rationalise the DSR studies. However, the design science research process (DSRP) model proposed by Peffers et al. (2006) was selected as the appropriate DSR methodology to conduct the research in this study. The rationale for doing so is due to the fact that it provides a graphical representation of the conceptual process for both carrying out and presenting the DSR. Such a mental model facilitates the application of the DSR and can also assist the authors in producing and presenting a high-quality DSR that would be accepted as valuable, rigorous and publishable within the field of digital forensics science (Montasari, 2018; Montasari, 2016a).

Peffers et al.’s (2006) DSRP consists of six components as shown in Fig. 9.1. The remainder of this section aims briefly to discuss the way in which we applied these six components to our study. For more details regarding the application of the DSRP to our research study, see Montasari’s study (Montasari, 2016a).

Fig. 9.1.The design science research process (DSRP) model after Peffers et al. (2006).

Activity 1 — Problem Identification and Motivation

A profound knowledge of the problem addressed by this research was acquired through a detailed analysis and assessment of the literature related to previous DFIPMs. Having drawn conclusions from the literature review, we were able to formulate the research problem that this study intends to address. Interactions with other experts and our own experience in the field of DF also provided insight into the stated problem.

Activity 2 — Objectives of a Solution

The research aim was formulated according to the definition of the problem. This approach is supported by Peffers et al. (2006), who state that objectives should be deduced rationally from the problem specification. Therefore, in order to formulate the stated aim, a deep knowledge was acquired of the state of the problem and its current solution in the form of previously proposed DFIPMs and their efficacy.

Activity 3 — Design and Development

Prior to designing and developing the SDFIPM, all previous DFIPMs were critically reviewed and assessed against three sets of assessment criteria to establish which could contribute to the new model. Law enforcement, commerce and incident response were the three environments on which this research focussed. Therefore, previous models within those three domains were considered for their possible contributions to the new model. Once the most reliable models were identified, their specific key contributions were determined for inclusion in the new model. Following this, the essential components necessary for the new model were identified from the specific key contributions. These formed the basic structure of the SDFIPM. The prevailing models were then built upon by the construction of a new set of domain-specific components. The components identified in the previous models contributed to the development of the new models, as did the new set of constructed components. The SDFIPM was graphically represented in the form of UML Activity Diagrams.

Having already applied the first three components of the DSRP to our research (Montasari, 2016a), in this chapter we focus on the remaining three components, namely Demonstration, Evaluation and Communication activities. The following sections describe how we intend to apply these elements to this study.

Activity 4 — Demonstration

Following the design and development of the SDFIPM, its implementation needs to be demonstrated within an appropriate environment based on the Demonstration Activity of the DSRP. Peffers et al. (2006) suggest the use of case studies as such an appropriate environment. Other researchers in the field (Valjarevic and Venter, 2015; Casey, 2011; Beebe and Clark, 2005; Carrier and Spafford, 2003; Ciardhuáin, 2004) have also used case studies as an appropriate environment to determine the applicability of their models. A case study pertaining to the different fields of law enforcement, commerce and incident response has been selected as an appropriate environment for testing the proposed model. Therefore, the SDFIPM will be applied to the selected case study in Section 9.5 in order to demonstrate its application and effectiveness within the three stated domains. We considered this activity important as it would enable us to address any shortcomings prior to the submission of the model to the external, independent experts for formal evaluation. Such an activity would also enable us to avoid impinging on the time of the external reviewers. The results of the Demonstration activity of the research will then determine whether the Design and Development stage needs to be repeated in order for certain alterations to be made.

Activity 5 — Demonstration

Based on the DSRP’s requirements, the SDFIPM also needs to be evaluated to determine how well it supports the solution to the stated problem. This activity will compare the SDFIPM’s application and effectiveness with the characteristics set out in the research problem. The Evaluation activity of this study, presented in Section 9.6, has involved the submission of the SDFIPM to DFPs within the three domains that are the focus of this research, namely law enforcement, commerce and incident response, and also to judges, barristers and researchers in academia. The aim of such an approach was to enable us to acquire insightful and reliable feedback as to the effectiveness of the SDFIPM from authoritative external reviewers. As with the Demonstration phase, once the evaluation has been carried out, we will be able to judge whether to repeat the Design and Development Phase of the SDFIPM in order to make improvements. Any such amendments will subsequently be introduced to the Design and Development Phase of the SDFIPM.

Activity 6 — Communication

Again, in accordance with the DSRP’s requirements, the problem addressed by this research and its importance, its solution (the SDFIPM), its utility and novelty, the rigor of its design and implementation, and its effectiveness will all need to be communicated to the intended user community. The Communication activity of the DSRP in relation to this research has already been covered through publications in well-known and peer-reviewed journals and conferences, and also via our attendance at various conferences, Digital Forensic Expositions and Cyber Security Summits. In addition, we aim to continue with further publications and also to initiate direct interactions with a wide variety of experts, including DFPs, legal practitioners and experts in academia, to communicate the importance of our proposed model.

9.4.Overview of the SDFIPM

The SDFIPM was designed using a top-down approach in order to enable DFPs to gain a better insight into its compositional components, namely Processes, Phases and Sub-Phases. The model consists of seven Processes, each of which contains a different number of Phases. Each Process provides additional lower layers of details, i.e. Phases and Sub-Phases. Figures 9.2 and 9.3 represent the first instance of the formal representation of the SDFIPM, i.e. the UML Activity Diagrams, the combinations of which make up the entire model. Since the Design and Development Phase of the model has already been extensively covered in Montasari (2016a), the following subsections provide only a brief overview of the model.

Fig. 9.2.The examination, analysis, interpretation, event reconstruction and reporting processes.

Fig. 9.3.The presentation, investigation closure and future readiness processes.

9.4.1.Examination process

During this Process, a large number of techniques should be used to access, find and extract the potential digital evidence into a humanreadable format (Montasari, 2016a; Montasari, 2016b; Kohn et al., 2013). The Survey Digital Crime Scene Phase enables DFPs to find apparent pieces of digital evidence for a particular category of crime in a swift manner. It also assists them in ascertaining the skill level of the suspect, which in turn will allow them to decide what examination and analysis techniques are required in the next process of the SDFIPM, the Analysis Process (discussed later). DFPs must survey the digital crime scene to locate potential evidence, possibly within unconventional locations on the system (Montasari and Peltola, 2015). It is preferable to perform this Phase in a digital forensic laboratory (DFL), using the image (working copy) of the system acquired during the Acquisition Process [8], as it provides a controlled environment and the results can be repeated with another copy of the system. In cases where DFPs might need to perform this phase also on a live system, they must conduct field searches (Montasari, 2016a; Montasari, 2016d) by booting the system into what Carrier and Spafford (2003) call a “trusted environment”. DFPs must adapt their investigative techniques based on the specific category of crime to expedite the subsequent Analysis activities as there is often a large volume of data to deal with. For instance, in cases involving server intrusions, DFPs should search for apparent signs of a rootkit installation, examine application logs and also search for new configuration files. Another example (Carrier and Spafford, 2003) concerns analysing network traffic to learn more about an incident; the Survey Digital Crime Scene Phase might analyse traffic for the incident time frame and filter out certain ports and hosts. In other cases, as suggested in Montasari and Peltola (2015), the investigators should also analyse the “common” and “uncommon” locations on the system that might contain artefacts related to the suspect’s browsing activities. Unallocated file system space must also be extracted and processed for deleted files, and a low-level timeline of file activity should be examined to trace the user’s activities. Often, there are large volumes of data to be examined (Kohn et al., 2013; Ciardhuáin, 2004), and automated techniques should be employed using tools such as FTK (AccessData, 2018) or EnCase (Guidance Software, 2018) in order to support the investigators. Furthermore, a large number of techniques might be performed to process the obfuscated data. For instance, deleted or hidden data can be processed by utilising sound digital forensic methods, as File Allocation tables or disk indexing might be deleted in some investigations. Therefore, this Phase will enable DFPs to ensure that files that have been partially deleted are recognized from the original evidence. DFPs can also reverse-engineer suspicious executables and examine encrypted files (Carrier and Spafford, 2003). It might also be necessary for DFPs to examine the contents of every cluster (physical search) or every file (logical search) (Casey, 2011).

After all data including partially discovered files and folders have been made visible, data then needs to be harvested by giving a logical structure to the entire data set. The file and folder structure should be indexed to provide structure to acquired data. Raw data will be shown as information, and the partially deleted files which were processed during the Examine Acquired Data Phase will become visible to the degree that they were rendered visible. The result of the Harvest Data Phase is the production of a logical structured data set (Kohn et al., 2013) where the extracted raw data has now become structured information (Kohn et al., 2013; Cohen, 2009). Therefore, the harvested information can now be displayed by the original file systems such as FAT or NTFS. The data examined during the course of a DFI can be very large and therefore must be reduced to expedite the Examination Process. Identifying known elements can enable DFPs to reduce data. Metadata and unique identifiers such as MD5 must be used to remove known system files and other application data (Casey, 2011; Cohen, 2009; Beebe and Clark, 2005). The data that remains will be modified data or data that could be uniquely attributed to the users of a specific computer system. This will result in the identification of the potential digital evidence from data that has been examined, harvested and reduced. DFPs should also group together digital evidence with similar identifying patterns by focusing on the incident type. Digital evidence also needs to be restructured so that the investigation can be conducted more appropriately. If similar types of incidents or crimes have taken place in the past and are known to DFPs, they should then use the known classification in order to compare the current digital forensic data to the similar past incidents or crimes. The output of the Examination Process becomes the input to the Analysis Process, discussed in the following subsection.

9.4.2.Analysis process

Based upon the results of the Examination Process, DFPs must now be able to define what the exact characteristics of the incident are and who is to be held accountable for the incident. The Analysis Process enables investigators to reconstruct fragments of data based on their significance and determine a possible root cause of the incident (Montasari, 2016a; Montasari et al., 2015). Once DFPs have addressed what is possibly known from the digital evidence (Montasari et al., 2015), they must now be able to formulate a hypothesis of how the incident took place. To do so, they need to reconstruct a sequence of events which has resulted in the current state of the system under investigation. Investigators must thoroughly analyse and test data that was organised in the Examination Process against the hypothesis that they have formulated. The legal validity of the possible digital evidence must also be questioned by considering issues such as relevance, admissibility and weight as discussed in Montasari (2017b), Montasari (2016a) and Kessler (2010). Digital evidence should then be linked and attributed to the root cause of the incident by correlating the results of the digital crime scene with physical evidence. For instance, DFPs might need to correlate data center access logs to logins, linking online chat activities found on the computer with the activity of an undercover officer, and correlating activity on a compromised server with activity on the suspect’s home system and network activity recorded by an ISP. Subsequent to the attribution, investigators need to evaluate their findings to ensure that their hypothesis holds true. At this stage of the Investigative Process, backtracking from the Analysis Process to the Examination Process is often to be expected as the investigators acquire a better understanding of the root cause of the incident. The output of the Analysis Process becomes the input to the Interpretation Process, discussed in the next subsection.

9.4.3.Interpretation process

The main purpose of the Interpretation Process is to use scientifically proven methods to explain facts discovered throughout the Analysis Process within the context of the investigation (Montasari, 2016a; Montasari, 2016b; Palmer, 2001). During this process, investigators need to interpret the digital evidence to produce meaningful statements in the legal context for later reporting and presentation. They must be able to reconstruct the events associated with the digital investigation by using the results of the analysis techniques from the Analysis Process to put together the pieces of the digital puzzle so that an accurate reconstruction of events can be carried out. The interpretation of any evidence should depend on the available information regarding the circumstances surrounding the creation of that item of digital evidence (Valjarevic and Venter, 2015; ISO, 2015). DFPs must obtain information from individuals involved in the day-to-day operation of the system under investigation so that they can carry out a more effective interpretation of evidence. Moreover, investigators must consider information concerning the goal as well as the scope of the investigation. In cases where the contextual information changes, investigators might also need to change the interpretation so that it can reflect any such changes regarding the contextual information. DFPs must also utilise link analysis and timeline tools to assist them with the digital reconstruction. The interpreted evidence then needs to be classified and evaluated in order to ascertain the amount of trust that can be placed in it. The interpreted digital evidence should also be organised according to relevance in such a way that more important digital evidence can be differentiated from others. After completing this process, DFPs should now be able to determine how the digital evidence came into existence and what its presence denotes. The output of the Interpretation Process becomes the input to the Event Reconstruction Process, discussed in the next section.

9.4.4.Event reconstruction process

During this process DFPs need to reconstruct a possible event sequence which reflects the incident result as accurately as possible. In order to reconstruct the events, investigators must utilise the series of events that they have deduced from digital evidence. Event Reconstruction should not be established as factual; instead, DFPs should use this Process to explain how the incident might have taken place. During this Process, the investigation findings must be consolidated and refined prior to assessing the review results against the original hypothesis, which was formulated in the Analysis Process. This will be to determine whether the DFPs have acquired all the evidence required to support the original hypothesis. If all the evidence has not been captured, investigators will need to backtrack to the Examination Process, in which this Phase and subsequent Phases form a cycle that needs to be repeated until the DFPs can identify additional evidence and explain the incident. As an example, in cases where a server intrusion has taken place, this iteration involves DFPs linking the exploitation of a service that is open to attack with the installation of a rootkit and utilization of a network sniffer. If the source IP address of the network connections is investigated, this could result in the acquisition of additional digital evidence to examine. If there is no need to iterate to the Examination Process, DFPs must identify and address any areas of improvement. The output of the Event Reconstruction Process becomes the input to the Reporting Process, discussed in the next subsection.

9.4.5.Reporting process
