Chapter 15

The European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)

Sérgio Tenreiro de Magalhães

Champlain College
Burlington, VT — USA
smagalhaes@champlain.edu

Algoritmi Research Center
Guimarães, Portugal
psmagalhaes@dsi.uminho.pt

ABSTRACT

This chapter presents the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) approved for the European Union, which has consequences not only for all the stakeholders of the information technology industry, but also for all of those engaged in industrial or commercial activities in the European Union.

The concepts and principles of the GDPR are presented and discussed as well as the implications of this regulation in data protection and in organisational cyber security practices. The financial implications for companies are discussed and an overview of the history of recent fines and recent trends is presented.

Conclusions are drawn on the importance of compliance and a recommendation is made that organisations choose to hire the services of multidisciplinary companies specialized in GDPR compliance.

Keywords: GDPR, cyber security, personal data, DPO, IT

15.1.Introduction

The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) was published in the Official Journal of The European Union (EU) on the 4th of May of 2016 as “REGULATION (EU) 2016/679 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data Protection Regulation)” (REGULATION (EU) 2016/ 679 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL — of 27 April 2016 — on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/ 46/ EC (General Data Protection Regulation), 2016). This long name is itself revealing of the two major objectives of this regulation: protection and freedom of movement for the personal data of natural persons (excluding, therefore, the data of other juridical persons, like corporations). This complete name also reveals that this is not a new issue and that this regulation ends the validity of the 95/16/EC Directive, which was more than 20 years old.

The GDPR has created an important change in the way businesses operate in Europe, no matter if they have a physical presence there or if they do not. As some of the concepts therein are hard to objectivize and/or are hard to operationalize, it has generated a lot of uncertainty, especially because the media has widely reported on the values of the fines that come with failing to implement this regulation.

While the publication of the GDPR dates from April 27, 2016, its application only became mandatory on May 25, 2018. This two-year period should have allowed for a smooth transition, but the fact is that the concerns about the application of the new regulation started much closer to the mandatory application date. A search in Google Trends shows that the public’s interest on the topic was focused mainly in late May 2018, both worldwide (see Fig. 15.1) and in the USA (see Fig. 15.2).

Fig. 15.1.Evolution of searches by GDPR worldwide.

Fig. 15.2.Evolution of searches by GDPR in the USA.

The following sections will present the legislative background, the main concepts of this new regulation with a special focus on the role of Data Protection Officer, the main implications for organisations and the current limitations of the GDPR.

15.2.Legislative Background

The GDPR is a piece of legislation that has a long history. To begin with, it replaces a directive from October 24, 1995 (Directive 95/46/EC) on the processing and movement of personal data (Directive 95/46/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 October 1995 on the protection of individuals with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, 1995). Therefore, the GDPR did not result from a void, even if a Directive is not a piece of legislation of the same nature as a Regulation. A Regulation is directly applicable to all European Union (EU) countries, while a Directive needs to be implemented by the countries through a national piece of legislation.

Directive 95/46/EC was actually quite advanced for its time and many of the concepts and procedures that now raise some surprise and controversy were already in it, even if the digital reality of 1995 was quite different from that of 2018.

Some of the fundamental concepts of the GDPR that Directive 95/46/EC contemplated are (Directive 95/46/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 October 1995 on the protection of individuals with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, 1995):

•Personal data, which is defined as “any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person”;

•Identifiable person, who is “one who can be identified, directly or indirectly”;

•Consent, which is defined as “any freely given specific and informed indication of his wishes by which the data subject signifies his agreement to personal data relating to him being processed”;

•Supervisory Authority, which is a national authority responsible for monitoring the application of the Directive. The existence of one or more supervisory authorities in each country of the European Community (the former name of the European Union) was mandatory.

•Right to Object. The data’s subject had the right to object, in certain situations, to personal data processing. This included situations where data is handled for the purpose of direct marketing.

•Protection from automated individual decisions. Directive 95/46/EC granted protection to all persons from any relevant decisions affecting him and produced solely by automated processing.

Other legal documents that provide context to the GDPR are the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (European Parliament, European Council, and European Commission, 2012) and the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (European Union, 2012). Both documents grant European citizens the right to the protection of their personal data. There are also other pieces of legislation that maintain their pertinence. Among those are:

—Directive 2000/31/EC (DIRECTIVE 2000/31/EC OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL, 2000);

—Regulation (EC) No. 45/2001 (Regulation (EC) No. 45/2001 of the European Parliament and of the Council, 2001);

—Regulation (EC) No. 223/2009 (Regulation (EC) No. 223/2009 of the European Parliament and of the Council, 2009);

—Directive 2002/58/EC (DIRECTIVE 2002/58/EC OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL, 2002);

—Directive 2011/24/EU (Directive 2011/24/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 9 March 2011 on the application of patients’ rights in cross-border healthcare, 2011);

—Regulation (EU) No. 536/2014 (REGULATION (EU) No. 536/2014 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL, 2014);

—The Convention for the Protection of Individuals with regard to Automatic Processing as it was amended in October 10, 2018 (Convention for the Protection of Individuals with regard to Automatic Processing of Personal Data as it will be amended by its Protocol CETS No. 223, 2018); and

—Directive 2016/680 (DIRECTIVE (EU) 2016/ 680 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL — of 27 April 2016 — on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data by competent authorities for the purposes of the prevention, investigation, detection or prosecution of criminal offences or the execution of criminal penalties, and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Council Framework Decision 2008/ 977/ JHA, 2016).

GDPR applies to the treatment, by any means, of personal data resulting of activities in the European Union or regarding persons living in the EU, regardless of where the treatment is made (inside or outside the EU).

15.3.Personal Data Under GDPR

GDPR defines personal data exactly as Directive 95/46/EC did, as “any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person” and it clarifies that:

“An identifiable natural person is one who can be identified, directly or indirectly, in particular by reference to an identifier such as a name, an identification number, location data, an online identifier or to one or more factors specific to the physical, physiological, genetic, mental, economic, cultural or social identity of that natural person” (REGULATION (EU) 2016/ 679 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL — of 27 April 2016 — on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/ 46/ EC (General Data Protection Regulation), 2016).

The concept of Personal Data is at the core of GDPR and is actually quite broad. While the definition does not provide any details on the extent of the underlying notion, the preamble does provide some examples of personal data, namely:

—Internet Protocol Addresses;

—Cookies;

—Radio Frequency (RFID) tags;

—Data revealing racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, or trade union membership;

—Genetic data;

—Biometric data used for authentication and/or identification;

—Data concerning health;

—Data concerning a natural person’s sex life or sexual orientation

This makes it clear that any technology solutions that can indirectly lead to the identification of a person fall under GDPR, which relates to the “identifiable” component of the definition of Personal Data.

Further clarification comes from the work of the Article 29 Working Party (WP29), created by Directive 95/46/EC. WP29 issued a set of guidelines, recommendations and best practices before its work was terminated on May 25, 2018, when the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) succeeded WP29. WP29’s Opinion 4/2007 focusses on the concept of Personal Data (Article 29 Data Protection Working Party, 2007, p. 4). This complex document decomposes and analyses the concept in its four parts:

—“Any information”, which the WP29 believes “calls for a wide interpretation of the concept regardless of the nature or content of the information, and the technical format in which it is presented”;

—“Relating to”, which the WP29 feels can be approached by looking into content, purpose and result;

—“Identified or identifiable”, which the WP29 considers the introduction of a context-dependent approach in the decision on what constitutes personal data, given “the means likely reasonably to be used”; and

—“Natural person”, which points to an application of the GDPR mostly limited to “living individuals”. It is important to notice that the chosen expression is used to refer to people already born and not yet deceased.

These clarifications are better understood through the given examples, showing that the following less obvious data is considered to be personal data under GDPR:

—Professional habits and practices;

—Customers’ recording of instructions;

—Video surveillance recordings containing images of individuals;

—Any information regarding the state of a person’s health, even if it can be recognized only by professionals (the example is of a child’s drawing created in a neuro-psychiatric test);

—The value of a person’s house;

—Car service records, which can hold personal data both from the car’s owner and from the mechanic that worked on the car.

—Telephone call logs (incoming and/or outgoing);

—Vehicle GPS tracking, including those used professionally;

—Some information included in minutes of meetings, like the presence of certain individuals and the statements made.

15.4.Data Processing

Another core GDPR concept is data processing. Different people can perceive this term in different ways, so the GDPR presents a definition that is quite clear and is almost the same as Directive 95/46/EC (Directive 95/46/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 October 1995 on the protection of individuals with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, 1995):

“Any operation or set of operations which is performed on personal data or on sets of personal data, whether or not by automated means, such as collection, recording, organization, structuring, storage, adaptation or alteration, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure by transmission, dissemination or otherwise making available, alignment or combination, restriction, erasure or destruction” (Directive 95/46/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 October 1995 on the protection of individuals with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, 1995).

This definition only differs from the previously existing one in two words: “structuring” (added in the new definition) and “restriction” (which replaced the word “blocking”). Some components of this definition deserve special attention, due to their consequences:

—“Whether or not by automated means”: The main consequence of this definition component is that the GDPR is not, as many might think, only applicable to digital data. Storing a paper that contains personal data is personal data processing, so it falls under the GDPR. This means that, for full GDPR compliance, most companies need to implement a clean desk policy, given that processing requires either a contractual/legal justification or the data subject’s consent, which is given for a specific purpose. Therefore, the information is to be internally shared on a need-to-know basis and limited to the extent that is required by law, contract or consent. Being so, it shouldn’t be accessible to just anyone with access to the space. For instance, cleaning crews don’t need access to the data subject’s data to perform their work.

—“Storage”: The fact that storing personal data falls under GDPR means that organisations need to apply it not only to information that they collect after May 25, 2018, but also to all the information that was collected before that but is still being stored. Given that there has to be either a legal/contractual justification or the data subject’s consent for the processing, organisations need to review all their stored data that doesn’t have storage consent attached. Either there is a legal/contractual reason for continuing to store that data or else they must destroy it immediately. Asking a posteriori for consent is not a legal procedure, both because the storage is illicit until the consent is received and because contacting the data subject with the purpose of requesting the consent is a non-solicited and nonconsented use of their personal data (the telephone number, e-mail address or physical address). If there is consent for storing the data, “safeguards should ensure that the data subject is aware of the fact that and the extent to which consent is given”.

Processing is limited to the conditions specified in Article 6 (lawfulness of processing), which specifies that this is restricted to situations where there is consent, a legal/contractual obligation to process, the need to process in order to protect the vital interests of a person or the public interest or when the processing is done in the exercise of an official authority.

15.5.General Principles

The whole GDPR, as complex as it is, has a set of general principles that guide the entire regulation and should guide its interpretation. These can be summarized as:

—Freedom of movement of personal data inside the EU. The EU currently has in its general goals the freedom of circulation inside its borders. The Schengen Agreement created an area without internal border controls and with common visa policies and the freedom to cross between countries for leisure or for work (“The Schengen Agreement — History and the Definition,” n.d.). Currently the Schengen area includes 26 countries (“Schengen Area — Visa Information for Schengen Countries,” n.d.). This principle expands that concept but includes tools to facilitate that portability. Organisations must provide facilitated ways for people to collect their personal information and transfer it to another organisation.

—Limitation to purpose. The data processing has to be consistent to the purpose driving its collection. Once the definition of processing includes gathering information, this means that an organisation cannot collect information that is not justifiably needed for a legitimate purpose. Legitimacy results from informed and unambiguous consent, necessary to pursue the objectives of a contract, or to take the steps needed to enter a contract, satisfy legal obligations, perform tasks of public interest or tasks executed under official authority and protect the vital interests of the data subject, or to satisfy legitimate interests of the organisation that don’t conflict with the data subject’s rights and freedoms. This also enforces data minimization, which means not only that the minimum amount of data gets collected, but also that organisations must destroy information that no longer satisfies the legitimacy criteria (as storing is also a type of data processing).

—Integrity and confidentiality. Organisations are responsible for ensuring that the data is stored in such a way that guarantees, to an extent that is reasonable to expect under the current knowledge of technology, that the data does not suffer illegitimate changes (integrity) and is not disclosed without consent or legitimate necessity (confidentiality).

—Demonstrated responsibility. It is the organisation’s responsibility to prove that it has collected informed consent to data processing and/or that there is a justifiable need for that processing. It is also the responsibility of the organisation to prove that it has implemented adequate processes, policies and technologies to protect the personal data under its control.

15.6.The Data Protection Officer

An important figure created by the GDPR is the Data Protection Officer (DPO). The DPO has a major role in all processes related to data in an organisation and the GDPR dedicates the entire Section 15.4 to it. There is also a Guidelines document endorsed by the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) that is extremely relevant to the interpretation of GDPR regarding DPOs, which is the Guidelines on Data Protection Officers (‘DPOs’), issued in December 2016 by the Article 29 Data Protection Working Party and revised and adopted in April 2017 (Article 29 Data Protection Working Party, 2017b).

The DPO can be a person, either an employee or someone external under a contract, or an organisation contracted to take that responsibility and assume the corresponding functions. The general recommendation is that the DPO is located in the EU, although there is the possibility of the DPO being located outside the EU if the data controller and/or processor has no establishment in the European Union (Article 29 Data Protection Working Party, 2017b). Even if this is the general recommendation, a lot of thought must go into deciding the location of the DPO and/or of his team, considering not only the work he has to do on a daily basis, but also its higher-level responsibilities. It is expected that the DPO maintain a high level of proximity to the administration and that he (or it, if the role is assigned to an organisation) be involved in decisions regarding data processing. These are arguments that favor locating the DPO wherever most of the data processing activity is located and wherever decisions are made, namely the headquarters of the company. On the other hand, the DPO is the connection between the organisation and the European authorities, which favours locating the DPO in Europe. For international organisations, this is truly a challenge and there is no one-size-fits-all solution.

Obtaining the knowledge needed to act as a DPO is itself a challenge. Although most organisations would benefit from nominating a DPO, not all are obliged to do so and not all have the financial conditions necessary to hire a competent DPO. Smaller organisations that deal with smaller amounts of personal data can opt to hire an information security consultant who can help them to establish the correct procedures and assist in case a personal-data-related incident occurs. It is important that they do so, given that they still have to be compliant with the regulation. An alternative is the hiring of a common DPO by an aggregation of organisations. This can be done through consortiums, through associations (like commercial and industrial associations) or through joint contracts. However, if this is the case, organisations must be particularly careful in the choice of a DPO and about the contract conditions, given that the DPO must be able to fully satisfy the needs of all the organisations that fall under the contract. Bigger consortiums or contracts are likely to choose an organisation, instead of an individual, to act as a DPO.

Organisations are obliged to nominate a DPO in one of the following situations (REGULATION (EU) 2016/ 679 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL — of 27 April 2016 — on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/ 46/ EC (General Data Protection Regulation), 2016):

1.If “the processing is carried out by a public authority or body, except for courts acting in their judicial capacity”. It is not clear why the legislator has decided to exempt courts from the obligation of nominating a DPO, but this is likely to be an effort to maintain the separation between legislative, executive and judicial powers. However, this does not mean that courts are exempt from following the GDPR. Relevant quotations from the regulation are:

a.“this Regulation applies, inter alia, to the activities of courts and other judicial authorities”;

b.“The competence of the supervisory authorities should not cover the processing of personal data when courts are acting in their judicial capacity”;

c.“Supervisory authorities shall not be competent to supervise processing operations of courts acting in their judicial capacity”.

2.If “the core activities of the controller or the processor consist of processing operations which, by virtue of their nature, their scope and/or their purposes, require regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale”. In this case it is necessary to clarify the meaning of “core activities”, of “regular and systematic monitoring” and of “large scale” and, for that, one should consult the guidelines emanated from WP29 and endorsed by the EDPB. Unfortunately, this document does not provide clear definitions for all of these concepts, but it does exclude some situations and clearly include others. According to WP29/EDPB, core activities are the key operations executed by the organisation to pursue its objectives. For an information security professional, this definition relates closely to the concept of critical processes. So, even if a company deals with a large amount of personal data that doesn’t necessarily mean that the organisation is obliged to nominate a DPO. For instance, salaries processing is not considered a core activity, therefore it does not fall into this category. Regular and systematic monitoring is any activity done, continuously or recurrently, either according to a system, a method or any organized process or as part of a plan or a strategy to track or profile data subjects, including but not limited to, over the Internet (Article 29 Data Protection Working Party, 2017b).

3.“The core activities of the controller or the processor consist of processing on a large scale of special categories of data pursuant to Article 9”. Those special categories are “Processing of personal data revealing racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, or trade union membership, and the processing of genetic data, biometric data for the purpose of uniquely identifying a natural person, data concerning health or data concerning a natural person’s sex life or sexual orientation”. One must notice that, in general, the GDPR prohibits organisations from processing these types of data without consent from the data subject in the cases where the national law does not prohibit that consent. However, there are several exceptions, presented in paragraph 2 of article 9, mostly related to the execution of legal obligations or public interest (REGULATION (EU) 2016/ 679 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL — of 27 April 2016 — on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/ 46/ EC (General Data Protection Regulation), 2016). In the cases where that processing is legitimate, the concept of large scale is critical. The guidelines for DPOs indicate that several factors must be considered to verify if a certain case can be considered large scale processing. Those factors are the number of data subjects (either in absolute numbers or as a percentage of the population), the volume of data, the range of different data, the duration of the processing activity and the geographical extent of the data activity. Examples of large scale processing include the processing of patient data in a hospital, the processing of individuals’ travel data in a city transportation system, the geo-location of clients in a chain of stores and the processing of consumer data by banks and insurance companies. Examples of situations where there isn’t large scale processing include patient data processed by an individual physician and the processing of criminal convictions and offenses by an individual lawyer (Article 29 Data Protection Working Party, 2017b).

The DPO “shall be designated on the basis of professional qualities and, in particular, expert knowledge of data protection law and practices and the ability to fulfil the tasks referred to in Article 39”. Those tasks include informing the organisation of and advising the organisation on the obligations resulting from the GDPR, monitoring compliance, assigning responsibilities related to data protection, raising awareness, providing training to staff involved in data processing, providing advice relative to data protection impact assessment and cooperating with the supervisory authority. The DPO also needs to take into consideration the risks associated with data processing operations (REGULATION (EU) 2016/ 679 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL — of 27 April 2016 — on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/ 46/ EC (General Data Protection Regulation), 2016).

This means that the DPO needs to have legal and technical knowledge. Given that each country in the EU can increase the level of regulation associated with the GDPR and that some dispositions are complemented by national laws, the mandatory legal knowledge might include regulations from up to 28 countries depending on the activity of the organisation. Also, because some data processing is frequently outsourced, the DPO should have some legal knowledge regarding contracts and, if the third party is in a different country, of international law. At the same time, the DPO should possess knowledge of privacy protection techniques, which in turn demands that he possess technical knowledge in a specialized domain: information security (data security, network security, etc.). Therefore, there aren’t a lot of professionals that can fulfill this task on their own. This calls for the constitution of corporations specially dedicated to this task, but that is not what is currently happening in Europe. While there isn’t any data on this, the author’s experience is that either companies hire one expert in either law or Information Technology (IT) or they hire the services of an existing company, usually one that already provides them with services. Again, most of those companies focus either on the technological aspects or on the legal aspects, when the GDPR calls for an integrated approach. There are only a few rare cases where legal and technological companies have come together to provide this service or when a company constitutes an interdisciplinary team that includes legal and technological experts. The recommendations of WP29/EDPB are that the DPO must also have some personal qualities like integrity and high professional ethics (Article 29 Data Protection Working Party, 2017b). While this relates to personality, it also calls for some knowledge on Social Ethics, Deontology and Theories of Justice. Therefore, ideally the DPO should have training in Philosophy. The WP29/EDPB also recommends that DPOs have knowledge of the business sector of the organisation that hires them and, if they are serving a public authority or body, that they have a sound knowledge of the administrative rules and procedures applicable to that organisation. Because raising awareness and training is one of the DPO’s responsibilities, he should also have knowledge of Education and/or Training.

In conclusion, one DPO is a super professional, with an impeccable social and professional record of “good behavior” and with a sound knowledge of several types of laws, several domains including IT, Philosophy, Education and Public Administration and the specific activity of the organisation. Again, this calls for joint teams, specialized in this activity.

One aspect of the Regulation that is very relevant for the choice of the DPO is the level of protection granted to this position. The GDPR clearly states in Paragraph 3 of Article 38 that the DPO “shall not be dismissed or penalised by the controller or the processor for performing his tasks” (REGULATION (EU) 2016/ 679 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL — of 27 April 2016 — on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/ 46/ EC (General Data Protection Regulation), 2016). This means that if the organisation choses to nominate a DPO from the existing staff it has to be careful to ensure that such a person has no conflict of interest and that if a situation arises where there is a need to dismiss that person no doubts will be raised regarding the reasons for the dismissal. If the DPO can correlate the dismissal with an action or a set of actions performed in the capacity of DPO, the organisation will not be able to dismiss him. This might be an incentive for organisations to hire external DPOs. Even if the protection is also applicable to them, at least there isn’t any risk of misunderstandings in cases which require dismissals.

Another argument for hiring external specialized DPOs is the fact that the DPO cannot have a conflict of interest. Even if it is not clear what a conflict of interest is, the existing guidelines indicate that senior managers (such as chief executives, chief operating officers, chief financial officers, chief medical officers, heads of marketing departments, heads of Human Resources or heads of IT departments) cannot occupy this position. This restriction also applies to those in the organisation that determine the purposes or means of processing (Article 29 Data Protection Working Party, 2017b). Therefore, it isn’t easy to find someone in the organisation with the technical capacity to perform the role of DPO and someone who can do so without any conflict of interest. It is also important to notice that the issue of conflict of interest also applies to external DPOs, under a contract. The common practice of hiring a company that is already a technology supplier is frequently a violation of the GDPR. Companies that provide consultancy on the means to process data (recommendations on software adoption, database manipulation maintenance, data analytics, data collection tools, etc.) are in clear conflict of interest if they also assume the position of DPO.

15.7.Data Protection Impact Assessment

Demonstrating compliance is a pillar of the GDPR. The document is based on the notion that organisations have the responsibility to protect personal data, but it is not a naive document. The legislator understands that absolute security can only happen in a utopia and that incidents can happen regardless of what measures are in place. Therefore, organisations need to be able to prove that they have done what is reasonable, considering the underlying risk, in order to protect the data they process. The Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) is the pillar tool of that demonstration.

Information security professionals know that any security plan starts with the identification of the assets to protect and a corresponding risk analysis.

The importance of the DPIA cannot be overestimated. Not only is it fundamental to the correct development of a security strategy, but it is also closely related to the fines that are associated with noncompliance. The WP29 wrote it clearly:

“Under the GDPR, non-compliance with DPIA requirements can lead to fines imposed by the competent supervisory authority. Failure to carry out a DPIA when the processing is subject to a DPIA (Article 35(1) and (3)–(4)), carrying out a DPIA in an incorrect way (Article 35(2) and (7) to (9)), or failing to consult the competent supervisory authority where required (Article 36(3)(e)), can result in an administrative fine of up to 10M€, or in the case of an undertaking, up to 2 % of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (Article 29 Data Protection Working Party, 2017c)

It is impossible to summarise the description of the guidelines and the procedures to follow when carrying out a DPIA and how to assess the level of the risk such that all this information fits in this section. But the guidelines (Article 29 Data Protection Working Party, 2017c) give a list of what to look for when deciding if a DPIA is needed. These items on that list deserve some consideration:

—“Evaluation or scoring of data subjects”: this type of data processing can have applications in many different situations, from work performance to health insurance. Whenever the data subjects get a comparative position towards other data subjects, organisations should consider this as an indicator of high-risk processing.

—“Automated-decision making with legal or similar significant effect”: automated decisions are a growing concern of legislators. The EU has a convention that covers this type of processing (Convention for the Protection of Individuals with regard to Automatic Processing of Personal Data as it will be amended by its Protocol CETS No. 223, 2018). It is important to notice that, under the GDPR, data subjects have the right to be informed that a decision was made using automated processes. They also have the right to have a human review that decision. It is also likely that in most cases humans will not change those decisions, given that companies design the automated processes to reflect the organisation’s policies and humans have to follow the same criteria. This might be a concern related to machine failure or to the imprecision of the existing algorithms. In fact, machine-learning techniques have been developed quite recently and have a level of error that is unneglectable. There is no way to know how the confidence level of the algorithms will evolve, but it makes a lot of sense to protect citizens from automatic mistakes.

—“Systematic monitoring”: the whole notion of systematic monitoring has already been discussed in this chapter.

—“Sensitive data or data of a highly personal nature”: the notion of sensitive data can vary according to the culture and ethics of a certain population. Health records, criminal records and data regarding sexual, political or religious orientation are usually considered sensitive data or highly personal data. But some less evident data can also be included in this category, either because of concrete temporary or regional circumstances or because they allow for indirect disclosure of highly personal or sensitive information. For instance, detailed lunch records can reveal food habits that provide clues on health problems or religious options. Other types of sensitive data are those related to personal communications, including metadata (dates, recipient, etc.) and many countries have specific laws regarding this.

—“Data processed at a large scale”: the concept of large scale has already been discussed in this chapter.

—“Matching or combining datasets”: this definition can be tricky. What is a dataset? This is a hard question to answer from the technological perspective. However, the spirit of the legislation seems to be that whenever there is no reasonable expectation of a common citizen to see two different sets of collected data as interrelated, then this is a red flag that elevates the risk. This type of situation, by definition, goes beyond consent, so it can only happen in special situations.

—“Data concerning vulnerable data subjects”: the definition of a vulnerable data subject can change with time and space. Usually children, elderlies and people with physical or mental disabilities fall under this category. Most laws consider employees to be a group vulnerable to their employers, so organisations have to treat data related to work with extra precautions. Other situations must be considered case by case, with consideration of the sociological context of the data subjects.

—“Innovative use or applying new technological or organisational solutions”: the fact that the GDPR has isolated this type of processing is a sign of the times and of the concerns that new technologies are creating. There is a fear of the unknown, so whatever is new is deemed to be particularly dangerous. Machine learning or Artificial Intelligence, combined with Big Data, are definitely a growing concern in society and so are the privacy concerns related to the Internet-of-Things. At the same time, the general population seems to accept them as part of daily life and whatever comes next is for no one to forecast, so the legislators took the safe path. WP29 includes in the description of this item biometric technologies like fingerprint and facial recognition, but it also cites the GDPR to refer to the current state of the art as the main referential for the evaluation of what is innovative (Article 29 Data Protection Working Party, 2017c). Most experts in biometrics would not consider fingerprint authentication methods an innovative technology, but a new algorithm for fingerprint biometrical authentication would definitely fall into this category. Some recent biometric technologies, like cognitive biometrics, can be of even more concern, given that they include health related data (heart beat patterns, brain activity patterns, skin conductivity, etc.) (Revett and de Magalhães, 2010).

—Processing that “prevents data subjects from exercising a right or using a service or a contract”: this seems to be directed at preliminary analyses of clients, so whenever this is applied, the first item of this list (“Evaluation or scoring of data subjects”) is likely to also be applied.

It seems clear that the decision on the legal obligation to do a DPIA, like the DPIA itself, should be carried out by an exempt third party with technical and legal knowledge of information technology (databases, network communications, encryption, authentication/identification, operating systems, web programming, etc.) and privacy laws and without any conflict of interest. However, even if there is no legal obligation to do a DPIA, this is still a valuable tool for any organisation and it can prove itself priceless in case of a data breach.

15.8.The Fines and the Press

The GDPR has become most famous for the value of the fines that come with the failure to comply with it. All countries must adhere to these administrative fines, which must be “effective, proportionate and dissuasive”. The formal exceptions are Denmark and Estonia, which have legal systems that exclude them for the direct definition of administrative fines by an EU Regulation. However, these countries will have to apply them either through the criminal courts (Denmark) or through the supervisory authority in the framework of a misdemeanor procedure. Fines can reach 20 million Euros or, in the case of an undertaking company, 4% of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding year.

Following a lot of curiosity around the period when the GDPR started producing effects, the topic lost public attention (Fig. 15.1 and Fig. 15.2), but, regardless of that, the second semester of 2018 brought the first GDPR fines and, as more countries create national regulations to the GDPR and empower their national authorities, more fines are expected. Therefore, media coverage will likely increase, which will, hopefully, raise awareness and promote compliance.

The first fine applied under the GDPR after May 25, 2018 was to a hospital in Portugal in July 2018. The national authority fined the hospital due to a lack of detail in the access control systems that protect health records, which allowed for any doctor or psychologist and even some social workers to access the medical records of any patient. The hospital didn’t have a policy for creation and/or deletion of account privileges, which allowed doctors who were no longer working there to continue accessing the files. The fine was of 400 thousand Euros and it is being disputed in court (“Portuguese Hospital Receives and Contests 400,000 € Fine for GDPR Infringement,” 2018).

Austria has also applied a fine under the GDPR, after accusations of trying to undermine the EU regulation by passing a law that would issue warnings to first time offenders (Nielsen, 2018). The Austrian authority issued its first GDPR fine in late September and it was quite modest: 4,800 Euros (Fritz, 2018). This fine was applied to a retail establishment that had a video surveillance system that captured the sidewalk. It remains to be seen how things will progress in this country.

In November 2018, Germany applied its first fine under the GDPR and, while this wasn’t of a high value it is an important case exactly because of that. The national authority fined the social media platform Knuddels.de 20 thousand Euros for a data breach of more than 300 thousand access credentials, including e-mail addresses and passwords. The fine didn’t result from the breach itself but from the lack of protection of the data, given that passwords were stored in plain text. The fine was especially low due to the consideration of two facts: the financial impact of the fine on the company and the level of cooperation showed by the company in their interactions with the national authority (Pressestelle, 2018).

It is important to notice that fines regarding data protection are not new in Europe. As discussed before, there was legislation in place that required companies to protect personal data and fines were applied quite frequently. Examples of both small and large fines can be found in many countries and in a variety of business areas.

The Italian authorities have applied several fines in the past years. Examples are:

—The 10,000 Euros fine issued to a hotel in San Felice Circeo (Federico Domenichelli, 2018);

—The 32,000 Euros fine applied to the celebrity blog 5-star movement controlled by the Rousseau Association (“M5s, dal Garante della privacy 32 mila euro di multa al blog delle Stelle,” 2018);

—The 600,000 Euros fine for aggressive telemarketing applied to Fastweb (“Telemarketing aggressivo, 600 mila euro di multa per Fastweb,” 2018); and

—The 960,000 Euros fine applied to the telephonic company TIM (“Violazione della privacy, multa da 960 mila euro a Tim,” 2018).

Like Italy, the United Kingdom authority has issued several fines in the past years. Examples are:

—The £120,000 fine to the University of Greenwich due to a data breach that exposed almost 20,000 staff and students (“University of Greenwich fined £120,000 for breach of sensitive data,” 2018); and

—The £500,000 fines (the highest fine possible prior to GDPR) issued to Equifax (“Equifax Hit With Maximum UK Privacy Fine After Mega-Breach,” 2018) and to Facebook (Waterson, 2018).

Several factors should contribute to the definition of the values of fines, from the categories of the data in question to the level of collaboration with the authorities with the intent to mitigate the effects of the infringement. WP29 issued detailed but vague guidelines on this matter and the EDPB endorsed the document (Article 29 Data Protection Working Party, 2017a).

At the same time that countries are adjusting their regulations and creating/empowering their national authorities, citizens are coming together in many countries to file suits against corporations for data breaches. There are indications that consumer associations have filed lawsuits against Facebook for violations of personal data rights in Portugal, Spain, Belgium and Italy (“DECO processa Facebook e pede indemnização de até 2000 euros por utilizador,” 2018).

With increasing fines, different mitigation techniques are likely to be considered and taking out insurance policies to transfer the risk is a possibility. Currently only Finland and Norway have legislation that allows insurance policies to cover GDPR fines and it is unclear if that is a possibility in eight other countries. In 20 jurisdictions GDPR fines are likely uninsurable (Leemans and Molony, 2018).

15.9.Information Technology and the GDPR

Technology is simultaneously the motor behind the need for a GDPR and a critical factor in GDPR compliance.

The proliferation of data services and data-enhanced business results from the development of IT domains like cloud technologies, social media and business analytics, the proliferation of computational devices (smartphones, Internet-of-Things, etc.) and the evolution of computer networks, not only cabled but also wireless. All these created business opportunities and enhanced the average quality of life, but also created privacy challenges that originated the need for regulatory legislation.

For companies to comply with the GDPR, they, paradoxically, will need to rely on technology, given that it is not possible to depend on humans to do all that is needed to elevate data security to acceptable levels.

One of the rights that GDPR grants to EU residents is the right to receive a copy of all the data that an organisation has on him and/or to transmit that data to another organisation, as long as that data was obtained from the data subject (actively provided or observed) and does not compromise the rights of other data subjects. This forces organisations to have integrated information systems and to develop automated forms of providing that data in a manageable format, not only due to the potentially high number of requests, but also because there is a time limit of one month, extendable in certain cases to three months, to satisfy the request (REGULATION (EU) 2016/679 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL — of 27 April 2016 — on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/ EC (General Data Protection Regulation), 2016).

Ensuring that data is not easily accessible by non-authorized parties forces organisations to both encrypt sensitive data and to implement adequate access control processes. Two of the existing (and discussed) cases of fines relate exactly to this compliance requisite. Given that there is no effective access control without effective identification and/or authentication mechanisms, organisations will need to evolve beyond the traditional password systems that suffer from the paradox that they must simultaneously be complex, so they are hard to guess, and simple, so that they are easy to remember. Biometric technologies can play a major role in this (de Magalhães, Revett, and Santos, 2008).

The right to be forgotten, when applicable, and the limitations to data storage also create a challenge. Organisations must be ready to delete any data subject’s data that is no longer required to be stored, without deleting any data that actually has to be stored and without affecting the stability of their systems. Again, organisations must rely on technology to be able to do this effectively and within the legal timeframe.

Accountability is also critical under the GDPR. Organisations carry the burden to demonstrate that they have done all that is reasonably expected to protect the personal data that they process. If an incident occurs, being able to trace the data path is critical to understanding what happened and where something went wrong. Insured accountability might even demonstrate deliberate actions taken by an employee in clear disrespect for the implemented policies. For this to be possible, solutions like Private Key Infrastructures (PKI) must be implemented. PKI can ensure accountability for instance in network storage (Yumerefendi and Chase, 2007) or in e-mail communications (de Magalhães, Santos, and Nunes, 2006).

Technology is, in many ways, the protection of a digital infrastructure and, therefore, it will need to be the base for a secure organisation. Nevertheless, it is important that the independence of the DPO remains intact. Therefore, technology suppliers cannot be the organisation’s DPO.

15.10.Conclusions

The revision of the main features of GDPR, of the adjacent guidelines and of the current application of this regulation show that this is a complex normative with profound implications on the way that companies do business in the EU market. However, at the same time, it is clear that many of the requirements of the GDPR were already in place before the EU passed this legislation.

In an increasingly connected world that relies on a fast growing and innovation-based technology industry, the number of incidents is likely to grow until the mindset changes and the hardware and software players realize that security by design and security as a process are part of the normal development of any solution. In the meantime, organisations will have to navigate their way between the GDPR, the particularities of each of the countries’ national regulations and all the applicable regulations. The latter include not only EU regulations but also other nations’ regulations, given that information services are usually offered worldwide, which means that, while dealing with the GDPR, organisations might find themselves having to deal with several different regulations. Examples of states with similar but distinct regulations are:

—The Australian Privacy Act of 1988 with all the updates made until November 2018 and its more than 300 pages (Privacy Act 1988, 2018);

—The California regulation on privacy protection (The California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018, 2018), which is likely to implicate changes in several states across the United States; and

—The Brazilian law on personal data protection, approved in August 2018 and set to be enforced in February 2020 (Lei no 13.709, 2018).

At the same time, organisations must also adhere to business specific regulations, like the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) regulations (34 CFR 99 — Family Educational Rights and Privacy, 2010) or the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996, 1996).

Companies definitely need to change their posture on personal data protection and understand that they must either hire a team to support them in the active protection of data or hire specialized services, as the challenges associated with this task are multidisciplinary. Companies will also need to avoid the temptation of hiring their technology suppliers as DPOs, under the penalty of not only failing to comply with the GDPR but also not being able to distinguish between what is a genuine data security concern and what is a commercially-driven concern.
